Title: Salem Ghost Train offers nighttime ghost stories and historic train rides in South Jersey
Article_Text:
September 19, 2026
A fall train ride through South Jersey gets a spooky twist this October when Woodstown Central sends passengers into the night for ghost stories and local legends told just outside Salem City.
The Salem Ghost Train runs Oct. 16, 17 and 24, departing at 6:30 p.m. from South Woodstown Station. The 2½-hour experience begins with a nighttime ride through Salem County farmland and woods before passengers step off at Fenwick Grove for live storytelling presented by the Salem County Historical Society.
The route covers about 18 miles round trip on Salem County’s first railroad line, which dates to 1863. At Fenwick Grove, storytellers share local legends, folklore and ghost tales in an outdoor setting just outside Salem City.
This is not a haunted house on rails. There are no jump scares, actors chasing people through the dark or haunted-house walkthroughs. The experience leans on local history, nighttime scenery and storytelling instead.
That makes the Salem Ghost Train a better fit for families and anyone who wants something spooky without intense scare tactics. The dark countryside and outdoor stop at Fenwick Grove provide the atmosphere, while the stories focus on Salem County’s past.
Tickets start at $35. Riders are asked to arrive 20 to 30 minutes before departure, and free parking is available on site. Woodstown Central also recommends bringing a small flashlight and wearing comfortable shoes because the stop at Fenwick Grove includes walking over grass, dirt and uneven terrain in low light.
Light snacks and nonalcoholic drinks are allowed aboard the train. Restrooms are available at the station and onboard.
Dates: Friday, Oct. 16; Saturday, Oct. 17; Saturday, Oct. 24
Departure: 6:30 p.m.
Duration: 2 hours, 30 minutes
Location: South Woodstown Station
Address: 650 Alloway-Woodstown Road, Woodstown, NJ 08098
Tickets: From $35
Route: Approximately 18 miles round trip
Includes: Nighttime train ride, stop at Fenwick Grove and live Salem County ghost stories and folklore
Parking: Free
Age: Family-friendly
Good to know: Arrive 20-30 minutes early, bring a small flashlight and wear comfortable shoes

Title: Sixers player preview: What kind of player is Ariel Hukporti going to be?
Article_Text:
September 19, 2026
Welcome to PhillyVoice's series of Sixers player previews ahead of the 2026-27 season.
After two years of volatility, Sixers fans entered this offseason teetering on apathy. Then came new Sixers President of Basketball Operations Mike Gansey, the architect of what became a dream summer. Gansey traded Paul George away, landing five-time All-Star Jaylen Brown from the Boston Celtics. As Gansey accumulated depth around Brown, Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and VJ Edgecombe, the door opened for an unfathomable addition.
LeBron James is a member of the Sixers, rounding out one of the most talented starting lineups in recent NBA history. And suddenly, the Sixers have cultivated more local and national interest than ever before. Games are not won on paper, but the Sixers are built to be full-blown championship contenders for however long James remains in Philadelphia.
As Sixers Media Day on Sept. 28 nears, our player preview series will focus on two key questions surrounding each member of the team's 14-player standard roster.
Up next: Ariel Hukporti, signed to a one-year, $3.4 million deal early on in free agency to add some more youth and athleticism to the Sixers' center depth chart. After two seasons of being a little-used understudy with the New York Knicks, Hukporti is entering a situation in which he will be relied upon for minutes much more often. Can he emerge as the Sixers' primary backup center and pay off their investment in him?
SIXERS PLAYER PREVIEWS
Joel Embiid | Labaron Philon Jr. | Dean Wade
Dominick Barlow | Adem Bona | Tyrese Maxey
VJ Edgecombe | Jaylen Brown | Ariel Hukporti
This question can be interpreted in many different ways; all of those interpretations are valid. From the physical aspect of playing on a nightly basis to the basketball side of being a rotation big, there is so much unknown about Hukporti with only 715 NBA minutes under his belt. (For reference: Trendon Watford played 864 minutes in 53 games for the Sixers last season.)
Hukporti is a massive athlete – a true seven-footer weighing in at 246 pounds – and, for a player of that stature, can really move. In some ways, he is a ball of clay the Sixers can try to mold into their ideal backup center. But for a team that will be focused on winning a championship, having that degree of uncertainty in what a player can actually be in the NBA is unusual.
One way the question above can be interpreted: Does Hukporti have the requisite endurance to hold up over 30-plus minutes in a game Embiid is sitting out? Hukporti and Adem Bona are both prone to experiencing foul trouble; either one of them picking up too many personals could lead to the other playing significant minutes. How will Hukporti handle a night when Sixers head coach Nick Nurse leans on him as much as possible?
Really, though, this question pertains to basketball – because Hukporti has just not played enough of it at the NBA level for his strengths and weaknesses to be clearly defined.
Hukporti has averaged 14.6 rebounds per 100 possessions, a fairly strong mark, and also committed a horrifying 3.7 turnovers per 100 possessions. But when a player has only exceeded 22 minutes in five individual NBA games, it is hard to say with any sense of confidence that rebounding is a strength of his or that he is completely unreliable with the ball.
For every team, scouting the players already in the building is just as important as evaluating players in other organizations. From practice performances to every regular-season appearance, the Sixers need to keep a watchful eye on Hukporti as they try to develop him into a long-term bench big.
SIXERS FILM STUDIES
Jaylen Brown's strengths | Jaylen Brown's weaknesses
Anfernee Simons | Dean Wade | Ariel Hukporti
Hukporti is not the only backup center this team hopes can answer this question in the affirmative. But for players with roles like the ones Hukporti and Bona will inherit on this team, having the trust of the quarterback of the operation is essential.
There is a chance that the majority of Hukporti's minutes will come as a screen-and-roll big partnered with James, a basketball savant capable of making every read a split second earlier than anybody else. Will Hukporti be able to get on the same page as James and start to detect those passes a tick early, too?
More importantly: When James puts the ball on a silver platter for Hukporti, will he take advantage of the opportunity or squander it? Bona having unreliable hands is a significant cause for concern when it comes to his fit with James because, even if Bona has chances to roll hard to the rim with open space, James will simply not make the pass if he calculates that Bona is unlikely to make a clean catch and finish.
The same questions linger for Hukporti. As James' legendary career winds down, does he want to be showing the ropes to his pick-and-roll partner? Hukporti and Bona have until the trade deadline to prove they are deserving of consistent minutes and the trust of their new superstar teammate. If they cannot pull it off, there will likely be a new backup center behind Embiid for the stretch run of the season.

Title: Torrid Padres take on Marlins, hoping to keep pace in NL wild-card race
Article_Text:
Torrid Padres take on Marlins, hoping to keep pace in NL wild-card race
(Photo credit: David Frerker)
Friday night couldn't have gone any better for the San Diego Padres.
Not only did they continue their scalding September with an 8-2 defeat of the visiting Miami Marlins, but losses by the Chicago Cubs and Philadelphia enabled the Padres (85-69) to forge a three-way tie atop the National League wild-card standings. And their magic number to clinch a playoff spot was reduced to four when the New York Yankees defeated Arizona.
San Diego will hope for similar results on Saturday when it looks to improve to 5-0 this season against Miami.
The Padres are presently flying on a rocket ship to the postseason. They've won 11 of their last 12 games and have scored at least six runs in seven of their last eight. The idea of actually hosting a wild-card series is now taking on serious traction.
While San Diego would lose any tiebreaker with the Phillies or Cubs, it is easily the hottest of the three clubs coming down the home stretch.
'The only thing that we can worry about is playing each game the best we can and playing to our standard,' said manager Craig Stammen. 'That first playoff game, we would love for it to be in San Diego.'
The Padres are 47-29 in Petco Park, including a 22-5 mark dating back to July 10. The only home series they've lost since late June came at Pittsburgh's hands in late August.
'We're in a good spot going into these last eight games,' said first baseman Ty France, who belted his career-high 21st homer to cap a six-run fifth inning Friday night. 'Hopefully, we can just keep things going.'
Casey Mize (6-9, 3.69 ERA) will try to string together consecutive wins for San Diego. He scattered eight hits over five innings Monday night in an 8-7 victory at Colorado, allowing two runs. He is 1-1 with a 2.31 ERA in two prior starts against Miami.
Eury Perez (7-11, 3.99) looks to escape the roughest patch of his season, one that's seen him allow 19 earned runs in his last four starts, covering 16 2/3 innings. The best start in that stretch came Sunday in a 6-4 win over the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Perez made it through five innings, allowing four hits and three runs with two walks and five strikeouts. Control has been an issue as he's doled out 12 walks in that span. He's 0-1 with a 3.75 ERA in two career outings against San Diego.
The loss came on July 25, when he worked seven innings and yielded three runs in an eventual 7-2 defeat that was the 11th game in a 12-game losing streak that eventually took Miami (76-78) out of the running.
With Miami out of the playoffs for a third straight season, it will use the remaining time to try to find answers for an inconsistent bullpen. Season-ending injuries to closer Pete Fairbanks and setup man Anthony Bender have made things harder.
Manager Clayton McCullough said he won't have a set closer over the final eight games.
'We just look at using the best people we have to get to that point and then whoever's left will get that opportunity,' he said.
--Field Level Media

Title: Yanks move on without Aaron Judge as D-backs fight to stay alive
Article_Text:
Yanks move on without Aaron Judge as D-backs fight to stay alive
(Photo credit: Kirby Lee)
The New York Yankees will play the rest of the regular season without slugger Aaron Judge. While they understand the magnitude of his loss, they enter the stretch run with belief.
The Yanks scored five runs in the first inning of a 9-2 victory over the Arizona Diamondbacks in the first game of a weekend series Friday, and the teams meet again Saturday in Phoenix as Arizona attempts to stay alive in the National League wild-card race.
'Obviously losing 'Judgey' hurts,' Cody Bellinger said. 'We all know he's the best hitter in the game. For us in here, our mindset is we're going to have to find a way. The talent in this room speaks for itself.
'I'm fully confident we have enough talent in here that we can go out and win and beat anybody.'
American League Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95 ERA) will face Arizona right-hander Brandon Pfaadt (7-3, 3.77) in the second game of the series.
The Diamondbacks (80-74) will ask Pfaadt to end a slump in which they have lost five of six. They are five games behind San Diego, the Chicago Cubs and Philadelphia (all 85-69) for the three NL wild-card spots with eight games to play.
'We know where we're at,' Arizona manager Torey Lovullo said. 'We can't afford to worry about things we can't control. I'm going to say there's time. There's always time.'
The Yankees (89-64) are 48-39 this season without Judge, who was placed on the injured list Friday with a strained right calf after missing three months earlier with a fractured right rib.
New York is also without injured regulars Jazz Chisholm Jr. (thumb) and Trent Grisham (hamstring), although manager Aaron Boone said Chisholm could return for the Tampa Bay series early next week.
The Yankees, who already have qualified for the postseason, are four games behind Tampa Bay in the AL East, and the teams have a four-game series at Yankee Stadium beginning Tuesday.
'There is no replacing a player as great as Aaron Judge, but we have high expectations that don't change now,' Boone said. 'One thing we do know is that we are in the dance.
'We've been built on the strength of our starting pitching all year.'
No one has been as strong as Schlittler, who is in his first full season and has made every start while Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodon have missed time with injuries or recovery time.
Schlittler has won four of his last five starts and has given up one run or fewer in each of his last seven. He was struck on the back of his right leg by Bo Bichette's 111.5 mph comebacker on his 94th and last pitch of a 2-0 victory over the New York Mets last Sunday, but shrugged it off.
'You have an ace at the top that has pitched like that,' Boone said. 'That's a good place to start. He's been dominant. This is largely in line with who we saw down the stretch last year.'
Schlittler has never faced the Diamondbacks, although Jesus Sanchez is 4 for 12 with three walks against him.
Pfaadt is 0-2 with a 5.74 ERA in his last five starts, and he gave up six runs and 10 hits in 6 2/3 innings in a loss to Texas on Aug. 12. He will be pitching on six days' rest after being pushed back so Eduardo Rodriguez could start the first game of the series.
Pfaadt lost his only outing against the Yankees, giving up six runs in 4 1/3 innings of a 7-1 loss as a rookie in 2023. Cody Bellinger is 2 for 7 with two solo homers against him and Luis Garcia Jr. is 3 for 7 with a homer.
--Field Level Media

Title: Opinion: Donbas Is More Than a Line on a Map: Lessons From Gettysburg, Normandy and Iwo Jima
Article_Text:
The Donbas is often discussed as though it were primarily a territorial question: a section of the map that might be exchanged, conceded or divided as part of a negotiated settlement. That framing misses a fundamental military reality. Terrain is not interchangeable. Some terrain provides such an advantage to the force that controls it that military professionals have a specific term for it: key terrain.
That concept is among the fundamentals of military art taught to young officers. A hill, ridgeline, river crossing or fortified city can matter far beyond its physical size because control of it determines what an army can observe, defend, attack or protect. The US has learned this lesson repeatedly in its own military history, from Gettysburg to Normandy to Iwo Jima. Americans considering the future of Ukraine should remember those lessons before treating the Donbas as simply another line on a map.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
                                                                                                                                                                         
At Gettysburg, Little Round Top was a relatively small piece of ground on the Union Army’s extreme left. On the afternoon of July 2, 1863, Brigadier General Gouverneur K. Warren recognized that the hill was dangerously exposed as Confederate forces moved against the Union flank. Union troops were hurried to the position, including Colonel Strong Vincent’s brigade, with Colonel Joshua Lawrence Chamberlain and the 20th Maine occupying its extreme left. The National Park Service describes Little Round Top as ideally suited for observation, artillery and defense; Union forces ultimately repelled repeated Confederate attacks and retained control of it.
Russia Enlists Yemeni Citizens for War in Ukraine, Ukraine Intel Says
Chamberlain and the 20th Maine became famous for their defense of the flank and their downhill bayonet charge after ammunition ran low. Their achievement has endured in American military culture not because Little Round Top represented valuable real estate, but because losing the position could have exposed the Union flank and altered the tactical situation across the battlefield. The significance of the ground came from what possession of it allowed one army to do to the other.
The same logic was evident on June 6, 1944, when US Army Rangers assaulted Pointe du Hoc during the Normandy invasion. The Rangers scaled cliffs approximately 100 feet high to attack a German artillery position overlooking the invasion area. They were not risking their lives for the intrinsic value of a few acres of Norman coastline. They were attacking terrain from which German forces could threaten the larger Allied operation.
                                                                                                                                                                         
The Marines who fought on Iwo Jima understood the principle as well. Mount Suribachi dominated the southern portion of the island and the exposed ground beneath it. Marine Corps histories describe the mountain as a major tactical obstacle whose capture was necessary before the advance north could proceed securely. The raising of the American flag on its summit became one of the most recognizable images of the Second World War, but the fight for Suribachi began as a military problem: an enemy-held dominant terrain feature overlooking American forces.
Gettysburg, Normandy and Iwo Jima were different battles in different wars, and historical analogies should not be pushed beyond what they can support. The Donbas is not Little Round Top, and Kramatorsk is not Pointe du Hoc. The enduring lesson is more basic: military terrain has value because of what it enables.
That is the lens through which the debate over the Donbas should be viewed. Russia continues to press toward Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, which sit at the center of Ukraine’s remaining defenses in Donetsk Oblast. Reuters recently described control of Donetsk as critical to both sides as Russian forces continue their offensive and Ukraine concentrates major defensive efforts there. A negotiated territorial concession in such an area therefore cannot be evaluated simply by calculating how many square kilometers would change hands. The relevant question is what military position each side would occupy afterward.
Fortifications, urban terrain, transportation networks, observation, maneuver corridors and the geography behind a defensive line all affect the answer. A defensive position built and improved over years cannot necessarily be recreated by drawing another line farther west. Surrendering key terrain can give an adversary through negotiation an operational advantage it has been unable to secure through combat.
This distinction becomes especially important when negotiations are described in the vocabulary of real estate transactions or commercial bargaining. Wars are not commercial transactions, and territory in war is not fungible property. A company negotiating the sale of an asset can often substitute money for ownership. An army surrendering commanding terrain cannot necessarily purchase equivalent geography somewhere else.
There is also a human dimension that makes the analogy to a real estate transaction particularly inadequate. The United Nations has documented increased pressure on residents of Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory to obtain Russian citizenship, restrictions imposed on people without it, penalties for expressions of Ukrainian cultural identity and continuing expropriation of private property. The disposition of occupied territory therefore determines not only where armies stand but also the political and legal conditions under which civilians will live.
None of this means military history dictates a particular diplomatic formula. Political leaders must weigh military realities alongside human costs, economic constraints, alliance considerations and the prospects for a durable peace. But any negotiation that contemplates territorial concessions should begin with an accurate understanding of what is being conceded and what advantage it may provide.
American military history provides a useful way to explain that distinction to an American public. Little Round Top was not important because Abraham Lincoln coveted a hill in Pennsylvania. Pointe du Hoc was not important because Franklin Roosevelt wanted cliffs in France. Mount Suribachi was not important because the United States wanted possession of a volcanic peak. In each case, Americans fought for terrain because of the military consequences of allowing the enemy to control it.
That is the lesson worth remembering as policymakers discuss the Donbas. Before asking whether Ukraine should surrender a piece of territory in exchange for a diplomatic agreement, they should first ask the question an officer would ask while studying a battlefield: What does control of that ground enable?
The answer may determine not merely where this war ends, but the conditions under which another one could begin.

Title: Titans trust index entering Week 2: Cam Ward slips, Anthony Hill surges
Article_Text:
The Tennessee Titans have much to weigh after their disappointing Week 1 defeat to the New York Jets. For fans, frustration has already reached a boiling point following consecutive 3-14 seasons. For the Robert Saleh era, bad preseason football carried over to the home-opener letdown.
The fanbase wants tangible results before buying into hope. The 2026 Titans must earn trust after damaging the relationship with fans. Patience is immediately running thin, with Saleh and his coaching staff tasked with responding.
Here is our first Titans trust index entering what already looks like a campaign-defining Week 2 showdown with the Philadelphia Eagles.
How the Titans' trust index works
We consider many factors when evaluating Tennessee's trust index. It considers performance levels and opportunity. It also considers comments from Coach Saleh and any mitigating circumstances, such as injuries.
Trust can waver from week to week. That's the nature of the NFL, and the Titans are no different with everything on the line this season.
Let's get to it...
The proving ground: QB Cam Ward
Fans are anxious to see sophomore Cam Ward grow into a franchise quarterback. Week 1 delivered more disappointment than excitement. Ward finished 19-of-32 with 140 yards and one touchdown. A chunk of his yardage and TD pass occurred in garbage time.
Nothing matters more for the 2026 Titans than Ward's growth and development. It was a rough start under first-year offensive coordinator Brian Daboll. Portions of the fanbase are already disappointed beyond belief, but Ward deserves a fair opportunity and a much larger sample size to show progress.
The alpha: HC Robert Saleh
Coach Saleh had to confront some difficult questions this week following the Titans' first regular-season performance under his leadership. It's understandable. Saleh's Titans were deplorable in all phases, and responsibility for such an unfathomable showing belongs to the head coach.
Fan frustration has carried over from the Brian Callahan-coached Titans. Saleh's squad desperately needs a better performance to bring closure to ugly narratives. The new-look Titans need to be just that.
The fast riser: LB Anthony Hill Jr.
The only bright spot from the Titans' no-show Week 1 performance was rookie linebacker Anthony Hill Jr. The former Texas standout registered a league-high 16 tackles across the complete slate of opening games. The rebuilding Titans need more difference makers, and Hill appears to possess legitimate upside.
The expectation is the Titans will start Hill and Cedric Gray at linebacker versus the Eagles in Week 2. That would give the Titans an ascending duo at linebacker made up of two growing defenders on team-friendly rookie contracts. Hopefully Hill stays in the starting lineup.
Initial disappointment: OC Brian Daboll
Fans were excited for Daboll's offense to make its debut after enduring the Brian Callahan experience. Unfortunately, it didn't look any better in Week 1. The Titans gained fewer than 200 yards of offense and managed one touchdown, with portions of the meager production occurring on a garbage-time possession.
Ward didn't appear comfortable in the pocket. The offense was chaotic, with spacing/route concept issues in the passing game. Daboll's offense has plenty to improve in an extremely tough Week 2 matchup with an elite Eagles defense.

Title: Padres blast Marlins to draw even in wild-card race
Article_Text:
Ty France clouted a three-run homer to cap a six-run fifth inning Friday night as the San Diego Padres stopped the visiting Miami Marlins 8-2 to forge a three-way tie atop the National League’s wild-card standings.
Winning for the 11th time in 12 games, San Diego (85-69) pulled even with the Chicago Cubs and Philadelphia, who both lost earlier Friday night. The Padres’ magic number for clinching a playoff spot dropped to five.
Nick Pivetta (3-2) earned the win by working the first five innings, yielding four hits and a run with a walk and four strikeouts. Marlins reliever Cade Gibson (5-2) was tagged with the loss after yielding the first two runs in the game-changing fifth.
Xander Bogaerts led off with a double and reached third on Jake Cronenworth’s single. Samad Taylor greeted reliever Tyler Zuber with a bunt single to fill the bases. After Ethan Salas’ shallow fly ball netted Zuber an out, Fernando Tatis Jr. tied the game with an RBI single to right.
Dustin Harris put San Diego ahead to stay with a two-run single up the middle. After Manny Machado lined out, France jacked a hanging sweeper an estimated 388 feet to left for his 21st homer, a career high.
All that happened after Miami starter Tyler Phillips worked 3 2/3 scoreless innings, permitting only two hits and a walk while fanning three. He left with Miami holding a 1-0 edge after Agustin Ramirez lined a one-out homer to left in the third, his fifth.
The Marlins’ other run came in the eighth via a two-out RBI single by Javier Sanoja that scored Otto Lopez, who doubled to left with one out. Ramirez collected three of their 10 hits, while Sanoja and Lopez had two each.
San Diego tacked on two more runs in its half of the eighth. Jackson Merrill led off by ripping his 26th homer of the year an estimated 432 feet to right. Three more singles, the last by Taylor, brought in Bogaerts.
Harris, France, Bogaerts, Cronenworth and Taylor each bagged two of the Padres’ 12 hits.

Title: Yankees score 5 runs in first inning to take down D-backs
Article_Text:
Ben Rice and George Lombard Jr. homered and the New York Yankees scored five runs in the first inning to cruise to a 9-2 victory over the Arizona Diamondbacks on Friday in Phoenix.
Lombard had two hits and three RBIs, and his two-run single capped the early five-run outburst against Eduardo Rodriguez (15-7), who walked three of the first four he faced.
Rice tripled and walked twice as the Yankees played without Aaron Judge, who will be placed on the injured list Saturday, retroactive to Thursday, with a right calf strain.
Gerrit Cole (9-9) gave up two runs on four hits in six innings. He struck out six, did not issue a walk, and retired 13 of the final 15 he faced after Corbin Carroll’s two-run homer in the second made it 5-2.
Carroll added a double and Geraldo Perdomo and Nolan Arenado had two hits apiece for the D-backs, who have lost five of six as their NL wild-card chances fade.
The D-backs (80-74) are five games behind San Diego, Philadelphia and the Chicago Cubs (all 85-69) for the three NL wild-card spots. The Padres were the only one of the four to win Friday.
The Yankees (89-64) have won four of five and eight of 10.
The Yankees trail Tampa Bay by four games in the AL East, and the teams will meet in a three-game series in Yankee Stadium starting Tuesday. They are 5 1/2 games ahead of Boston for the first AL wild-card spot.
Rodriguez, on pace to post a career-low ERA, gave up five hits and seven runs in 5 1/3 innings, leaving after Lombard’s homer made it 7-2 in the sixth. He struck out five and walked four.
The Yankees forced Rodriguez to use 45 pitches in their big first. Paul Goldschmidt walked to open the game and took third on Cody Bellinger’s single before Heliot Ramos and Rice walked on 3-2 counts to force in the first run.
Amed Rosario followed with an RBI single and Ramos scored on a wild pitch before Lombard capped the inning with a two-run single.
Rice homered to lead off the third, Lombard homered in the sixth, and the Yankees turned an infield single and two Arizona errors into a two-run seventh to close the scoring.

Title: MLB roundup: Braves top Astros, wrap up postseason berth
Article_Text:
Michael Harris II, Ronald Acuna Jr. and Matt Olson slugged two-run home runs and deadline acquisition Tyler Mahle continued his exceptional pitching for the visiting Atlanta Braves, who secured a postseason berth with a 6-2 victory over the Houston Astros on Friday.
Atlanta qualified for the postseason for the eighth time in nine seasons. The Braves lowered their magic number to clinch the National League East to three over the Philadelphia Phillies.
Harris provided Mahle a 2-0 lead when he followed a one-out single by Matt Olson with an opposite-field blast to left off Astros starter Peter Lambert (8-10) in the fourth inning. Harris (3-for-5) drove a first-pitch slurve from Lambert 367 feet for his 26th homer of the year.
Mahle (7-10) improved to 4-1 with a 1.28 ERA over eight starts since his acquisition from the Giants. He allowed one run on three hits and one walk with six strikeouts over six innings.
Guardians 5, Athletics 3
Jose Ramirez hit a solo homer in the sixth inning for his 1,000th career RBI after rookie Travis Bazzana went deep in the fifth, fueling host Cleveland to a victory over the Athletics.
The Guardians have won three in a row to move a game ahead of the second-place Chicago White Sox in the American League Central. Joey Cantillo (10-9) threw six scoreless innings in relief, and Cade Smith handled the ninth for his 38th save.
Zack Gelof belted a three-run homer in the first inning for the Athletics, whose losing skid reached four games. Reliever Scott Blewett (2-1) permitted one run on one hit in 1 2/3 innings.
Padres 8, Marlins 2
Ty France clouted a three-run homer to cap a six-run fifth inning as San Diego stopped visiting Miami to forge a three-way tie atop the National League wild-card standings.
Winning for the 11th time in 12 games, the Padres pulled even with the Chicago Cubs and Philadelphia Phillies, who both lost. San Diego’s magic number for clinching a playoff spot dropped to four.
San Diego starter Nick Pivetta (3-2) worked five innings, yielding four hits and a run. Marlins reliever Cade Gibson (5-2) was charged with the first two runs in the game-changing fifth. The Padres’ Jackson Merrill and the Marlins’ Agustin Ramirez homered.
Mets 6, Phillies 3
Zac Thornton tossed six solid innings, Juan Soto homered among his three hits and host New York beat Philadelphia.
Soto went 3-for-5 for the Mets, while Francisco Lindor and Carson Benge each collected two hits. Thornton (5-5) gave up two runs on five hits.
Edmundo Sosa finished 3-for-3 with a homer and Derek Hill also went deep for the Phillies, who fell to 7-9 this month. Newly acquired Jose Urquidy threw 4 2/3 shutout innings after opener Tim Mayza (3-4) surrendered three runs while getting just one out.
Reds 6, Cubs 4
Cincinnati scored three times in the sixth inning in a back-and-forth win over visiting Chicago.
Elly De La Cruz had two hits, two walks and two runs for the Reds. Cincinnati starter Chase Burns and reliever Julian Aguiar (1-0) each allowed two runs on four hits in three innings.
Cubs starter Clay Holmes (6-8) surrendered six runs on three hits in 5 1/3 innings. Ian Happ homered for Chicago, and Michael Conforto amassed three hits.
Twins 3, Angels 0
Connor Prielipp allowed two hits over a career-high seven innings and fellow rookie Walker Jenkins went 3-for-4 with a home run as Minnesota topped Los Angeles in Anaheim, Calif.
Travis Adams pitched a 1-2-3 ninth inning to pick up his third save. Jenkins, who began his career going 4-for-45, homered for the second straight game on his sixth consecutive hit in the series.
Jose Siri had two hits for the Angels. Grayson Rodriguez (4-8) gave up three runs on eight hits in 6 2/3 innings.
Brewers 6, Orioles 5 (10 innings)
Sal Frelick singled home a 10th-inning run and visiting Milwaukee pulled out a victory against Baltimore.
Trevor Megill (3-3) was the winning pitcher despite a blown save. Chad Patrick retired the Orioles in order in the bottom of the 10th for his sixth save.
Milwaukee’s Jackson Chourio and Baltimore’s Pete Alonso hit three-run homers early in the game. Gunnar Henderson and Coby Mayo both collected three hits for the Orioles.
Dodgers 8, Giants 2
Mookie Betts homered twice, including his 53rd career leadoff homer, and Josue De Paula hit a tiebreaking double to help Los Angeles produce a victory over visiting San Francisco.
The Dodgers socked five home runs while winning for the 12th time in the last 15 games. Max Muncy and Kyle Tucker hit back-to-back homers in the eighth, and Betts and Will Smith repeated the feat later in the frame. Tyler Glasnow (5-1) gave up two runs and three hits while striking out a season-high 10 in six innings.
Jung Hoo Lee homered and Jonah Cox had an RBI single as the Giants fell for the fifth time in seven games.
Yankees 9, Diamondbacks 2
George Lombard Jr. had two hits and three RBIs, and his two-run single capped a five-run first-inning outburst as New York cruised past Arizona in Phoenix.
Ben Rice and Lombard homered and Rice added a triple as the Yankees won for the fourth time in five games. Gerrit Cole (9-9) gave up two runs on four hits in six innings.
Corbin Carroll homered and doubled for the Diamondbacks, who have lost five of six to see their NL wild-card chances fade. Eduardo Rodriguez (15-7) yielded seven runs in 5 1/3 innings.
Red Sox 4, Rays 2
Roman Anthony homered and had three RBIs, Jahmai Jones went deep and Boston cooled off first-place Tampa Bay in St. Petersburg, Fla.
Anthony went 2-for-5 while Caleb Durbin was 2-for-3 for the Red Sox. Boston starter Ranger Suarez (8-4) fought control issues but allowed one run on three hits in 5 2/3 innings.
Junior Caminero doubled, walked twice and drove in a run for the Rays, who had only five hits as their six-game winning streak ended. Ian Seymour (9-7) allowed four runs on seven hits in five innings.
Rangers 7, Blue Jays 1
Corey Seager capped a four-run second inning with an RBI double as Texas topped Toronto in Arlington, Texas.
The Rangers drew 10 walks and moved into a first-place tie with Houston in the American League West. Jake Burger had two RBIs for Texas, which won for the fifth time in six games. Texas took a 4-0 lead in the second inning against Dylan Cease (11-6), who allowed four runs (one earned) on three hits over 2 2/3 innings.
The Blue Jays fell two games back of the White Sox for the final AL wild-card spot. Myles Straw had two hits with an RBI for Toronto, which committed three errors and lost for the third time in four games.
Tigers 11, White Sox 8
Dillon Dingler delivered the go-ahead single and Riley Greene followed with a two-run homer in a five-run eighth inning as visiting Detroit stormed back from six runs down to beat Chicago.
Hao-Yu Lee went 4-for-5 with a homer, three RBIs and two runs for the Tigers. Kevin McGonigle finished 2-for-5 with four RBIs. Drew Sommers (2-4) threw two shutout innings, fanning five, and Kenley Jansen blanked the White Sox in the ninth for his 21st save.
Colson Montgomery and Miguel Vargas each had two hits and three RBIs for the White Sox, who have lost three out of four. Sean Newcomb (2-5) got only two outs in relief while allowing three runs.
Pirates 8, Royals 5
Konnor Griffin had four hits and two RBIs and Spencer Horwitz delivered a tiebreaking two-run single in the seventh as Pittsburgh rallied to beat visiting Kansas City.
Pittsburgh trailed 4-0 after the top of the third inning and 5-2 entering the bottom of the fourth. The Pirates won their second straight after losing four of their previous five.
Vinnie Pasquantino and Michael Massey each homered as the Royals scored five runs against Pittsburgh ace Paul Skenes, who scattered six hits in his six innings. Royals starter Randy Dobnak allowed four runs on seven hits over 3 2/3 innings.
Nationals 9, Cardinals 1
Cade Cavalli pitched five scoreless innings and recorded the 200th strikeout of his first full major league season, leading Washington to a victory at St. Louis.
Cavalli (13-5), who agreed with the Nationals earlier in the day on a four-year, $47 million contract extension, allowed four hits and struck out six. Dylan Crews hit a two-run homer and Yohandy Morales added a two-run double for Washington.
Cardinals starter Kyle Leahy (10-5) allowed seven runs, six earned, on five hits over three innings. Leo Bernal went 3-for-4.
Mariners 5, Rockies 4
Lazaro Montes homered leading off the top of the ninth, J.P. Crawford went deep to open the game, and Seattle beat Colorado in Denver.
Randy Arozarena finished with three hits as the Mariners logged their second win in a row. Carlos Vargas (2-0) recorded one out in relief, and Andres Munoz earned his 28th save with a scoreless ninth inning.
Cole Carrigg, Connor Norby and Jake McCarthy had three hits apiece and Ezequiel Tovar contributed two hits for the Rockies, who have lost three in a row and 11 of 12. Jordan Romano (0-4) served up Montes’ homer.

Title: Phillies turn to improving Andrew Painter in clash vs. Mets
Article_Text:
Field Level Media
                
19 Sep 2026, 17:35 GMT+10
            
(Photo credit: Dale Zanine)
Christian Scott, Zac Thornton and Nolan McLean are providing the New York Mets hope that they eventually will be part of a rotation for a playoff contender.
The Philadelphia Phillies need rookie Andrew Painter to continue proving that now.
Painter will take the mound for the Phillies on Saturday afternoon when they visit the Mets in the third contest of a four-game series between the National League East rivals.
Painter (3-9, 5.54 ERA) will oppose Scott (4-5, 3.76) in a battle of right-handers.
The Phillies missed a chance to take over sole possession of the top wild-card spot in the NL on Friday night, when Thornton and two relievers combined on a six-hitter in the Mets' 6-3 win.
The Phillies, Chicago Cubs and San Diego Padres are tied for the NL's three wild-card spots at 85-69. The Cubs lost to the Cincinnati Reds 6-4 before the Padres created the three-way tie hours later with an 8-2 win over the Miami Marlins.
The Arizona Diamondbacks reside five games behind the Phillies, Cubs and Padres.
The importance of Painter was further magnified Friday, when Philadelphia fell to 0-2 in bullpen games necessitated by the absence of left-hander Jesus Luzardo (shoulder, 15-day injured list).
The All-Star was scratched from his scheduled start against the Atlanta Braves last Saturday, when the Phillies used six pitchers as the Braves rolled to a 12-2 win. On Friday, opener Tim Mayza got just one out and allowed three runs while pitching in Luzardo's spot.
The Phillies' bullpen also is being taxed by injury and ineffectiveness.
Right-hander Jonathan Bowlan departed Thursday's game vs. the Mets with a tight right groin. On Friday, Orion Kerkering gave up Juan Soto's three-run blast in the sixth inning -- the second homer surrendered by Kerkering in his last three outings, during which he has a 13.50 ERA.
'Anybody that gives up runs, when things aren't going good, your confidence is not sky high like when you're getting all your outs and everything's going smoothly,' Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said. 'But we've got to get past that at this point.'
Painter is 2-1 with a 3.58 ERA in nine starts since being recalled from Triple-A Lehigh Valley on July 31. He didn't factor into the decision in his most recent start last Sunday, when he gave up one run over five innings as the Phillies beat the Braves 9-4. He has yet to face the Mets in his career.
The Mets (70-84) have been under .500 since April and officially were eliminated from playoff contention earlier this week. But McLean and Thornton continued to provide optimism for 2027 by combining to allow just three runs over 12 innings in the first two games of the series.
McLean took the hard-luck loss Thursday, when he gave up one run in six innings in the Phillies' 3-0 win.
Thornton, McLean and Scott have a combined 3.40 ERA in 66 starts. Thornton and McLean are rookies while Scott is in his second big-league season after Tommy John surgery cut his 2024 campaign short.
'I think you have to train like you've never won anything and compete like you've never lost,' Mets interim manager Andy Green said Friday night about Thornton. 'I think you have to live in that space constantly.'
Scott took the defeat Sunday after allowing two runs over six innings in the Mets' 2-0 loss to the New York Yankees. He is 1-0 with a 1.80 ERA in two career starts against the Phillies.
--Field Level Media

Title: LCCC premieres Skilled Trade Career Fair
Article_Text:
NANTICOKE – Hundreds of students are exploring exciting career opportunities and learning about a program designed to rejuvenate Pennsylvania’s skilled trades.
Luzerne County Community College held its inaugural Skilled Trade Career Fair for local career-and-technical-center students Friday. The fair on LCCC’s main campus featured representatives from businesses and unions and a ceremony launching a new workforce-preparation program at the college.
LCCC President John Yudichak said the fair and new program were designed to invest resources into crucial, but long-neglected, career pathways.
“For too long, careers in the skilled trades were often overlooked,” Yudichak said. “For too long, Pennsylvania has lacked the statewide education ecosystem to meet the need for skill-trade workers….”
The businesses and unions attending the fair stationed tables throughout the James T. Atherton Gymnasium to meet with students and discuss possible careers.
Greg Ellsworth, a former high school career-and-technology teacher who now works for Milnes Engineering, Construction, & Surveying, said the fair was an opportunity to connect students with possible career paths in growing fields.
“CTE (career-and-technical education) rocks, I always say,” Ellsworth said. “We wanted to be here for their kickoff opening to be a part of helping kids to understand the other careers and hands-on trades that are out there.”
John Behm, an apprentice coordinator for Insulators Local 38, said the career fair was a way to introduce students to a vital labor organization that can offer a great career.
“We’re one of the smaller internationals, we’re one of the smaller unions,” Behm said. “But, we play a very important part in construction,”
Warren Faust, the president of the NEPA Building & Construction Trade Council, called on students to embrace the opportunities laid out before them Friday. He also called on businesses and public officials to reciprocate with a pledge to support apprenticeships.
“Look here, when you require apprenticeship, this is what you’re giving,” Faust said. You’re giving opportunity to all these students….”
Before touring the career fair, students gathered in an assembly to hear a presentation on near workforce-preparation initiatives — with a focus on the L3C Building & Construction Trade Apprenticeship Readiness Academy.
The L3C academy will teach students the skills that will help them enter registered apprenticeship programs in construction and the building trades. TradesFutures, a national non-profit organization that promotes union construction careers, is licensing its Multi-Craft Core Curriculum to LCCC for the academy’s use. Joe Gusler, the apprenticeship coordinator of the Pennsylvania Building & Construction Trades Council, said the program would provide students relevant training while connecting them directly with labor unions that could employ their new skills.
“Work is extremely busy across the commonwealth,” Gusler said. “And we’re confident that this program will assist our local unions in recruiting new members into their apprenticeship programs.”
“We’re hoping that some of you end up as some of our members in the very near future thanks to programming like this,” added Marissa Bankert, the president and CEO of the Eastern Pennsylvania Association of Builders & Contractors. “Now is the time for you to grab this opportunity.”
This program is meant to address a coming, statewide skilled-trade labor deficit forecasted to reach 300,000 skilled-trade workers by 2030.
“With no skill-trade educational system in place, Pennsylvania expects to be short more than 300,000 skill-trade workers by 2030,” Yudichak said. “Students, that’s 300,000 jobs waiting for you.”
The fair and announcement of the initiatives seemed to be sparking interest among students.
Alayna Arnet, a freshman at the West Side Career & Technology Center said she was considering a career in broadcasting or a field in engineering and cutting-edge technologies. During the fair, she took interest in the company HITT and its demonstration of a four-legged robot named “Spot.”
“It’s good so far,” Arnet said of the career fair.
Lesley Betz, of Berwick Industries Inc., said she is counting on sparking that youth interest. A ribbon and bow manufacturing company that sells its products across the country, Berwick Industries has struggled to recruit youth workers, especially the machinists needed to manufacture their boutique parts the company makes itself.
Given those challenges, Betz said an LCCC graduate Berwick Industries recently hired has been “amazing.”
“We have a really aging workforce,” Betz said. “So we need to get people involved.”
The L3C curriculum is part of a statewide effort to promote workforce preparation in the trades. In May, the Pennsylvania Commission for Community Colleges partnered with TradesFuture to launch apprenticeship readiness academies in all 15 of the state’s community colleges.
“It is really earthshattering for Pennsylvania to collaborate in this way,” PACCC President Tuesday Stanley told students. “So, I encourage you to take full advantage.”

Title: NFL Week 2 predictions: Upsets, fantasy sleepers, stat lines
Article_Text:
Week 2 of the2026 NFL season is off to an exciting start, as the Bills defeated the Lions 41-31 in the first game at Highmark Stadium. But what will happen in the remaining 15 games? We have 15 predictions from our NFL experts.
First,betting analyst Pamela Maldonado picks two underdogs who could win outright. Then, analytics writer Seth Walder projected out stat lines for three players. Fantasy football writerEric Moody gives three sleepers, and analyst Matt Bowen suggests three players who will find the end zone. Finally, analyst Ben Solak lays out four wild-card predictions.
Could the Bengals upset the Texans? Will we see big receiving days for the Dolphins' Malik Washington and Caleb Douglas? Can Eagles running back Saquon Barkley find the end zone? And is it finally time for the Jets to snag an interception? Let's make 15 big predictions for all of Sunday and Monday's action.
Jump to:
Upset picks | Projected stat lines
Fantasy sleepers, surprises
TD scorers | Other predictions
Jacksonville Jaguars +2.5 at Denver Broncos (+124)
Denver's offense hasn't shown enough to justify laying points. The Broncos produced only 176 yards and 3.7 yards per play in their Week 1 loss to the Chiefs, with quarterbackBo Nix turning it over twice. Jacksonville is bringing a pass rush that generated five sacks against Cleveland, while QBTrevor Lawrencethrew four touchdown passes. Defense makes the Broncos the favorite, but the Jaguars have the more trustworthy offense to win outright.
Cincinnati Bengals +2.5at Houston Texans(+120)
The Bengals' biggest weakness looked better against the Bucs, as quarterbackJoe Burrow was sacked only once. If that holds, he gets a Houston defense that just allowed 10.4 yards per pass to Buffalo in Week 1.Houston can obviously pressure Burrow, but if Cincinnati's offensive line continues to improve, it should have enough through the air withJa'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins.
Rhamondre Stevenson, RB, New England Patriots: 16 carries, 63 rushing yards; 5 receptions, 42 receiving yards, 1 receiving touchdown
Since 2023, running backs catch passes on 8% of dropbacks against man coverage but 15%against zone coverage. Why does that matter here? Because in Week 1against the Falcons, the Steelers ran zone coverage 89% of the time under new defensive coordinator Patrick Graham. So I expect Stevenson to have a big day in the receiving game.
And while I don't expect the Patriots will be as run-heavy as they were in Week 1-- which certainly didn't work out for them! --New England should be ahead by enough early to run the ball late in the game. All in all, it should be a healthy workload for Stevenson.
Riq Woolen, CB, Philadelphia Eagles: 34 coverage snaps, 1 reception allowed for 7 yards on four targets, 1 interception
Woolen had a strong Week 1 against the Commanders, allowing just one reception for 1 yard. Granted, that one reception was a touchdown to WRStefon Diggs, but I'm not sure that play was entirely on him. Either way, it was a strong game for Woolen, who also scored highly in my cornerback metric. Now, he gets to face second-year Titans QBCam Ward, who struggled against the Jets in Week 1. Woolen should have the advantage againstCarnell Tate, Calvin Ridley or Elic Ayomanor.
Malik Washington, WR, Miami Dolphins: 7 receptions, 77 receiving yards, 1 touchdown
Washington ran a route on 84% of Miami's dropbacks in Week 1, the highest rate on the Dolphins. He was also targeted eight times but had just three receptions. His 99 incomplete air yards was tied for second among all players, a number that indicates some positive regression could be coming in Week 2.
The Dolphins threw a little more than expected versus the Raiders, and they'll have to pass plenty against the 49ers since this looks likely to be a blowout loss. Washington, who frequently plays out of the slot, historically runs shorter routes and could be an option underneath in garbage time.
Jordan Love, QB, Green Bay Packers (rostered in 43.9% of ESPN leagues)
Love threw for 387 yards in Week 1 against the Vikings, the second-highest total of his career, and scored 19.4 fantasy points on 42 pass attempts. Green Bay struggled to run the ball without Josh Jacobs, and its offensive line will still be banged up in Week 2 against the Jets. But with Christian Watson and Matthew Golden combining for 48.2 fantasy points last week, Love should be an appealing streaming option.
Caleb Douglas, WR, Miami Dolphins (34.9%)
Douglas caught five of seven targets for 94 yards, scoring 14.4 fantasy points in his NFL debut against the Raiders. He played more than 90% of Miami's offensive snaps and led all rookies in targets, receptions and receiving yards. The Dolphins enter Week 2 as double-digit underdogs against the 49ers, so Douglas could benefit from a pass-heavy game script.
Mack Hollins, WR, New England Patriots (5.2%)
Hollins outsnapped Romeo Doubs in the first half against the Seahawks in Week 1, and he led the Patriots receivers in snaps after A.J. Brown exited with an ankle injury. Hollins should continue to see significant playing time against Pittsburgh now that Brown is on injured reserve.
Holins received at least six targets in four games last season, averaging 12.8 fantasy points in those contests. He finished with five targets and 9.1 fantasy points in Week 1.
Derrick Henry, RB, Baltimore Ravens
Henry rushed for three touchdowns in the Ravens' Week 1 win over the Colts -- including two on carries inside the 5-yard line. Under new coordinator Declan Doyle, the Ravens used schemed zone concepts and creative tight end movement to put Henry on a north/south track. That should work versus a Saints defense that allowed two rushing scores in New Orleans'Week 1 loss to the Lions.
George Pickens, WR, Dallas Cowboys
Pickens caught just three of six targets for 28 yards in the Cowboys' Week 1 loss to the Giants, including two drops. But that doesn't mean quarterback Dak Prescott will stop going to Pickens for big plays. The vertical pass game is a key element of Dallas' offense, and it could lead Pickens into the end zone.
Saquon Barkley, RB, Philadelphia Eagles
Barkley did have 15 carries in the Week 1 win over the Commanders, with two goal-to-go attempts, so we can bet on him seeing the ball in scoring position. Plus, he has home run ability to score from outside the red zone. Yes, the Eagles need more up front to create consistent daylight for Barkley, but he gets a matchup against a Titans defense that gave up just 152 rushing yards to the Jets.
Raiders RB Ashton Jeanty will lead the league in scrimmage yards
Jeanty led the Raiders in both rushing yards (102) and receiving yards (45) last week in the Raiders' win over the Dolphins. Without Brock Bowers(meniscus trim) for another week and facing another light box defense from theChargers, I expect Jeanty to once again thrive on the ground and in the air. Jeanty was seventh last week with 147scrimmage yards, but his longest play was only 15 yards. With a couple home run plays on Sunday, he could knock on the door for 200.
The Jets will get their first interception
The last Jets pick was on Jan. 5, 2025 -- 623 days from their matchup with the Packers on Sunday. Green Bay's pass protection is a glaring issue, and while quarterbackJordan Love is around league-average in his interception rate, the 16 hits he took in Week 1 could have him looking to get rid of the ball faster in Week 2. I'm banking on safety Minkah Fitzpatrick to track down a deep heave and end the drought.
Did I predict the Jets to break the drought last week? Yes. Will I do it again next week if they fail again? Who's to say?
Falcons QB Jack Strandwill score a touchdown
Who? Strand is an undrafted free agent out of Minnesota State-Moorhead, a Division II school just opposite Fargo on the border of North Dakota and Minnesota. He was the QB4 on the roster during training camp, but with Michael Penix Jr. and Tua Tagovailoa still hurt, Strand is the QB2 behindCooper Rush, who had a rough Week 1 showing.
Even with Rush getting the Week 2 start, Strand is an enormous player (6-foot-5, 240 pounds) who should get short-yardage usage as a QB sneak expert. If the Falcons get inside the 2-yard lineagainst the Panthers, they should feed Strand.
There will be another weird forward pass/fumble ruling
Early doors, but it feels like the forward-pass-or-fumble line will be blurry this season. Lions quarterbackJared Goff had a fumble that was called an incomplete pass in Week 1 for the simple intention to throw the ball forward.Bo Nix had another one on "Monday Night Football" that was at least a little closer to the gray area.
There's always one refereeing decision that gets the spotlight every season -- complete pass, offensive tackle false starts and illegal forward motions are recent examples -- and this particular plane is ready to take off. One bad call in a key moment, and then it's conspiracy theory time.
]

Title: Dallas Cowboys vs Washington Commanders biggest storylines for Sunday
Article_Text:
I don’t think anyone expected things to go the way they did in the Dallas Cowboys vs. New York Giants game. Without dwelling too much on a game in the rearview mirror, the Dallas defense caught many by surprise considering the overhaul over the offseason. Guys like Jalen Thompson, Rashan Gary, and Caleb Downs were supposed to usher in something different.
Important Cowboys vs Commanders storylines on Sunday
What do you think is the biggest storyline entering Sunday?
Unfortunately, it was more of the same.
Here’s the good news. It was Week 1. The Cowboys still have 16 regular-season games left, and they have plenty of time to turn things around. They have to do it in a must-win way this week against the Washington Commanders.
Here are five points to watch for as the game kicks off on Sunday.
First point: More of the same?
Heading into their matchup with the Giants, one of last week’s five points was limiting Jaxson Dart in the running game. The Cowboys had 54 yards on the ground to Dart, averaging almost five yards per carry. Dart’s ability to scramble kept Dallas’ defense on the field, which we all know how that went.
The Cowboys have another quarterback coming up on Sunday who can hurt them with his legs: Jayden Daniels. Last week against the Philadelphia Eagles, Daniels didn’t run for as many yards as Dart did in Dallas, but he was an effective runner when he had the opportunity or needed to make a play. He had five carries for 31 yards, averaging over six yards every time he would run.
Dallas needs to make sure last week’s mistake doesn’t happen again, because it’ll lead to more of the same, with the Commanders extending drives and keeping the Cowboys offense on the sidelines.
Second point: The terror twins or the DeVille twins
Somehow, someway, the Cowboys need to get CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens the ball early and often against the Commanders. Brian Schottenheimer has talked about wanting to run the ball and set the tone, but the team’s real playmakers are on the outside.
On a great day, both wideouts can have over 100 yards each and be a terror to opposing defenses. Against the Giants, it just seemed like Pickens and Prescott weren’t always on the same page, and we’ve seen how Lamb can take time to get going if things don’t go his way early in a game.
The best version of Lamb and Pickens earned them the nickname “the terror twins.” That version of the duo needs to be on display vs. the Commanders’ smaller cornerbacks. Last year against the Commanders at AT&T Stadium, Lamb went for 110 receiving yards and Pickens had 85. Both players averaged over 20 yards per catch. What we don’t need to see are the DeVille twins, which, if anyone has seen the show Rugrats, you know what I’m talking about.
Third point: A rookie DC in DC
The Commanders have the same question at defensive coordinator as the Cowboys do: Is this moment too big for them? Head coach Dan Quinn went out and hired two first-time coordinators on both sides of the ball this offseason, which could make him look like a genius or get him fired.
Washington’s DC should be a familiar name to Cowboys fans since he was in the running for the same position with Dallas: Daronte Jones. He spent most of his coaching career with the Minnesota Vikings and learned under Brian Flores over the last three seasons. Unlike Christian Parker, Jones was actually a defensive coordinator in college in 2021 for LSU. That was his only season holding the position.
Against the Eagles, the Commanders defense looked good and got the Philly offense out of rhythm on multiple drives. However, a few explosive plays happened where it looked like the secondary didn’t know what was going on (sound familiar).
It’ll be interesting to see the storylines coming out of the game because one of these teams will be 0-2, with a ton of questions surrounding their first-time defensive coordinators and whether they were the right guys for the job.
Fourth point: Reading between the linebackers
Before offseason training and the NFL draft, the Cowboys’ linebacking corps was seen as a glaring need, even with Jaishawn Barham and Dee Winters coming aboard. DeMarvion Overshown’s health was a question, and Dallas needed to keep developing second-year pro Shemar James.
As time went on, the questions around linebacker seemed to shift towards the pass rush and secondary. We should have stuck with our first instincts. With Overshown leaving Week 1 with a hamstring injury that could cost him one to two weeks, the Cowboys linebacker room looks even thinner heading into Week 2.
Barham could be called upon as the next man up with green-dot responsibilities, but with growing concerns about the defense’s ability to communicate calls properly, should a rookie be trusted to make the right calls? Dallas has Curtis Robinson and Justin Barron on the practice squad and could elevate one of them to the active roster for Sunday, but they aren’t on the same level as Overshown to fill the void.
The Cowboys were impressed by what they saw from Barham all offseason and in the first preseason game. If that player is still there, which he should be, the Dallas defense will need him in a big way this weekend.
Fifth point: Kicking and screaming
No need to panic; this is an under-the-radar point my colleague RJ Ochoa brought up on Twitter.
Dating back to last season, Dallas Cowboys kicker Brandon Aubrey has now missed a kick of some kind (field goal or extra point) in 3 straight games.
This is the first time in his career he has a 3-game streak of such kind.
Aubrey is one of, if not the best, kickers in the NFL. However, if the defense struggles to start the season and the offense needs to score as many points as possible in their opportunities, missing kicks can’t happen. Questions lingered about the special teams unit’s performance last year under Nick Sorensen, and doubt remains about his return this offseason.
Sorensen stuck around, and so far, after one game, the special teams unit has not looked any better in year two. Aubrey signed a historic deal this offseason, and deservedly so. But if he starts missing critical kicks in games that could come down to three points, it could raise alarm bells about what’s happened to one of the league’s most clutch kickers.

Title: Kevin Alan Metzger
Article_Text:
Milton, Pa. — Kevin Alan Metzger, 55, passed away unexpectedly on Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026.
Born May 15, 1971 in Danville, son of the late Carl W. and Burrtell E. (Labour) Metzger, Kevin graduated from Danville Area High School. Following high school, he enlisted in the United States Navy, where he proudly served his country for 22 years as a Hospital Corpsman and Fleet Marine Force (FMF) Corpsman “Doc” before retiring in 2012. His time in the service included two foreign wars: the Gulf War and Operation Iraqi Freedom.
He continued his education at George Mason University, where he earned his Bachelor of Individualized Studies degree in Athletic Training. He worked as an Athletic Trainer for Loudoun County Public Schools, as a Physical Therapy Assistant for Officer Candidates School and the Naval Health Clinic at Quantico.
Kevin was a member of Milton Lutheran Church and a life member of the Veterans of Foreign Wars.
While in school he participated in the marching band as the drum major, played football, ran track, and was in the Boy Scouts where he earned the rank of Eagle Scout.
An outdoor enthusiast, Kevin enjoyed hunting, fishing, cycling, and camping. He enjoyed sports cheering on his favorite teams the New York Giants and Penn State University, and the St. Louis Cardinals. With a playful spirit and a gift for being a goofball, Kevin brought laughter to those around him. His love of the Minions perfectly reflected his own mischievous humor and fun-loving personality. He will be remembered for his dedication to his country, his sense of humor, and the joy he brought to those who knew and loved him.
Surviving is his wife, Alison Stroop; three daughters, Hailey E. Metzger of Tampa, Fla., her mother and his former spouse, Stefanie C. Koster of Tulsa, Okla., Carley C. Metzger and Sydney P. Metzger, their mother and his former spouse, Kimberly C. Metzger, all of Burke, Va.; two step-children, Mason Stroop of Philadelphia and Abigail Stroop of Montoursville; siblings, Carla S. Wetzel (Dan) of Danville, Flint C. Metzger, of Danville, Brian J. Metzger (Linda) of Mechanicsburg; Wendy L. Kohut (Pstachu) of Nashville, Tenn.; and a boat load of nieces and nephews whom he loved.
A burial with military honors will be held at 1:30 p.m. Wednesday, Sept. 23 at the National Memorial Cemetery at Quantico, 18424 Joplin Road, Triangle, Va. 22172. A memorial service to honor Kevin’s life will be held 1:30 p.m., Thursday, Sept. 24 at Milton Lutheran Church, 1125 Mahoning St, Milton, Pa. 17847.
Memorial donations in Kevin’s name may be made to Veterans Services Foundation. In the memo line please include “In Memory of Kevin Metzger,” PO Box 100, Richmond, VA 23218.
Online condolences may be made on Kevin’s memorial page at www.SandersMortuary.com
For guidance or help please call 988 (suicide and crisis lifeline) or 800-273-8255 (Veterans Crisis Line).

Title: Stephen Curry finally admits he tried to recruit LeBron James to Warriors
Article_Text:
The Golden State Warriors will enter the 2026-27 season on rather precarious footing. The front office missed out on their high-end targets this offseason, and the team remains largely the same from the one that missed the playoffs in the previous campaign. Apparently, even Stephen Curry dipped his fingers into the recruitment war, but ultimately to no avail.
Just recently, Curry himself admitted to actively recruiting LeBron James this summer before the superstar ended up signing with the Philadelphia 76ers instead, adding that anybody would be a fool not to try their luck to land the living legend. That basically confirms what fans and pundits speculated about his desire for the Warriors brain trust, which is to snag a new star for a possibly final hurrah for the title.
Well, obviously, that has already become a moot point.
The Western Conference has become so top-heavy that it is simply too difficult for an aging team like the Warriors to keep up with the likes of the San Antonio Spurs and the Oklahoma City Thunder. The barrier to entry just to be in the conversation with those teams is mightily high, and there is no way they are moving the needle as a collective given the stale summer they just had.
Aside from having an old nucleus, the Warriors are also not going to be at full strength to begin the campaign. Jimmy Butler will be sidelined for the rest of the calendar year as he rehabs his ACL injury, and their core players are not the most durable of cogs, either.
LeBron may not even be enough to catapult Golden State into the title conversation, but he definitely could have helped a ton with this group. He is still an elite playmaker and finisher, and those are traits the Warriors highly value in their system.
Now, after missing out on James, Curry and the Warriors will aim to get back to the postseason. Normally, that would have been a no-brainer for them, but given the circumstances, another playoff absence is well within the realm of reality for this group.

Title: Ed Sheeran returns to stage after Palestinian controversy
Article_Text:
Protesters and police were expected to greet concertgoers in Philadelphia on Saturday for pop superstar Ed Sheeran's first show since he became embroiled in controversy set off by his opening act's pro-Palestinian comments.
Rapper Macklemore was booted from Sheeran's US Loop Tour on Monday after the owners of stadiums hosting upcoming shows objected to his shouting "Free Palestine" onstage in New Jersey earlier this month.
Sheeran has denied being behind the decision to remove Macklemore, saying his tour's promoter was responsible.
But four supporting acts soon quit the "Shape of You" singer's tour. They included Sheeran's backing band as well as performer Finneas, who rose to fame collaborating with his pop superstar sister Billie Eilish.
At a time when a growing number of artists are speaking out against the conflict in Gaza and West Bank settler violence, the 35-year-old British performer has maintained his apolitical stance.
"I am not complicit. I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care," he said on Instagram on Tuesday.
However, he said, "those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum."
The former busker-turned-superstar, accused by critics of failing to stand up to the stadium owners, has been targeted by boycott calls over the controversy.
"Clearly, there's some real discontent around how this whole situation is being managed, and he's definitely having to do some brand reputation management," said Gretchen Larsen, a professor specialising in the music industry at Durham University Business School in the UK.
No new opening acts or backing bands have been announced, and it was not known how Sheeran planned to carry out his show at Lincoln Financial Field in the eastern US city of Philadelphia on Saturday night.
A pro-Palestinian rally organised by local groups was scheduled to take place near the venue in the afternoon.
City police told AFP there would be an "appropriate police presence" to "help ensure the safety of concertgoers, employees and neighborhood residents."
On the resale market, tickets for the show have been changing hands at a slightly brisker pace since Monday when compared to previous dates on Sheeran's tour, according to tracking site TicketData.
"Some share of the audience isn't tuned in to anything political, or is completely indifferent to it, and has only just now become aware that Ed Sheeran is even playing their city. They're buying tickets with zero connection to the controversy," site founder Keith Pagello said.
The price of the cheapest tickets had fallen from US$123 on Monday to US$67 by Friday afternoon.
Pagello said the decline was not necessarily linked to the row, as it is common for concert ticket prices to drop as the event date approaches. - AFP

Title: Media Monitor: NPR Music Weighs Rap Lyrics on Trial After Lil Durk Acquittal, Macklemore Tour Fallout
Article_Text:
NPR Music is reporting that rapper Lil Durk was acquitted on all charges last week after a three-day jury deliberation in his murder-for-hire trial. It said Durk remains in detention awaiting a second federal trial next month on racketeering charges. NPR Music said his lyrics and an unreleased music video were shown to jurors, and that he assembled a defense team that included Brian Steel, who led Young Thug's defense in the YSL/RICO case.
NPR Music said the outcome gave new meaning to a viral 2018 photo of Young Thug and Lil Durk, and it raised broader questions about how street artists will handle increased legal scrutiny of their lyrics. It said scholar Erik Nielson, co-author of "Rap On Trial: Race, Lyrics and Guilt in America," warned that using artistic expression as evidence could chill that expression and lead artists to self-censor. NPR Music also cited podcaster Wallo267, who said hip-hop did not have a target on its back when he was growing up and that some lyrics can be incriminating.
Separately, NPR Music is reporting that the dispute between Macklemore and Ed Sheeran unfolded rapidly this week. It said Macklemore, a Grammy-winning rapper, was removed as an opening act on Sheeran's stadium tour after making a statement in support of Palestine on stage in New Jersey. NPR Music said the situation now involves billionaire sports team owners, other musicians quitting the tour in solidarity and millions of dollars in donations. It said the tour is scheduled to continue in Philadelphia.
NPR Music is also reporting that the battle over whether The Kennedy Center will close for renovations, have President Trump's name added to its facade, or possibly be torn down cycled again through the courts and the press this week.
It said Neil Young was interviewed about his 50th studio album, "Second Song," which includes new material and songs he wrote as a teenager. NPR Music said songwriter Edgar Barrera leads the Latin Grammy nominations with 10, while Karol G, Rosalía, CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso and Jorge Drexler each received seven. It said folkloric music is having a huge year.

Title: New laws trigger a fresh legal fight over Nazi-looted art in Los Angeles and Auschwitz museums
Article_Text:
By Canadian Press on September 19, 2026.
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Jewish heirs of Holocaust victims and their representatives have filed two lawsuits in California staking their claims to Nazi-looted paintings that still hang on the walls of prominent museums in Los Angeles and Auschwitz.
This pair of lawsuits are the first to be filed after the recent passage of laws by California and Congress, which strengthen U.S.-based claims to artwork that were forcibly taken from Jewish families during World War II.
One lawsuit was filed in Los Angeles Superior Court on Monday by the Jewish Federation of Greater Los Angeles and its board chair Daniel Gryczman against Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena for the return of “Adam and Eve.” These are two life-size oil-on-panel masterpieces created by Lucas Carnach the Elder in 1530.
The other lawsuit was filed in federal court in Los Angeles the same day by the daughters of the late Dinah Gottliebova Babbitt, a Holocaust survivor and California-based animator who was held in Auschwitz. It demanded the return of watercolors of fellow prisoners that the artist was forced to paint for Josef Mengele, a Nazi physician who had earned the nickname the “Angel of Death.”
Spokespersons for both museums say the museums legally hold titles to the works, and intend to continue displaying them to the public. The lawsuits don’t specify the monetary value of the paintings.
Artworks pit Jewish families against museums
The issue of Nazi-looted art is an emotional, legally and ethically charged topic that pits Jewish families that have suffered inter-generational trauma against museums that say they are trying to preserve a painful, yet important, chapter of history. Between 1933 and 1945, the Nazi regime orchestrated the largest art theft in world history, seizing over 600,000 works of art across Europe from Jewish families, collectors and museums. Decades later, many of these masterpieces reside in prominent museums around the world, making the push for their recovery more complex than a simple property dispute.
Rabbi Noah Farkas is president and CEO of the Jewish Federation of Los Angeles, the organization to which Marei von Saher, sole heir of Dutch Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker, has signed over her rights. The paintings were seized from Goudstikker’s collection by Hermann Goring, Adolf Hitler’s second-in-command and changed a number of hands before being sold in the 1960s to the Pasadena Museum of Modern Art, which was renamed Norton Simon Museum in honor of its benefactor.
Farkas said the federation plans to use most of the net proceeds from the recovered art to provide much-needed help to the about 2,500 Holocaust survivors living in the Los Angeles area.
“These are incredibly beautiful European masterpieces stolen from a Jewish family to enrich the Nazi party and fund the war and death machine against the people,” he said. “It’s our honor to take on this role on behalf of the community and use most of the proceeds to help these elderly survivors live out the last years of their lives in dignity, comfort and peace – something their family members were denied during the Holocaust.”
Marei von Saher, in a statement, said she is grateful to the Jewish organization for taking up her family’s cause.
“This effort represents a meaningful step toward justice for Holocaust survivors and victims of Nazi era atrocities,” she said.
New legislation gives lawsuits second wind
California Assemblyman Jesse Gabriel, D-Woodland Hills, wrote Assembly Bill 2867, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom in September 2024, which requires that the state law must apply in lawsuits brought by California residents or their heirs to recover art seized during the Holocaust or during other acts of persecution. Gabriel, who co-chairs the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, introduced the legislation in response to a federal court ruling, which allowed the state-owned Thyssen-Bornemisza National Museum in Madrid to keep a multimillion-dollar Camille Pissarro impressionist masterpiece.
That painting had been taken by the Nazis from the Cassirer family in 1939. This case, which prompted this new law, is expected to be heard in federal court in California next month.
Gabriel said it’s time for museums to “do some deep introspection on whether they want to be on the right side of history.”
Museums want to preserve paintings for posterity
Norton Simon Museum released a statement pointing out that a federal court in 2018 unanimously determined that the museum had proper title to the Cranach paintings. In May 2019, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to get involved in the case, leaving in place lower court rulings.
They said the Cranach paintings, which originally belonged to the Stroganoff family, were put up for sale in 1931 by the Soviet Union in an illicit auction in Berlin where they were purchased by Goudstikker. After a complicated journey, the paintings were sold to the museum by a Stroganoff family descendant. The museum later restored and preserved the pieces.
“For nearly 50 years, they have been on view at the Norton Simon Museum and will continue to be accessible to the public for years to come,” the statement said.
Pawel Sawicki, a spokesperson for the Auschwitz Memorial, said the watercolors of Roma victims that Gottliebova Babbitt was forced to paint by Mengele to document his horrendous experiments and racial research, “must remain in the Memorial” to document the man’s crimes. He said these paintings must not be mischaracterized as “Nazi-looted art” because Gottliebova Babbitt painted them against her will as a prisoner and therefore didn’t have ownership of the watercolors.
While he understands the family’s sentiments, Sawicki said the portraits of Roma and Sinti victims are among the few remaining documents of Mengele’s criminal experiments and should be treated as unique documents related to the history of the Auschwitz concentration camp.
“While fully respecting the rights of people who created some of the documents here, we are of the opinion that any loss in the collections of the Memorial will constitute irreparable harm,” he said. “ … The loss of even the smallest part of the documentation is an irreparable loss and blemish on the memory of the victims of Auschwitz.”
Advocates hope cases will now be heard on their merit
Joel Greenberg, founder of Art Ashes, a Philadelphia-area nonprofit that helps Jewish families track down and recover Nazi-looted art, said in addition to the California law, President Donald Trump signed into law and updated the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025. This new law permanently eliminated the expiration date to allow Holocaust survivors and their heirs to indefinitely pursue the recovery of these works of art.
Greenberg said the new federal law gave families the right to reclaim their art for up to six years from the time they find out in whose possession they are.
“These new laws mean that technical defenses will no longer stick in court,” he said. “Every case will be heard on its merits.”
He said the new legislation also ensures that these Jewish families have their day in court and a fair process to determine ownership of the stolen art.
“It will make sure the stories of what happened to European Jewry is not lost and forgotten,” he said. “The art can still be returned to the rightful owner.”
