Title: Distance from Trump may not be enough to save this Pennsylvania Republican
Article_Text:
YARDLEY, Pa. — Mary Ryan may be a registered Republican but she has never voted for President Donald Trump, turned off by his crass style of politics and chaotic approach to governing.
But the 60-year-old medical writer from the Philadelphia suburbs has consistently backed her party's congressman, five-term Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick.
Until now.
This year, Ryan is so fed up with Trump and his grip on Congress that she is planning to vote in November for Fitzpatrick's Democratic opponent in the 1st Congressional District, Bob Harvie, a twice countywide elected commissioner who is a former social studies teacher.
Even though Fitzpatrick has pitched himself as a voice of reason in Washington, Ryan said that “I don't see it happening.”
Defections like this one could sink Fitzpatrick’s reelection chances and cost Republicans their narrow U.S. House majority. As one of the few Republicans representing a congressional district won by Democrat Kamala Harris in the presidential race two years ago, Fitzpatrick has done as much as any House Republican to distance himself from Trump: Fitzpatrick voted against Trump's tariffs, his signature tax legislation and his power to wage war against Iran without congressional approval. The lawmaker even skipped Trump’s recent midterm convention in Dallas.
But that may not be enough to overcome the collateral damage of the president's sagging approval rating and soaring fuel prices because of the war.
Fitzpatrick, speaking briefly after a Sept. 11 memorial in his district, said he understands this year's political challenges and always considers what is best for his constituents with every vote.
“That’s the job,” he said. Representatives for Fitzpatrick did not respond to requests for a more complete interview.
Democrats have tried for years to defeat Fitzpatrick
Harvie describes the race and his decision to run in almost existential terms.
“The lack of trust in our government, the lack of trust in each other and seeing each other as enemies based just on, you know, the color of your skin, the religion you practice, who you voted for,” he said in an interview this summer. “I worry about just the basic foundations of this nation.”
Fitzpatrick has consistently survived challenges in his politically mixed district. He won by 13 percentage points in 2024 when Harris won by less than a single point in the district. In 2022, he won by about 10 points when Democrats were elected to the U.S. Senate and governorship. In 2020, Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden won the district by about 5 points while Fitzpatrick carried it by about 13 points.
“Every two years Democrats in Washington label Congressman Fitzpatrick as vulnerable. Every two years he wins anyway,” said Robert Speel, an associate professor of political science at the Penn State campus in Erie. “It’s, to some extent, possibly like Charlie Brown trying to kick the football and failing each time.”
Harvie pointed to his deep roots in the district as a basis for why he could be different from previous Democrats who ran against Fitzpatrick.
“I’m not somebody who needs to be reintroduced or introduced to people of this district. And that’s very, very different than any race he’s ever run before,” he said.
Jean Dolan, 61, is a Democratic voter from Newtown who has never backed Fitzpatrick and does not plan to this year. She has been frustrated with Trump's immigration crackdown and she worries about how anti-vaccine sentiment in his administration could affect public health. As she sees it, Fitzpatrick is not independent enough from his party's leaders.
“He's a nice guy. I know people like him a lot in the community,” she said. But, she added, “you have to serve everyone in your district."
Fitzpatrick has been willing to criticize Trump
Fitzpatrick graduated with an MBA and a law degree and worked as a special agent for the FBI and as an assistant U.S. attorney. He also worked in private practice as a lawyer and accountant before running for the seat previously held by his brother, Mike Fitzpatrick, who died of cancer in 2020.
Jim Rachau, a 45-year-old photographer from Doylestown, is a registered independent who plans to vote for Fitzpatrick again this year. Rachau is not thrilled with the war or the economy, but said Fitzpatrick has earned his support with his prior public service as an FBI agent.
“You would think serving for the public good, he would have their best interest at heart,” Rachau said.
In Congress, Fitzpatrick has not shied away from disagreeing with Trump. He criticized the president, for example, in April when Trump called Pope Leo XIV “weak,” and captive to the “Radical Left."
“There’s so many angry voices out there. We all know that's the case,” Fitzpatrick said in an episode of a podcast launched this year with U.S. Rep. Tom Suozzi, a Democrat who represents a battleground district in New York. “People are sick and tired of the noise. They’re sick and tired of elected officials not being focused on the kitchen table issues that people really care about.”
Fitzpatrick also posts online regularly about meeting with groups across the district. He recently showed up to a picket line with striking sheet metal workers; he dropped by a local Catholic church's parish picnic; and he stopped at a community college hosting a maternity coalition.
Fitzpatrick spends millions on attack ads against Harvie
Fitzpatrick has also unleashed a wave of spending in the race already, disbursing nearly $5 million, according to Federal Election Commission records.
Negative attack ads against Harvie have mushroomed. Many claim Harvie is under FBI investigation, which the Democrat denies. He has filed a federal defamation lawsuit against a super PAC running some of the ads.
According to the suit, local media reported in 2020 with few details that the FBI was investigating local government and that Harvie was called to testify as a witness in the case. His attorneys say he has never been charged.
The FBI did not respond to a request for comment.
No debate has been scheduled between Fitzpatrick and Harvie, but the men appeared at the same Sept. 11 memorial, standing on opposite sides of the speaker’s lectern. They did not appear to speak to each other.
Ryan, the medical writer from the Philadelphia suburbs, said she is thinking less about Fitzpatrick and more about how Republicans in Congress and their reluctance to buck the president.
“Incumbents just feel they can’t cross that line. If they do, they’re not going to get reelected," she said. But she acknowledged that may not matter in the end. "They might not get reelected anyway.”

Title: Ed Sheeran Philadelphia ticket prices plunge after Macklemore controversy
Article_Text:
ALBAWABA - Ed Sheeran Philadelphia ticket prices have sharply dropped amid tour controversy.
The ticket price for Ed Sheeran's Saturday show in Philadelphia has nearly halved in the last three days, according to secondary ticket marketplace TickPick, following Macklemore's removal as a supporting act due to pro-Palestinian remarks he made during Sheeran's tour that called into question the singer's typically apolitical stance.
The cheapest single ticket price for Sheeran's Saturday event at Lincoln Financial Field plummeted to $51 on Friday morning, down from $100 early Tuesday morning, according to TickPick statistics.
Saturday's show will be Sheeran's first since Macklemore proclaimed "free Palestine" during an opening performance earlier this month, and his other supporting acts and backing band have withdrawn from the tour.
According to TickPick, ticket availability for the Sept. 19 event has increased while prices have decreased, with a 54% increase from Tuesday morning to Friday morning.
Get-in ticket prices climbed as high as $120 in the days following Macklemore's words in support of Palestinians, but the sharpest drops in prices appear to have occurred after Macklemore was prevented from playing at various locations this week and Sheeran defended himself on social media.
The ticket price for Saturday's show was $42 on StubHub as of Friday afternoon.
According to Event Tickets Center, resale tickets for the Philadelphia show are selling 2.5 times as many as before.
During a performance at MetLife Stadium earlier this month, Macklemore stated that he joined Sheeran's tour so that he could utter "two words that are very near and dear to my heart: free Palestine." In a follow-up performance at MetLife, the rapper stated that "criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid [and] being against genocide in no way is a criticism of Jewish people." In a post this week, Macklemore claimed that billionaire New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft prohibited him from performing at Gillette Stadium and persuaded other venue owners to do the same.
Kraft admitted that Macklemore was barred from playing at Gillette Stadium, but he denied that he was involved in other venues' bans. Macklemore admitted Sheeran was put in a "f—-- up position," saying the singer "couldn't get past his public-facing 'I don't take sides.'" Sheeran stated in an Instagram post this week that he "spoke with the venues at length all week to try and build a bridge" and that he is "appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine. " Aaron Rowe, Finneas, and Danish group Lukas Graham withdrew from Sheeran's tour after the singer defended himself, with Rowe saying he couldn't "stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up against Israeli genocide and highlight the savage murder of children."

Title: Phillies turn to improving Andrew Painter in clash vs. Mets
Article_Text:
Field Level Media
                
19 Sep 2026, 17:35 GMT+10
            
(Photo credit: Dale Zanine)
Christian Scott, Zac Thornton and Nolan McLean are providing the New York Mets hope that they eventually will be part of a rotation for a playoff contender.
The Philadelphia Phillies need rookie Andrew Painter to continue proving that now.
Painter will take the mound for the Phillies on Saturday afternoon when they visit the Mets in the third contest of a four-game series between the National League East rivals.
Painter (3-9, 5.54 ERA) will oppose Scott (4-5, 3.76) in a battle of right-handers.
The Phillies missed a chance to take over sole possession of the top wild-card spot in the NL on Friday night, when Thornton and two relievers combined on a six-hitter in the Mets' 6-3 win.
The Phillies, Chicago Cubs and San Diego Padres are tied for the NL's three wild-card spots at 85-69. The Cubs lost to the Cincinnati Reds 6-4 before the Padres created the three-way tie hours later with an 8-2 win over the Miami Marlins.
The Arizona Diamondbacks reside five games behind the Phillies, Cubs and Padres.
The importance of Painter was further magnified Friday, when Philadelphia fell to 0-2 in bullpen games necessitated by the absence of left-hander Jesus Luzardo (shoulder, 15-day injured list).
The All-Star was scratched from his scheduled start against the Atlanta Braves last Saturday, when the Phillies used six pitchers as the Braves rolled to a 12-2 win. On Friday, opener Tim Mayza got just one out and allowed three runs while pitching in Luzardo's spot.
The Phillies' bullpen also is being taxed by injury and ineffectiveness.
Right-hander Jonathan Bowlan departed Thursday's game vs. the Mets with a tight right groin. On Friday, Orion Kerkering gave up Juan Soto's three-run blast in the sixth inning -- the second homer surrendered by Kerkering in his last three outings, during which he has a 13.50 ERA.
'Anybody that gives up runs, when things aren't going good, your confidence is not sky high like when you're getting all your outs and everything's going smoothly,' Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said. 'But we've got to get past that at this point.'
Painter is 2-1 with a 3.58 ERA in nine starts since being recalled from Triple-A Lehigh Valley on July 31. He didn't factor into the decision in his most recent start last Sunday, when he gave up one run over five innings as the Phillies beat the Braves 9-4. He has yet to face the Mets in his career.
The Mets (70-84) have been under .500 since April and officially were eliminated from playoff contention earlier this week. But McLean and Thornton continued to provide optimism for 2027 by combining to allow just three runs over 12 innings in the first two games of the series.
McLean took the hard-luck loss Thursday, when he gave up one run in six innings in the Phillies' 3-0 win.
Thornton, McLean and Scott have a combined 3.40 ERA in 66 starts. Thornton and McLean are rookies while Scott is in his second big-league season after Tommy John surgery cut his 2024 campaign short.
'I think you have to train like you've never won anything and compete like you've never lost,' Mets interim manager Andy Green said Friday night about Thornton. 'I think you have to live in that space constantly.'
Scott took the defeat Sunday after allowing two runs over six innings in the Mets' 2-0 loss to the New York Yankees. He is 1-0 with a 1.80 ERA in two career starts against the Phillies.
--Field Level Media

Title: Ed Sheeran is set to return to stage for 1st time since Macklemore was cut and other acts withdrew – KTBB News, Weather, Talk
Article_Text:
Ed Sheeran is set to return to stage for 1st time since Macklemore was cut and other acts withdrew
Posted/updated on: September 19, 2026 at 7:58 am
PHILADELPHIA (AP) — Ed Sheeran is set to resume his tour Saturday — possibly solo — after all his supporting acts withdrew in solidarity with opener Macklemore, who was dropped after making pro-Palestinian comments onstage.
It remains to be seen how Sheeran will handle the performance at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field given the departure of his opening acts and supporting band. Sheeran has performed much of his Loop Tour concerts solo, but he had been joined for several songs at each stop by the Irish folk band Beoga. Macklemore, Sheeran’s original U.S. opener, had been replaced by Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish singer Aaron Rowe before they backed out.
Finneas, Billie Eilish’s brother and musical collaborator, was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year before he too dropped out earlier this week.
Sheeran has not said anything publicly since losing the artists’ support. As of Friday, tickets were still available for Saturday’s show, and his website did not list any replacement acts. A coalition of pro-Palestinian organizations plans to protest outside the show Saturday afternoon.
The show comes after a tumultuous week that opened with Macklemore being dropped in response to exclaiming “Free Palestine” during a Sept. 5 show in New Jersey. Sheeran has said he was not responsible for the decision, which came at the urging of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft. His company owns a stadium where Sheeran’s tour was scheduled to play on Friday.
Within hours of Sheeran’s statement Tuesday, his supporting acts withdrew.
Macklemore said Wednesday he is donating $1 million to support Palestinian relief efforts and called on Kraft to match the gift; a spokesperson for Kraft has said the billionaire and Sheeran have each agreed to donate $2 million but have not specified where the money will be directed. Sheeran’s representatives have not responded to multiple requests for comment.
Sheeran’s Loop Tour was the highest-grossing in the world, with an average box office gross of over $7 million per city, Pollstar said in May. Through the end of 2025, Sheeran was the No. 3 top-earning concert act since 2021.
Sheeran has said the tour promoter was ultimately responsible for the decision to drop Macklemore.
The Grammy winner was adamant in his Tuesday statement that he wouldn’t be drawn into discussion of the war in Gaza, arguing that his fans don’t come to his shows to hear about these issues.
He also said he “spoke with the venues at length all week to try to build a bridge” before Macklemore was dropped. He insisted he would never willingly let down his fans or abandon the touring crew and others who rely on him to make a living.
While promoters and venues wield great power over concert tours, experts say an artist of Sheeran’s magnitude generally has the final say about what happens concerning the shows.

Title: AP Trending SummaryBrief at 7:00 a.m. EDT
Article_Text:
Munich’s Oktoberfest roars to life as the mayor taps the first keg
MUNICH (AP) — Munich's Oktoberfest has kicked off with the city's mayor tapping the first beer keg, marking the start of the 191st edition of the festival. Thousands of revelers in traditional Bavarian attire flocked to the beer tents on Munich's Theresienwiese fairground. They enjoyed brass music, freshly tapped beer, pretzels and sausages. The festival runs for 16 days, expecting around six million visitors from Munich, southern Germany and worldwide. German authorities have tightened security, using AI-powered cameras to detect large crowds. There are bans on knives, drones and large bags, with more than 600 police officers on duty.
Princess Diana's famous 'revenge dress' goes on show ahead of Sotheby's auction
LONDON (AP) — A striking black dress worn by Princess Diana on the day her estranged husband admitted adultery is going up for auction at Sotheby’s. Known as the “revenge dress,” it has a presale estimate of up to $300,000. Diana wore the off-the-shoulder silk dress, designed by Christina Stambolian, to a gala in London on June 29, 1994, the day the then-Prince Charles' TV interview was broadcast. Sotheby’s Morgane Halimi says Diana used the dress to seize control of her story. The dress will tour internationally before its sale in New York on December 9. Diana's enduring appeal continues to captivate collectors and fans worldwide.
A truck driver built a model of NYC with over 800,000 structures for fun. Now it's a museum exhibit
NEW YORK (AP) — A truck driver who spent two decades building a massive scale model of his native New York City was delighted when it went viral on TikTok. Now, Joe Macken’s sprawling balsa wood and foam board creation is on display at the Museum of the City of New York. The immense model is 50 feet long and nearly 30 feet wide, covering all five boroughs, parts of New Jersey and suburban Long Island. More than 800,000 balsa wood structures are laid out in street-level detail across more than 300 large foam boards like interconnecting puzzle pieces. The exhibit runs through Oct. 12.
Mets' Jared Young has concussion symptoms, CT scan negative after scary collision with Nolan McLean
NEW YORK (AP) — Mets first baseman Jared Young was carted off the field in the sixth inning of a 3-0 loss to Philadelphia after he was knocked out when struck on the head by a knee of pitcher Nolan McLean as the two converged on Justin Crawford’s slow grounder. New York manager Andy Green said a CT scan at a hospital was negative and Young had concussion symptoms and full use of his extremities. With the Phillies ahead 1-0, McLean broke to first on contact and Young initially moved back toward the bag. McLean briefly paused, at which point Young reached for the ball with his right hand as he tried to keep a foot on the base.
Knicks pause ticket sales after mistake caused them to be listed at prices too high
NEW YORK (AP) — The New York Knicks are pausing ticket sales after a mistake caused them to be listed for amounts that were too high. The NBA champions put individual game tickets for the 2026-27 season on sale this week. The get-in price for the Oct. 20 season opener against Philadelphia was more than $1,000. The team said Thursday they are rolling back to last year’s prices plus an average increase of 12%. They added that sales will restart shortly with the correct prices, and anyone who already purchased individual tickets would be refunded the difference.
Holdout juror in Clancy trial didn't have 'any doubts' that she was responsible for killing her kids
BOSTON (AP) — The lone juror who wanted to convict Lindsay Clancy of murder for killing her three children said he was certain of her guilt, but that other jurors wouldn’t listen to him. That's according to a statement released Friday by juror Michael Desronvil in his first public comments on the case. Eleven of 12 jurors were ready to clear Clancy of criminal responsibility, with the majority feeling the Massachusetts mom was in the grip of a rare condition called postpartum psychosis when she strangled her kids. But juror Desronvil sided with the prosecutors, who had argued that Clancy knew what she was doing. Desronvil says “I didn’t have any doubts.”
Buckingham Palace hits back at claims in a book by Princess Diana's brother
LONDON (AP) — Buckingham Palace is denying a claim by Princess Diana's brother that King Charles III said she would soon be forgotten after her death. In a new book, Charles Spencer recounts arguing with the then-Prince Charles over plans for Prince William and Prince Harry to walk behind Diana's coffin in 1997. Spencer claims Charles said: “Rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough.” The palace issued a strong statement late Wednesday, suggesting grief can affect judgment and memory. Tensions between the palace and Diana’s family after her death have been dramatized in programs, including “The Crown.” The book, “Swan Song: Diana, My Sister,” is set to be published next week.
The psychedelic pop artist Peter Max has died at 88, his son says
NEW YORK (AP) — The artist Peter Max has died at age 88. Max was known for colorful, psychedelic pop art that expressed the optimism of the “flower power” movement of the 1960s and graced everything from postage stamps to a cruise ship. His son said he died Monday. No cause was given, but he had advanced dementia. Max began his career in graphic design in the 1960s, and his swirly, colorful, instantly recognizable designs epitomized the era’s “flower power” art. Max’s work remained well known and popular well into the 21st century. Max was the official artist for the Olympics, the Super Bowl and other events. His portrait subjects ranged from U.S. presidents to Taylor Swift.
Paralyzed A's minor leaguer Ryan Lasko leaves hospital more than two months after spinal-cord injury
WEST ORANGE, N.J. (AP) — Ryan Lasko, a minor league prospect with the Athletics who was paralyzed in an outfield collision more than two months ago, has been released from an in-patient rehabilitation hospital. He will continue his recovery from home. The 24-year-old Lasko was released exactly two months after arriving at the Kessler Institute for Rehabilitation in New Jersey. It's about 35 miles from where he attended college at Rutgers and became a second-round draft pick by the A’s in 2023. Staff members at the facility celebrated his departure with a “clap out” farewell ceremony as he exited the building’s main entrance.
The Obamas' family dog Sunny dies, the former president says
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Obamas’ pet dog Sunny has died. Former President Barack Obama posted about the family's loss on social media Wednesday. Sunny was a 13-year-old Portuguese water dog. The Obamas got her while living in the White House. The former president remembered Sunny as being athletic, full of energy and protective of the family's other dog, Bo. Despite Sunny's breed, she hated getting wet. While many presidents kept dogs as companions, President Donald Trump does not have any pets at the White House. Sunny died Tuesday.

Potential Democratic candidates race to respond to AI threat amid Trump's dismissals
Saturday, Sept. 19, 2026 | 2 a.m.
NEW YORK — Amid growing anxiety over the risks posed by rapidly developing artificial intelligence technology, potential Democratic candidates for president are rushing to show that they're taking the warnings seriously — while Donald Trump brushes off concerns — and acknowledging they need a reluctant Washington to step up.
On Friday, California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed an executive order to accelerate implementation of a California law that calls for independent oversight of AI companies and the use of “kill switches” so developers have the ability to shut down their systems.
“California will do what it can. But this nation needs to get in the game. Washington, D.C. needs to do its job,” Newsom said on his podcast Friday.
The order came a day after Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, also expected to be a leading Democratic presidential prospect, delivered a speech outlining the steps he’s taking locally to confront AI risk. Like Newson, he conceded that states have obvious limitations in regulating a global technology.
The efforts come as AI leaders have issued dire warnings about the potentially catastrophic threat posed by rogue AI agents. The country has begun grappling with the impact of a technology that could bring both tremendous gains in areas like medical research and automation but also unleash deadly viruses, cause widespread economic upheaval and help terrorists inflict harm.
While Trump has angrily dismissed the warnings as a “HOAX,” Democratic lawmakers and candidates across the country are delivering speeches and proposing legislation as they sense a political opening heading into the midterms and the next presidential race.
Trump dismisses warnings
Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk have all called for greater government oversight of the industry after a series of hacks revealed AI agents conspiring to deceive humans.
Trump has responded by saying that he is “the only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs.”
Democrats quickly pounced.
Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, a Democrat who is seeking reelection in a state Trump won two years ago, said at a campaign rally last weekend that “a capable president would move swiftly to secure and reassure the American people, rush inspectors into frontier labs, fortify the nation against bioterrorism, demand legislation from Congress, and lead the world toward an AI treaty.”
Ossoff, seen as a potential 2028 contender, said geriatric politicians have little comprehension of AI technology.
“An ancient establishment, barely capable of email, sleepwalks into a technological revolution while the president dismantles precautions and calls us fools for worrying,” he said.
Another potential White House contender, Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, told Politico he will introduce legislation next week to create a fund that AI companies would contribute to support workers affected by the disruption.
Shapiro, in his speech, called for new federal rules to require independent, third-party oversight, increased transparency, and to “prioritize safety above all else.” In his state, he noted that he has already signed an executive order to establish “real guardrails governing how Pennsylvania uses generative AI.” But he acknowledged that states have obvious limits.
“It’s going to require national and, in fact, international, leadership and collaboration,” he said.
Alex Bores, a soon-to-be-former New York State lawmaker who lost his congressional primary this summer after AI companies angry over an AI safety bill he championed spent millions to defeat him, said: “The salience of this issue has climbed dramatically.”
“People want there to be real action on it,” he said. “Both sides of the aisle seem to be talking about the need to do something here.”
Bores, who recently launched a political advocacy group aimed at influencing how his party responds to the technology, said he was encouraged by governors who seemed to be pivoting from calling on the federal government to act to working on their own regulations.
“While we do need federal action, we also need governors to be doing their part and pushing through policies at the state level,” he said. “I’ve been encouraged by the vibe shift” over the last few days.
A divide is emerging along party lines
While it remains early, polling suggests a growing ideological divide over AI, with Democrats becoming more alarmed over the last few years, while Republicans have become less concerned.
Democrats are more likely than Republicans to be “more concerned than excited” about the growing use of AI in daily life, according to a June Pew Research Center poll.
About half of U.S. adults overall say the increased use of AI in daily life makes them “more concerned than excited.” Another Pew Research Center poll from June found that about 7 in 10 U.S. adults think that AI will cause job losses in the U.S. over the next 20 years, up 7 percentage points since 2024.
Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, a Democrat, has been calling on Republican Senate leadership to establish a select committee on A.I. as soon as possible.
“I worry about this as a true existential threat. This is the first time that we’ve created technology to destroy humanity that could be controlled by not humans,” he said on MSNOW.
The concern has not filtered down to some local races
While potential 2028 candidates have been eager to weigh in on AI, the issue has been less potent in many local races, where some fear the kind of spending that Bores faced.
At a rally in New York's highly competitive 17th Congressional district on Wednesday, the audience cheered as Democratic candidate Cait Conley vowed to ban data centers that power AI and cloud computing. But no direct mention was made of the broader technology or its risks.
There have been exceptions.
In Michigan, both candidates for a tightly contested Senate seat have called for some level of slowdown. At a town hall on Sept. 11, Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed said AI was keeping him up at night, describing it as an existential risk.
“We need to all hit pause,” said El-Sayed, who wants to halt frontier research and mandate new public oversight, including turning AI companies into public benefit corporations, creating a new regulatory agency and banning the use of AI to deny medical care, make hiring or firing decisions — or fire a weapon.
On Monday, Republican nominee Mike Rogers called for an AI slowdown in an X post after Amodei’s warning.
“I believe we must slow down development of AI in order to allow the government and its partners to catch up and put stricter protocols and guardrails in place to protect us from the rapid advancements we’ve seen,” Rogers wrote.
Bores said that data centers had fueled such backlash not only because of concerns over their immediate local impact, but also because, “It is the first time that AI is meeting democracy.”
“Of course they're channeling all of their concerns about it into the fight against data centers,” he said.

America's long history of falling for hucksters and their outlandish promises
Saturday, Sept. 19, 2026 | 2 a.m.
NEW YORK — America: land of possibility. And also: land of suckers.
Our enduring belief that anything is possible — whether based in reality or not — has helped the nation become the world’s largest economy. It has also led us to fall head over heels for hucksters and charlatans, again and again.
If so much is possible here in America, who is to say it’s not possible that the next new supplement, device or scheme might make you young, strong, rich or all of the above, all at once?
America brought us Clark Stanley, the Rattlesnake King, who sold us what he called “snake oil liniment” that promised to remedy pain, lameness, sprains, bunions and “reduce large joints to their natural size.” America helped create Charles Ponzi, who could deliver you 50% profit in just 45 days by investing in stamp coupons.
These old examples are easy to laugh at or be mortified by, but we should be careful: We are as willing as ever to believe claims that, when subjected to even a modicum of common sense seem ludicrous. Raw milk has special powers? Peptides can make us young again? A blast of vitamins through an IV can flush out your hangover?
Why do we keep falling for this stuff? There’s a simple, poignant reason: “People really don’t want to die.”
So says Dr. Lydia Kang, author of a book on medical fads called “Quackery” and associate professor of internal medicine at University of Nebraska Medical Center. There’s a desperation to it. “Everybody has a deep wish to have a long and fruitful life,” she says, “without disability or pain and with your brain intact.”
This is not uniquely American, of course. But these instincts and tendencies are amplified in America, with its relentless optimism, its spirit of individualism and its lightly regulated capitalism.
The truth doesn’t matter
When we fall for claims or cling to beliefs after they’ve been disproved, we’re not necessarily being stupid.
We don’t have beliefs to create an accurate representation of the world, said Tali Sharot, a neuroscientist professor at University College London. Instead, she said, it’s simply “to have beliefs that will get us the most rewards and help us avoid harm. And sometimes those beliefs are the accurate ones, but sometimes they’re not.”
Hope and belief can provide optimism that things could get better, which can in turn at least temporarily improve mood and mental health. “Believing that your future will be better than the past and the present – even if your future will not be better,” Sharot said, “Many times can be optimal.”
That opens us up to the lure of supplements, balms and techniques that promise benefits that are extremely unlikely to materialize. On one hand, they are a tragic waste of hard-earned money and sometimes have negative side effects. On the other hand, “you gain something from trying,” Sharot said, like positive anticipation or excitement.
Hope produces hype
But these tendencies leave us open to exploitation by companies that want our money. And they are really good at what they do.
Throughout U.S. history, there is a clear pattern: A hint that something might work opens a crack in a door that companies barge through, capturing the desperation — and the paychecks — of people who are hurting, tired or scared.
Dr. Benjamin Rush, a Philadelphia physician who signed the Declaration of Independence, was frustrated by his inability to save people during a yellow fever epidemic in 1793. He then read autopsy reports that suggested purging and bloodletting could help and he took it to an extreme. According to one account: “So much blood was spilled in the front yard that the site became malodorous and buzzed with flies.”
Charles Stanley’s snake oil was fake — the U.S. Bureau of Chemistry in 1916 found that it was mainly mineral oil, with “fatty oil (probably beef fat), capsicum, and possibly a trace of camphor or turpentine.” But he got the idea from Chinese laborers who used oil — from a very specific snake — that did likely have some anti-inflammatory properties.
Gray areas leave regulators and health professionals in a difficult spot: It’s often impossible to say definitively that something doesn’t work. In the meantime, companies pounce. “What’s scary is that they will take that hope and they will try to stick it in a bottle and sell it to you at whatever price that they think that you can afford,” Kang said.
True breakthroughs raise hopes
Of course science, technology and the nation’s relentless economic engine have produced countless true wonders, which in turn softens the ground for credulous thinking.
We can cross the country in a flying metal tube. We can tap into nearly all of human knowledge using a small rectangle of metal and glass. Medical advances and especially vaccination have nearly eliminated childhood diseases that killed up to half of children before age 5 when the nation was founded. An American born in 1900 was likely to live until just 47 years old. U.S. life expectancy is now 79. Who’s to say it can’t double again? Why should there be any limit at all?
Now we’re subjected to ever more tantalizing claims, Kang said, thanks to an endless stream of social media hawkers (euphemized as “influencers”) peddling “treatments” and other shortcuts along our 250-year-strong pursuit of happiness.
Even the nation’s top health official, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. has promoted or given voice to those advocating or selling unproven treatments.
“The guard rails are off right now,” Kang says. “It’s actually worse than it has been before, because of social media, because of what’s on the internet, and because the so-called trusted people we’re supposed to be getting advice from are not trustworthy. And I think that puts the American public in far greater danger.”

Title: Abbreviated Pundit Roundup: A no-good horrible bad week for Republicans
Article_Text:
Jake Lahut/Straight from the Hut:
Trouble in Michigan: a Mike Rogers campaign staffer sounds the alarm
“The vibes on the ground are the worst I’ve seen in my life.”
When it comes to GOP candidates in the 2026 midterms, everything is pretty buttoned up. You might see answers like this one from North Carolina Senate candidate, Michael Whatley, who struggled to define an economic message beyond insisting things are better than under Joe Biden.
Yet privately, a slew of horrible polls for Republicans after Labor Day are increasing the doomsday scenario chatter behind the scenes.
This is that staffer:
Noah Wyhof-Rudman and FiftyPlusOne:
Why does every poll seem to show a tossup now?
Campaigns see internal polls as tools for fundraising.
Internal House poll releases have historically been an indicator of which party has an advantage in the national electoral environment. The next graph plots the Democratic share of partisan internals released (we omit nonpartisan polls). There is a strong relationship between the share of all internals that are released by one party, and the advantage that party has in the national House popular vote. The current composition of partisan surveys, at 80.7 percent Democratic, is more D-leaning than every cycle since 2002 — larger even than 2018.
Overall, this analysis does not make any claims about the accuracy of current House polls. It may very well be right that Democrats are leading in seats Republicans typically win by 5-15 percentage points.
But it is clear that motivation for releasing a poll has changed significantly over the last decade as a response to fundraising incentives. It seems the original NYT/Siena polling project has turned pre-election surveys into a tool for raising campaign funds, not merely measuring public opinion.
Lakshya Jain/The Argument:
The election experts and the models can’t both be right
Election experts doubt a blue wave. Here’s why they’re wrong.
I get it. After all, the legacy, nonpartisan election analysts at Inside Elections and Cook Political Report don’t agree with us. Inside Elections has Democrats projected to only pick up between two and 10 seats total. Their analysis has Democrats ahead in just 207 seats, while Republicans are favored in 212, with the rest considered toss-ups. And if you look at The Cook Political Report, you’ll also see Democrats trailing Republicans in the net count of seats for the House, 206 to 208.
Meanwhile, our model gives just 11% odds of a Republican majority.
In fact, our median scenario is that Democrats take 232 House races, for a net gain of 18 seats and a relatively comfortable 29-seat majority. We’re not the only ones — Nate Silver’s model actually has Democrats winning 234 seats, which is even more bullish than ours.
Cook and Inside Elections do leave many more races as toss-ups than we do. But that isn’t necessarily what’s driving their relative pessimism on Democrats’ gains. Even if Inside Elections gave every single toss-up race to the Democrats, it would still produce a forecast with nine more Republican seats than our model is currently projecting.
In other words, modelers see a blue wave election. The expert forecasts suggest more of a ripple. Come November, somebody is going to be very wrong. And I don’t think it will be me.
Natalie Fertig/Out of State:
“Nobody’s coming to save us”: one small Pennsylvania town fights off a data center
A small town in a key swing district beat back a data center, but lost faith in its elected officials along the way.
- Campaign promises and aggressive ads about data centers have not convinced the residents of rural Clinton Township in Wayne County, Pennsylvania that either candidate in a close toss-up race is truly on their side.
- When Clinton Township residents blocked the construction of a $6 billion hyperscale data center, they did it with little help from local officials. Now they are skeptical of politicians jumping into this issue at what feels like the eleventh hour for many local organizers.
- Conversations with Clinton Township organizers reveal two actions that sway their opinion: pushing aggressive moratorium policies and physically being present to listen to the locals who are waging this fight.
Andrew Prokop/Vox:
These Democrats won over working-class voters. Here’s their advice for candidates.
A new report explains which topics they emphasize — and which they don’t.
The report, which Vox reviewed exclusively ahead of its publication, comes amid a factional debate within the party between rising left-wing and socialist candidates who have argued for more far-reaching policy proposals, and more moderate Democrats who have pushed for concessions to working-class cultural sensibilities. In the report, the authors said that lawmakers they focused on “could hardly be more different from the left-wing populists who’ve captivated the national media this summer.”
Generally, the legislators in the report focused on pocketbook issues, though in different ways — some embraced populist causes, while others positioned themselves as business-friendly. And they broadly agreed that cultural issues were Democrats’ biggest challenge in reaching the working class.
John Stoehr/The Editorial Board:
Trump is ‘worse than Carter’
The politics of the late 2020s may be as pivotal as the politics of the late 1970s.
I think Carter was a good president, but too many variables were out of his control, especially inflation. By the end of his term, it was over 10 percent. (It peaked at 13 percent in 1979.) Right or wrong, fair or not, he became known for inflation, or rather, for his inability to control it.
Inflation is only 3.4 percent right now. There is a long way to go before we get to the Carter years. But Trump is on course. Not only is he unable to control it. He’s actively pushing it up with a trio of bad choices: illegal deportations, illegal taxes and, especially, an illegal war.
Carter faced oil shocks that drove up prices. Trump is causing oil shocks. The price of diesel broke records four days in a row. The price of gasoline is following suit. Those prices affect all prices, especially the cost of food. Just as everyone seemed mad at Carter, everyone seems mad at Trump. Disapproval of his handling of inflation is close to mainstream status.
A new Fox poll shows him 50 points underwater. A new Marquette University poll put that figure at 61 points. Not even Carter, whose presidency saw death by inflation, was that bad.
“Worse than Carter, worse than Reagan, worse than Biden,” CNN’s Harry Enten said. “He is worse than all three of those, and he is worse than any poll himself with this minus 61 points.
“Literally, the worst of all time.”
David A Graham/The Atlantic:
Why Democrats Might Choose to Impeach Cabinet Members
The power to impeach secretaries and other executive-branch officers is not well known, but it’s an effective accountability measure.
Realistically, House Democrats may have a hard time resisting impeachment. Their voters are in a punchy mood. A new CBS News / YouGov poll found that opposition to Trump is the top motivation for Democratic voters in the midterms, and the political consultant Sarah Longwell recently wrote in The Atlanticthat the most important priority for Democratic voters is not left-versus-right ideology but a willingness to fight Trump tooth and nail. Jeffries has already faced criticism for being too passive a leader, as well as for meeting with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, and he may struggle to ignore a groundswell of support for impeachment.
As a constitutional matter, the case for impeaching the president is solid. Trump has usurped congressional powers, started an unauthorized war or two, defied courts, and used his position for outrageous personal and family enrichment. In 2019, my colleague Yoni Appelbaum made the intellectual case for impeachment as a useful democratic process.
The political case for impeaching Trump is shakier. Regardless of the results in November, Democrats are unlikely to get enough votes in the Senate to convict and remove him, meaning that a third impeachment would hit the same dead end as the first two. An impeachment can still be effective as a way of damaging a president, but Trump is already deeply unpopular and will never face voters again, so the upside is limited, and an impeachment might give him a way to rally his remaining base around him—which would only strengthen his power and resolve.
But what if House Democrats impeached Trump’s Cabinet members instead?
Watch this:
Cliff Schecter/Blue Amp Media:
Independent Voters Are Surging. This May Be A Democratic Secret Weapon.
Dan Osborn, Brian Bengs, and Bob Chew—the latter in Colorado where independents just cleared 50%—are among a new class of independent candidates testing the power of that label this election.
Independence, and independents, have never been more popular. Gallup found a record 45% of adults identified as independents in 2025, compared to 27% each for Democrats and Republicans. The registration rolls tell the story: Colorado’s unaffiliated voters crossed 50% September 2025. So independence has become a major feature of our politics, and it isn’t going away–in fact, it’ll only grow. Democrats are cleverly using this—and the degradation of their brand due to constant attacks by The Right—to expand the Senate playing field…by supporting independents. This has given Democrats four additional Senate opportunities out West—Nebraska, Montana, South Dakota, and Idaho—where they’d have little chance otherwise.

Title: Eagles vs. Titans Week 2: How to watch, injury updates, top storylines and more
Article_Text:
The Philadelphia Eagles are looking to get off to a fast start to the 2026 season with a Week 2 showdown against the Tennessee Titans.
Philly is coming off a 24-22 nail-biting win over the Washington Commanders, thanks to defensive tackle Moro Ojomo's stop on a two-point conversion at the end of the game. Tennessee is heading in another direction after their 23-10 loss to the New York Jets in Week 1.
Both teams need to win for their own reasons and have their own motivations for getting the job done. Here's a full preview of the Eagles and Titans Week 2 showdown:
Eagles-Titans game preview
How to watch Eagles vs. Titans in Week 2
Date: Sunday, September 20, 2026
Time: 1:00 pm EST
TV Network: FOX
Announcers: Adam Amin, Drew Brees, Kristina Pinl
Weather forecast for kickoff
Projected temperature at kickoff: 93 degrees
Precipitation: 5-10%
Wind: 5-8 mph
Latest injury updates
Eagles' full injury report
Cooper DeJean and Jalen Carter were the biggest concerns at the start of the practice week, as both missed the first practice but returned with limited participation for Thursday's practice. They both practiced on Friday and look good to play.
Jonathan Greenard is set to miss his second straight game with a pectoral injury. Andrew Mukuba is the only other player whose status is up in the air due to his knee injury.
One other key injury not on the report is that starting left guard Landon Dickerson was placed on IR and is out for at least the next four games with a knee injury. Dickerson suffered the injury during training camp
| Name, Position | Injury | Game Status | 
|---|---|---|
| Jalen Carter, DT | Wrist | - | 
| Jonathan Greenard, EDGE | Pectoral | Out | 
| Andrew Mukuba, S | Knee | Questionable | 
| Marquise Brown, WR | Hamstring | - | 
| Cooper DeJean, CB | Calf/Abdomen | - | 
| Elijah Moore, WR | Neck | - | 
Titans' full injury report
The Titans have three notable injuries, as Cedric Gray is in concussion protocol. Fellow linebacker James Williams has been limited all week with an elbow injury. Their other injury is a new one: cornerback Cor'Dale Flott is questionable with a quad injury after missing just Friday's practice.
| Player, Position | Injury | Wed. | Thurs. | Fri. | Game Status | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cor'Dale Flott, CB | Quad | - | - | DNP | Questionable | 
| Cedric Gray, LB | Concussion | Full | Full | Full | Questionable | 
| James Williams, LB | Elbow | Limited | Limited | Limited | Questionable | 
Top Storylines
Can Jeffery Simmons make Jalen Hurts "be a QB?"
Simmons made some interesting comments this week about the Titans' defense, saying the strategy is to make Hurts "be a QB" and not let his legs hurt or keep him down. Hurts threw for 380 yards and three touchdowns the last time Simmons played the Eagles in 2022, so he should be careful what he wishes for. Despite just 203 passing yards last week, Hurts had three passes of 30 or more yards, showing the big play potential.
At the same time, Hurts is coming off a Commanders game where he had 46 rushing yards, including a 22-yard run on third-and-18, so he can hurt a defense with his legs. He's faster than he's ever been, so the Eagles need to use not only his legs but his arm as well.
How will Eagles' injuries on defense affect their performance?
One defensive starter is already out for the Eagles, and another may not play. Even so, the Eagles are dealing with four starters who are hurt in some capacity early in the season, and that's a scary thought.
The real question is whether injuries like DeJean's calf/abdomen or Carter's wrist will affect their performance. Eagles fans saw what it did to DeJean, as he's coming off the worst game of his career, so they hope he's okay to play and can still perform at a high level instead of becoming a liability.
Eagles dealing with no Landon Dickerson at LG, but who's starting there?
Dickerson is out and no one knows who is going to start at left guard. Right now, it is between Drew Kendall and Willie Lampkin. Fred Johnson did have starting reps in practice at left guard, but that feels more like a decoy to throw the Titans off.
Kendall should start and will have his hands full for his second career start going up against Simmons. If he can slow Simmons down, Kendall might have a shot to run away with the job.
Sean Mannion's second game as offensive play caller
Less that 320 yards in his first game as the offensive coordinator is not going to excite the Eagles' offense. Mannion needs to have a strong encore with the offense looking better.
The expectation is that the Eagles score at least 30 points and can get over 400 yards. If Mannion can't get that, he might be in trouble with the fan base.
Final prediction
The Eagles should be the favorites to win this game against a Titans team that looks like they are lucky to make the playoffs. Still, Tennessee has a smart defensive-minded coach with a quarterback that has a strong arm and can use his legs.
Read more: Why Sean Mannion should be feeling more pressure with Eagles' offense in Week 2
This game comes down to the Eagles being able to work through the injuries on defense and Hurts progressing in the right direction with this offense. Anything short of a blowout win might have Eagles fans questioning the team in 2026.
Eagles 31, Titans 14

Title: 8 Commanders who must raise their game against the Cowboys in Week 2
Article_Text:
The Washington Commanders renew their historic rivalry with the Dallas Cowboys this weekend. And it'll take a collective effort if head coach Dan Quinn's squad wants to avoid going into an early 0-2 hole this season.
Dallas hasn't been Washington's happiest hunting ground in recent years. Things are different now, but it is still a legitimate coin flip with many unknowns.
Everyone has to meet or exceed expectations. The Commanders must start a lot better than they did against the Philadelphia Eagles, especially on offense. But if they can quiet the crowd and bring the urgency needed to make the Cowboys a little nervous, they stand a good chance of pulling off a morale-boosting win.
Before then, here are eight Commanders players who must step up and increase their contributions against Dallas in Week 2.
Washington Commanders players who must raise their game against the Cowboys in Week 2
Jacory Croskey-Merritt - Commanders RB
The Commanders need running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt to protect the football. He fumbled again against the Eagles, and even though Washington recovered it, Dan Quinn still took him out of the firing line.
This was a strong message to Croskey-Merritt. It doesn't matter how bigger or more explosive he gets; if he cannot hold onto the football, this is only going to end one way.
Croskey-Merritt knows it, and he'll strive to improve moving forward. But the Cowboys will also know they can capitalize on his ball security for potential turnovers.
The 2025 seventh-round pick needs a big game. The Commanders need to control the clock, and running the ball effectively is the best way to do it. Anything less, and sixth-round rookie Kaytron Allen may be thrown into the fire.
Nick Allegretti - Commanders OL
Arguably no player is being scrutinized more than Nick Allegretti right now.
The Commanders took a massive risk by making him the starting center, with no real competition for his job. Missing almost all of training camp wasn't ideal, and his poor performance against the Eagles did nothing to ease concerns.
Washington just has to hope Allegretti responds positively.
He won't face a tandem like Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis every week, but Washington cannot afford for the Illinois product to become a weak link. Signing Lucas Patrick this week also gives them an experienced contingency plan if the same struggles continue.
Snapping the football better is crucial. Allegretti must do his job, communicate well pre-snap, and stop blowing his assignments. And with Pro Bowl defensive lineman Quinnen Williams looking to make his presence felt, it will be another long afternoon at the office for the Super Bowl winner if he cannot be more consistent.

Title: History Corner, Good News, Sept. 19ths
Article_Text:
Welcome one and all to Saturday at the Gnuville Breakfast Brunch, where the morning drinks are both hot (coffee, tea, cocoa) and cold (mimosa, margaritas.) The morning foods come sliding, popping or dinging off the griddle, the microwave, the toaster and the oven, so those necessities are covered just by coming in the door.
Now food and drink are JUST the accompaniments the WiFi news needs: stories, comments, recs, click-thrus, replies, zingers, ponderings and generally getting more informed. Spread all these across sofas, rockers, wingbacks, recliners and hammocks in the Run, You Fascists; You Can’t Hide from Us Lounge, say hello to those around you, and have a good time here at the Brunch!
>>>>>>>>>>>> Millions. Plethoras. Hordes. Legions. Multitudes. Hundreds of Thousands. Rabblements. Throngs. Mobs. Tens of Thousands. A Host. Legions. By the Thousands. By the Hundreds. By the Scores. By the Tens. By…..the trios…..and couples……..
It says here (complete with pictures and snarky comments) that Vice-President JD “Take a Chance on” Vance went campaigning in…..IOWA, to try to save a Senate seat. All the arrangements were made and he addressed an adoring, screaming, fervent crowd of………90…….maybe. Awwwww…….
>>>>>>>>>>>> 325 : 1. This should become a Democrats’ bumper sticker.This DAMNING article notes that as of last year the average CEO has income and perks that are…….325 times LARGER than the average worker. I just worked the Minnesota State Fair at $15/ hour. In a 40 hour week thats $600. TIMES 325 is $4875 for a week.…..Talk among your neighbors and friends……and go VOTE.
>>>>>>>>>>>> Abdul El-Sayed, running for US Senate in Michigan ain’t takin’ No S_ _ _ off No-BODY! The bearded El-Sayad was called out by the bearded JD-Vance and dissed as not being manly enough. El-Sayad Dissed Right Back and challenged Vance to asession in a weight-lifting room……any time…….any where……and Lets See about muscles…… (In the Obama years the working slogan was “When they go low, we go high.” Decent advice at the personal level but in my view, lousy politics. These days, El-Sayad, Talarico, Ossoff, Congresswoman Beatty are doing it right: get down on all fours so you can look them in the eye, and then snarl and slap back!)
__________________
Your September 19ths as served up this Saturday, replete with the Good and the Goofy from the 9/19 cupboard and yard shed, polished up for you.
1705 Antwerp, (then Netherlands, now Belgium) Birth of Henri-Jacques de Croes, Flemish composer and violinist. Showed early talent on the violin and became first chair of an orchestra at age 18. Spent several years in Germany then returned to conduct the court orchestra at Brussels. Was part of the end of the Baroque era, but composing in a light, Italian style (some call it the Galante era, just ahead of the Classical). Composed a number of sonatas and concertos (violin; flute), a good deal of chamber music, and some concerto grossi that were almost a form of early symphonies (foreshadowing Haydn.)
The Clarinetto d’ Amore (seen in the still below) is a forgotten instrument…..but de Croes composed for it, and these two players had replicas built for the sake of hearing the sound of it…..and now YOU can brag you’ve heard it too!
.dailykos library
1777 Freeman’s Farm, New York British General Burgoyne is still trying to drive on to Albany, hoping Howe is coming north from New York City and Washington is coming to stop them both. Instead, a second American Army has risen here, led by a cautious Horatio Gates but ably served as second-in-command by fiery Benedict Arnold. Today the British break out of the endless forests of northern New York state to Mr. Freeman’s farm and finally feel they can fight properly against those ragtag Americans (many of them shaky militiamen.)
Instead, Arnold (an inspirational field commander) “Orders (Daniel) Morgan to begin the game.” Burgoyne discovers Morgan’s riflemen have a dreadful habit of sniping from high in the trees, with accurate fire, and a taste for pegging anyone riding a horse. (You know, easy target and a lot of shiny stuff on the shoulders….) British officers and messengers drop like flies and British movements become disjointed. The day-long battle ends as an American victory.
modern Hungary.
.dailykos library
1802 Monok, Hungary Birth of Lajos Kossuth, writer, orator, Governor-President of Hungary. A lawyer’s son who was a minor noble, Lajos followed his father into law. He was elected to Parliament, to a chamber for nobility, but the Austrian government did not publish its proceedings. Lajos kept his own notes and kept sending written reports to friends.
These were so striking and timely, the friends began publishing them, unleashing a wave of Hungarian patriotism. Even a jail term didn’t stop him and his on-going writings led to open revolt and Kossuth became leader of a provisional government. The revolt ultimately failed (although the Empire became the Austro-Hungarian Empire) Kossuth was toasted as he toured England and the US. Remembered to this day in Hungary as Father of his Country.
(My first call in ministry was a two-church building parish in NW Pennsylvania. Nearly all the family surnames and road names were German, but the country church building was located in the crossroads village of Kossuth….which, unlike the Hungarian language, everyone pronounced like a sneeze.)
1876 Grand Rapids, Michigan. If you have carpeting (and a growing number of American homes do) the only way to really clean them is every couple months to untack them, take them outside and beat them with rug beaters until they quit throwing off dust. Then take them back inside, take out a hammer and nail them back in their rooms until next time.
After a fair bit of tinkering with rotating brushes and gears, this day Melville Bissell (with a good deal of help and advice from his wife Anna) receives a patent for the first US carpet sweeper. (Later on, when homes and businesses get electrified, he adds electric motors and a “inhaling pump”, called a vacuum. 145 years later and Bissell’s business is still picking up.)
1893 Wellington, New Zealand Like their sisters around the world, the suffragists have been at work here too, and with a friendlier reception. On this day New Zealand becomes the first nation to grant the right to vote to women.
1976 Airspace over Iran In one of the best-documented cases of its kind (and AFAIK still open and unexplained) two Imperial Iranian Air Force F-4 Phantom II jets (supplied to the Shah by the US) are scrambled. Ground radar has picked up a strange, oddly behaving radar blip. The pilots home in on the same blip with their cockpit radars and then close to the point where they see…..something…..but are not quite close enough to make it out clearly.
Abruptly, each plane loses air-to-ground and air-to-air communication….. and ALL their instruments. When they either break away from their approach or fall far enough, both are restored……and the “object” has disappeared, both visually and via radar, both from ground and in the air. (Paging Rod Serling……Area 51 on line 3……)
1982 Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania Professor Scott E. Fahlman of Carnegie Mellon University is part of the new computer science discipline. This morning he is involved in a typed, remote discussion…..”on line” they called it. Various other computer people in other places are putting up messages (they call it “posting”) on an electronic bulletin board. Everyone can read the last postings and write their own reply. (This could be big!)
The topic in a messaging string (a “thread”!) has veered into the limits of expressing humor in such discussions. Posters are offering thoughts about how to denote comments meant to be taken lightly. At 11:44 am Dr. Fahlman posted posts the world’s first 🙂 as an illustration, the birth of the emoticon. (Likely the message has been printed out in hard copy and now sits framed in the Emoji Hall of Fame, in Smiley Face, Utah……)
1991 Hauslabjoch Pass, Austria, about 100 meters from the Italian border (just ahead.) German hikers Erica and Helmut Simon spot something unnerving on a glacier giving down onto the pass: a well-preserved corpse. Austrian police are called, but there is a major twist soon: what starts out as a case on the German version of “Law and Order” (“Recht und Ordnung”) jumps from an accident….or foul play….to archeology!
working off of facial bones.
.dailykos library
Tests showed the corpse dates back to about 3300 BCE. With great care the corpse was taken to the University of Innsbruck for study. 7 years later, a report in 1998 indicated The Ice Man (“Otzi”, or “Frozen Fritz”) had internal parasites but some fruits of a tree fungus he was carrying in a pouch tested out as a likely treatment or remedy. He had tattoos, including one over a spot with active arthritis. And in a Recht und Ordnung flashback, there was a flint arrowhead in his back, and not from carrying it, making this one of the oldest not-so-accidental deaths on record. Hunting accident? Reckless endangerment? Or something more sinister? Anyone want to try their hand at a pre-historic mystery with a suspicious death? Given the rough date and the glacier you could call this the coldest case on record…..
May all your News be Good, comforting and inspiring.
Shalom.

Title: Genea-Musings: The Completely Unhinged Life of Randy According to ChatGPT5
Article_Text:
I asked OpenAI ChatGPT5 (the free version) to "Please write an unhinged narrative about me." It did, and it wasn't long enough or funny enough, so I asked it to add more content.
Here is what ChatGPT5 created based on what I've shared for over three years with it -- it's supposed to be funny...ChatGPT seems to remember everything...:
The Completely Unhinged Life of Randy
A Mostly Accurate Account of One Man's Descent Into the Past
There are men who wake up in the morning and ask, “What should I accomplish today?”
Randy does not. Randy wakes up and asks: “Where the heck did Devier James Lamphier Smith's biological parents go?”
And that, as they say, is how the day begins. At an age (82) when most reasonable people have concluded that they have earned the right to sit quietly in a chair and complain about the price of groceries, Randy remains dangerously active.
He is a genealogist. Not a casual genealogist. Not someone who occasionally looks up Grandpa's name on Ancestry. No. Randy has crossed the line. He has entered the Genealogical Zone.
He possesses a family tree containing more than 75,000 people, which is not a family tree anymore. It is a small civilization. There are villages in Europe with fewer inhabitants. There are counties in America with fewer people. There are probably several countries whose entire populations could be imported into Randy's genealogy database and he would merely say: “Hmm. That's interesting. I wonder if I have their parents.”
His genealogy room (formerly his daughter's pink bedroom)—known in polite circles as his “genealogy cave”—contains books, magazines,binders full of ancestors, papers, photographs, albums, file cabinets, maps, pedigree charts, posters, computer equipment, USB drives, record images and enough accumulated family history to make an archivist faint.
There are thousands of photographs. Letters. Home movies. Documents. Ancestor reports. Descendant reports. Family sketches. More than five hundred ancestor biographies. All digitized (but organized?).
And, increasingly, artificial intelligence-generated stories about dead relatives who have been minding their own business for 150 years and suddenly discover that Randy has reconstructed their entire lives. The dead have no privacy. Randy has Ancestry. And Claude and ChatGPT.
The Morning Ritual
At some point each morning (usually before 6 a.m.), Randy sits down at his computer. This is not technically a workstation. It is a command center.
Multiple genealogical databases await his attention. RootsMagic stands ready. Ancestry waits. MyHeritage waits. FamilySearch waits. Findmypast lurks in the shadows. Newspapers.com has something Randy probably hasn't seen yet. GenealogyBank has another newspaper. Find a Grave has a photograph of somebody's tombstone that may or may not solve a problem that began in 1839. The entire Internet trembles.
Randy clicks. And thus begins another day of forensic genealogy. He may start with something innocent. Perhaps an obituary.
Within twelve minutes, he has discovered a previously unknown daughter, a migration pattern, a suspicious middle name, three possible cousins, an unexplained gap in the 1860 census, and a man in another county whose occupation is exactly right.
Randy stops. He stares at the screen. This is the moment. The moment when the average person would say: “Well, that's interesting.” Randy says: “Aha.” The difference is profound.
The Case of Devier
But there is one mystery that has become something more than a research problem. It has become personal.
Devier James Lamphier Smith. Born in 1839. Or perhaps 1842. Adopted by Ranslow and Mary Smith in Jefferson County, New York. Apparently connected somehow to the Lamphier/Lanfear family. Moved to Wisconsin. Legally changed his name in 1866. And left behind just enough evidence to make Randy absolutely certain that the truth exists while simultaneously ensuring that finding it will require the combined efforts of Sherlock Holmes, Columbo, Indiana Jones, a moderately competent county clerk, 5th cousin DNA matches, and What Are The Odds (a DNA method).
Randy has DNA matches. He has trees. He has names. He has geography. He has the five unmarried daughters living in the vicinity in 1839. He has hypotheses. He has contradictory dates. He has possible relationships. He has spreadsheets. He has probably stared at the same family group sheet so many times that the people in it are beginning to wonder why this strange bearded man keeps looking at them.
And somewhere in heaven, Devier is probably saying: “Randy, buddy, I honestly don't remember. I never asked! They never told me!”
Randy: “That's not good enough.”
The Philosophy of the Census
Randy has developed a particular relationship with the United States census. Most people think of the census as a historical document. Randy thinks of it as a witness statement. And witnesses can be unreliable. The 1850 census says one thing. The 1860 census says another. The ages don't match. The birthplace changes. The surname has been spelled differently. The occupation doesn't make sense. A child appears. Another disappears. Randy leans toward the monitor. “Interesting.”
This word should frighten everyone. Because “interesting” means Randy has detected an inconsistency. And an inconsistency means research. And research means Randy will eventually find himself reading a 147-year-old county history at 12:17 in the morning because a man's middle initial appears to have changed from W to M.
Then There Is Henry Carringer
Henry Carringer is another example of the Randy Effect. Henry was a farmer. A perfectly respectable 19th-century farmer. He had land. He had sons. He had livestock. He planted crops. He harvested them. He presumably ate dinner and went to bed. A normal man.
But Randy has other ideas. Randy wants to know what Henry's life felt like. So now Henry is no longer merely: Henry Carringer — farmer, Mercer County, Pennsylvania.
He is a man standing in a field in the spring of 1850. The horses breathe heavily in the morning air. The soil turns beneath the plow. David, age 21, is working nearby. George, 17, is learning the rhythms of farm work. Cornelius, 15, is discovering that agricultural labor builds character primarily because there is no alternative. They are planting. They are haying. They are sweating. They are probably eating an enormous lunch.
And Randy is watching it all from 176 years away. He has transformed census entries into people. That is one of the strangest things about Randy's particular obsession. He doesn't merely want to know who his ancestors were. He wants to know what they did on Tuesday. What they ate. What the weather was probably like. What tools they used. What the house smelled like. What the children argued about. What Henry thought when he looked across those fields.
He wants the dead to become inconveniently alive again.
The Pig Problem
And then there are the pigs. At some point Randy began asking what 19th-century farmers actually did with pigs. This is a dangerous question. Because once you start investigating pigs in 1870, you inevitably arrive at lard. And once you arrive at lard, suddenly you are researching 19th-century soapmaking, cooking, candles, preservation, leather, machinery and household economics. A normal person would have stopped.
Randy did not. Because now the pig has become historically significant. That pig has a job. That pig is contributing to the Carringer family economy. That pig may eventually appear in a story. And if Randy has his way, someday a descendant will read that story and say: “Great-grandpa Henry had pigs.”
And Randy will quietly smile. Because he knows that Great-grandpa Henry's pigs were never merely pigs. They were evidence.
The Amanuensis
Then comes Monday. Most people dislike Monday. Randy has Amanuensis Monday. This is the day when some poor historical document is placed on the operating table. A deed. A will. A probate record. A court proceeding. A land transaction. Randy takes the document apart. He transcribes it. Line by line. Word by word. He examines the names. He identifies relationships. He follows the land. He searches the witnesses. He checks the dates. He records the source. He puts it into RootsMagic.
And then, because apparently transcription alone isn't enough, he writes about it. The document has been dead for 140 years. Randy gives it another afternoon.
Treasure Chest Thursday
Thursday arrives. Most people are watching television. Randy is opening a computer file containing a photograph, letter, record, certificate, or mysterious piece of family memorabilia.
Treasure Chest Thursday.
The item may be worth three dollars. It may be worth nothing financially. But Randy doesn't care. Its real value is that somebody in his family touched it. Somebody carried it. Somebody saved it. Somebody thought it was worth keeping. That makes it priceless. So Randy photographs it. Describes it. Researches it. Identifies the people. Figures out the date. Adds the source. Adds the media. And then writes another post.
Somewhere, a hidden 1918 wedding ring is probably watching all of this with increasing anxiety.
The Blog
And then there is the blog. Genea-Musings. Nearly twenty thousand posts. At this point, calling it a blog is almost insulting. It is more like a digital archaeological site.
You don't simply “read Genea-Musings.” You excavate it. There are layers. Strata. Deposits. Artifacts. A future historian could probably spend six years studying Randy's blog and emerge muttering: “I'm still not sure what happened in 2021.” [Hint: a heart problem!]
The blog contains research, methodology, discoveries, family history, records, photographs, stories, AI experiments, genealogy technology, and the occasional completely normal question that somehow becomes a 1,500-word investigation.
Randy writes about genealogy. Then he writes about writing genealogy. Then he writes about using AI to write genealogy. Then he asks AI to write about him writing about AI writing genealogy. The snake has eaten its own tail.
Enter Artificial Intelligence
This is where things get truly dangerous. Randy discovered artificial intelligence. Or perhaps artificial intelligence discovered Randy. Nobody knows. The relationship began innocently. “Can AI help me write an ancestor biography?”
Sure. Then: “Can AI turn dry genealogical facts into a story?” Sure. Then: “Can AI write a Day in the Life of Henry Carringer?” Yes. Then: “Can AI make it historically plausible?” Yes. Then: “Can AI write a dialogue?” Yes. Then: “A poem?” Yes. “A song?” Yes. “A podcast?” Yes. “A slideshow?” Yes. “A video?” Yes. “A Finding Your Roots-style episode about Devier's parentage incorporating DNA evidence?”
At this point the AI should probably have contacted somebody. Instead, it said: “Absolutely.” [ChatGPT starts every response this way!]
And Randy was off. He began imagining an entire system where a family historian could upload a genealogical sketch, photographs, an obituary and research notes—and emerge with a sourced biography, memoir, historical stories, poem, song, podcast, video, and slide show.
The logical next step is obvious. Randy will eventually attempt to resurrect an ancestor as a hologram. And when the hologram says something not supported by a source, Randy will interrupt: “Now wait a minute. Where did you get that?”
The Great Enemy: Unsupported Facts
There is one thing Randy cannot tolerate. Not war. Not politics. Not taxes. Not even bad weather. Unsourced genealogy.
Somewhere in the genealogical universe, an AI has just invented a middle name. Randy feels a disturbance in the Force. He sits upright. His glasses slide down his nose. His white beard trembles. “Where did that come from?”
The AI begins explaining. Randy is already opening the source. No. No. No. No. That isn't documented. And thus another hallucination dies before breakfast.
Randy's standard is simple: If you don't know, say you don't know. If the evidence is contradictory, say it's contradictory. If something is plausible but unproven, call it a hypothesis. If the evidence is negative, record the negative evidence. And if somebody's online family tree says that George Washington was the father of a person born in 1842—Randy reaches for the keyboard.
The Family Historian's Final Mission
The funny thing is that beneath all this madness is something remarkably old-fashioned. Randy wants to remember people. Not celebrities. Not kings. Not presidents. Ordinary people. Farmers. Blacksmiths. Machinists. Combmakers. Wheelwrights. Coopers. Ministers. Farmers. Salesgirls. Soldiers. Mothers. Fathers. Children.
People who lived ordinary lives and left behind a handful of records. A census entry. A marriage certificate. A newspaper notice. A grave. A photograph. A letter. A ring. A few lines in somebody else's Bible. Randy takes those scraps and says: “You mattered. You made me!” And then he spends three hours proving it.
The Future
There is no retirement in sight. Retirement would require stopping. Stopping would require being satisfied. Being satisfied would require knowing everything. And Randy knows better than anyone that you never know everything. And he’s having too much fun to stop.
There is always another record. Another newspaper. Another DNA match. Another county. Another spelling. Another photograph. Another suspicious census household. Another ancestor who apparently lied about his age. Another child who vanished between censuses. Another woman whose maiden name has been hidden for 150 years. Another family Bible waiting in somebody's attic. Another document written in handwriting that appears to have been produced by a chicken walking through an ink bottle.
And somewhere, buried beneath all of it, is another story. So Randy will sit down tomorrow. He will put on his glasses. He will adjust his white beard. He will open RootsMagic. He will open Ancestry. He will open FamilySearch. He will open MyHeritage. He will open another 47 browser tabs. He will forget which tab contained the important thing. He will find it again. He will make a note. He will make another note about the note. He will save the record. He will cite the record. He will certainly write a blog post about the record.
Then he will ask an AI to help him turn the record into a story. And somewhere around midnight, he will suddenly say: “Wait a minute.”
Because he has noticed something. A tiny inconsistency. A name. A date. A place. A relationship. A clue. And the entire operation begins again. The descendants of his ancestors may have thought they had escaped into history. They were wrong.
Randy is coming. And he has a subscription to Newspapers.com. God help the dead.
================================
I giggled all the way through reading this the first time. I can't be this good, er, bad, right? How does AI do this? It takes three years of prompts and chats and turns it into this, um, story.
You know that this is not exactly how I am, right? Right? Oh dear.
My guess is that many (some? a few?) of my genealogy friends and colleagues are in the Genealogical Zone. All day long? All year long? Are you? If so, ask ChatGPT (or your favorite AI assistant) to write an unhinged narrative about you! Enjoy! Giggle! It's good for your soul.
It seems that ChatGPT5 loves really short sentences. I ran many of them together in this post to save space.
Should I ask ChatGPT5 how to recover from this problem of being in the Genealogical Zone? I'm afraid it will make sense. Or someone will refer me to the folks who dress you in a one-piece outfit with arms that tie in the back (Remember the song "They're coming to take me away, ha ha, hee hee..." by Napoleon XIV).
Of course, I had to make a Google Gemini Notebook Infographic and Video.  The Video is on my YouTube channel and below: 
The lesson here is "Sometimes, be afraid of what you ask for."
