Title: Revenge of the labor movement: Democrats with union backgrounds aim to retake Congress
Article_Text:
The US labor movement is having a banner election year.
More than three dozen nominees for open House and Senate races across the US have backgrounds as labor union representatives or members.
Several nominees are running in heavily blue districts, making it almost certain they will win the seat in November’s midterms, while others are in highly contested races that are likely to determine control of the House and possibly the Senate. Most are Democrats, though some are running as independents.
The early success of so many candidates with ties to labor comes as Democrats work to rebuild their support among working-class voters, centering their campaign messaging around affordability issues.
But the messenger matters, too.
“In a political environment that’s been dominated by wealthy elites for decades, union candidates provide a level of trust and credibility that’s simply unmatched,” Steve Smith, a spokesperson for the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of labor unions in the US, told the Guardian. “These candidates are at long last returning the levers of power to the people.”
A 2024 study by Cal State and UCLA researchers found working-class voters are 6.4 percentage points more likely to prefer a political candidate with a working-class occupation over one with an upper-class occupation.
Yet a 2026 report by the Center for Working-Class Politics found working-class candidates make up just 8-14% of Democratic and 5-8% of Republican congressional candidates.
Union candidates invoked pro-worker themes 159% more than non-union candidates, the report found. Running more union members as candidates, its authors argued, could increase the representation ordinary Americans have in Congress, by elevating people who can speak to and deliver on issues that affect the working class.
“Voters want elected leaders who understand the struggles working people face in an economy rigged against us,” Smith said. “In every area of the country, at every level, union members are running for office and winning because they bring lived experience in leveling the playing field for workers and creating a brighter future for our families.”
Americans overwhelmingly favor labor unions, according to recent annual Gallup polls, with 68% approving labor unions in 2025. But union density has been on a decline in recent decades, from more than 30% in the 1950s to 10% in 2025, correlating to a drastic increase in wealth and income inequality in the US.
In 2024, Donald Trump sought to woo labor leaders and blue-collar voters with populist trade promises. But exit polls and surveys conducted after the presidential election found little evidence that union members had shifted toward Trump.
According to the VoteCast survey conducted for the Associated Press and Fox News after the 2024 election, union members preferred Harris over Trump by 16% in 2024, 57% to 41% for Trump, matching Biden’s 16% lead over Trump with union households in 2020.
Trump was formerly a union member, but he resigned from the Screen Actors Guild in February 2021 rather than facing disciplinary charges from the union for violating its constitution regarding his actions and role in inciting the attack on the US Capitol on 6 January 2021.
In his resignation letter, Trump wrote “Who cares!” and accused the union of never doing anything for him. In response to his resignation, the union issued a two-word statement: “Thank you.”
Meet the Senate and House candidates identified as having labor union backgrounds who are running to join the roughly 25 current members of Congress who have previously worked in the labor movement or in a job represented by a union.
Todd Achilles
Candidate for US Senate, Idaho
Independent Todd Achilles, a former American Federation of Teachers member from his work as a public policy professor and lecturer, is running for the US Senate in a race where the Democratic nominee withdrew in July.
Abdul El-Sayed
Candidate for US Senate, Michigan
Abdul El-Sayed is a former American Association of University Professors member and other higher education unions from his time working as a professor and scholar at Columbia University, Harvard University, the University of Michigan, Wayne State University and American University. The union made its first ever national political endorsement in endorsing his Senate campaign.
In an interview with the Guardian in July, El-Sayed explained his critique of the economy and the impact of concentrated corporate power.
“If the markets actually worked the way they’re supposed to, you might have some efficient movement of money,” he said. “The problem is, we don’t live in capitalism, we live in oligopoly.”
Troy Jackson
Candidate for US Senate, Maine
Troy Jackson worked several past union jobs as a member of the unions of Painters and Allied Trades (IUPAT), the Machinists (IAM), Operating Engineers (IUOE), United Auto Workers (UAW), and Laborers’ International Union of North America (Liuna).
“Everything Troy fights for comes from his working-class roots as a logger from Allagash and the 1998 blockade, when he stood up to powerful landowners undercutting Maine workers,” Jackson’s campaign manager, Dan Gottlieb, said in a statement.
Gottlieb added: “Mainers know whose side Troy is on: theirs. For him, solidarity isn’t a slogan – it’s how he’s lived his life.”
Angie Nixon
Candidate for US Senate, Florida
Angie Nixon is a state legislator in Florida and the Democratic nominee for Senate in a special election to fill Marco Rubio’s vacated seat. She previously has worked as a union organizer, directing the Florida Public Services Union’s (FPSU) higher education campaign.
Dan Osborn
Candidate for US Senate, Nebraska
Dan Osborn, a former president of Bakery, Confectionery, Tobacco Workers and Grain Millers International Union (BCTGM) Local 50G, which represents Kellogg’s workers, is running for the US Senate in Nebraska as an independent. He faces Republican Pete Ricketts, the heir to billionaire Joe Ricketts, co-founder of TD Ameritrade.
James Talarico
Candidate for US Senate, Texas
As a public school teacher, James Talarico was a member of the San Antonio Alliance of Teachers and Support Personnel. He is also a longtime member of the Texas State Employees Union (TSEU – CWA Local 6186).
Colin Allred
Candidate for Texas’s 33rd congressional district
The former congressman Colin Allred is running again this cycle in a newly redrawn Democratic-dominant district in Texas. He is a former member of the NFL Players Association, the union representing National Football League players.
Chris Backemeyer
Candidate for Nebraska’s first congressional district
Chris Backemeyer, a former US state department employee and the Democratic nominee for Nebraska’s first congressional district, is a member of American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE) Local 1534.
Mitchell Berman
Candidate for Wisconsin’s first congressional district
Mitchell Berman worked a union job in college at UPS, where he was a member of Teamsters Local 344. As a nurse, he has worked several union jobs including as a member of the Wisconsin Federation of Nurses & Health Professionals and National Nurses United.
“Coming from a working-class background, understanding what folks are going through [and] having walked a mile in my neighbor’s shoes gives me the ability to look at legislation from the perspective of having some empathy and understanding for what people are dealing with,” Berman said in August.
Bob Brooks
Candidate for Pennsylvania’s seventh congressional district
Bob Brooks, a former president of the Pennsylvania Professional Fire Fighters Association, is running to flip one of the state’s swing districts.
“We need to change who’s representing us and who’s making the rules and the laws,” Brooks said in June. “That’s what inspired me to do this. I think we need more everyday people down there, because everyday people are the ones that are struggling.”
Connie Chan
Candidate for California’s 11th congressional district
A former member of the International Federation of Professional and Technical Engineers (IFPTE) Local 21, Connie Chan is in a general election runoff to replace Nancy Pelosi’s vacated seat in California’s 11th congressional district.
Darializa Avila Chevalier
Candidate for New York’s 13th congressional district
In one of the biggest primary upsets in 2026, Darializa Avila Chevalier defeated Adriano Espaillat, the incumbent congressman and chair of the Congressional Hispanic caucus, and she is expected to easily win the general election in a district that leans heavily in favor of Democrats.
She is a union member of the United Auto Workers Local 2325.
“That really changed the course of my education and my PhD program, to be able to be part of a union that fought for me, my work conditions, my wage, and made it possible for me to continue my program,” she said in June, reflecting on her experience joining the union. “I was able to teach at a pace that was manageable, right, with a workload that was manageable, but also be paid enough to actually lead a dignified life.”
Carmela Conroy
Candidate for Washington’s fifth congressional district
Carmela Conroy was a union member represented by the American Foreign Service Association.
Sam Forstag
Candidate for Montana’s at-large congressional district
Sam Forstag served as the vice-president of the Forest Service Council Local 60, an arm of the National Federation of Federal Employees.
“There is genuinely a fundamental lack of representation for working people in federal office right now, and that has serious, substantive effects on what kind of policies they actually prioritize and what they pass,” Forstag said in February. “The primary function of government is to step in when the market is not meeting a need and to make people’s lives materially better. And it seems like some people at the national level forgot about that.”
Chris Gallant
Candidate for New York’s first congressional district
Chris Gallant served as the president of his local union with the National Air Traffic Controllers Association.
Vince George
Candidate for West Virginia’s first congressional district
Vince George was a member of the West Virginia Education Association and is a retired union member of American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees (Afscme).
Bob Harvie
Candidate for Pennsylvania’s first congressional district
A teacher for more than 20 years, Bob Harvie is a former member of the Bucks County Technical High School Education Association.
Missi Hesketh
Candidate for Missouri’s seventh congressional district
Missi Hesketh is a teacher and a member the National Education Association and a former member of the Missouri State Teachers Association.
Bill Hill
Candidate for Alaska’s at-large congressional district
Bill Hill, an independent, is a former union construction worker. The leading Democrat in the race dropped out and endorsed his campaign.
Amanda Hollowell
Candidate for Georgia’s first congressional district
Amanda Hollowell was the state director for 9to5 in Georgia, a worker-led organization that arose from women-led worker organizing in the 1970s.
Jake Johnson
Candidate for Minnesota’s first congressional district
A high school math teacher, Jake Johnson served as an official with his local teachers’ union.
“To me, a lot of the great things that happen in public schools happen because of unions. We’re the ones fighting for smaller class sizes. We’re the ones fighting for reasonable wages,” Johnson said in July. “That’s happening because of teachers’ unions. We’re the ones that are raising the bar as far as teacher quality.”
Tanya Lloyd
Candidate for Texas’s 27th congressional district
Tanya Lloyd is a former union member of the Texas American Federation of Teachers.
Donavan McKinney
Candidate for Michigan’s 13th congressional district
A former organizer with the Service Employees International Union, Donavan McKinney defeated incumbent representative Shri Thanedar in the Democratic primary and is expected to easily win the district that favors Democrats by 22 percentage points, according to Cook Political Report’s Partisan Voting Index.
Analilia Mejia
Candidate for New Jersey’s 11th congressional district
Analilia Mejia, who won a special election in New Jersey’s 11th congressional district in April, is a former union organizer with the Service Employees International Union, Unite Here, and United Food and Commercial Workers.
Jena Nelson
Candidate for Oklahoma’s fifth congressional district
The former Oklahoma teacher of the year in 2020, Jena Nelson is a teachers’ union member. The district last flipped blue under Trump’s first term in 2018, but Republicans took back the district in 2020.
Richard Pan
Candidate for California’s sixth congressional district
Richard Pan, a pediatrician, is a member of the Union of American Physicians and Dentists – Afscme Local 206.
Brian Poindexter
Candidate for Ohio’s seventh congressional district
An ironworker, apprenticeship instructor and former organizer, Brian Poindexter is running to unseat Max Miller, the congressman who is facing calls to resign due to domestic assault allegations from his ex-wife, the daughter of Republican senator Bernie Moreno, and similar allegations made against him by Stephanie Grisham, a former White House press secretary under Trump’s first administration.
“People are working harder and harder. We’re getting less and less and we’re getting more and more of the burden,” Poindexter said. “I’d like to see an economy that works for all of us, not just the wealthy. We need to build an economy that rewards work, not just wealth.”
Chris Rabb
Candidate for Pennsylvania’s third congressional district
Chris Rabb helped organize adjuncts at Temple University with the United Academics of Philadelphia, while he worked as an adjunct professor at the university.
Kyle Rable
Candidate for Texas’s 19th congressional district
Kyle Rable is a member of the Texas State Employees Union, CWA Local 6186.
Lauren Reinhold
Candidate for Kansas’s first congressional district
A former federal employee, Lauren Reinhold served as a union steward and officer while working at the Social Security Administration and National Labor Relations Board (NLRB).
Ceretta Smith
Candidate for Georgia’s 12th congressional district
Ceretta Smith is a past president and current member of AFGE Local 2017 and also serves as the fair practices coordinator and women’s coordinator for AFGE Council 172, which represents Defense Commissary Agency workers. The US army veteran has worked as federal employee for more than 20 years.
Katy Padilla Stout
Candidate for Texas’s 23rd congressional district
Katy Padilla Stout is a former teachers’ union member with the American Federation of Teachers, which has endorsed her campaign.
Trina Swanson
Candidate for Minnesota’s eighth congressional district
Trina Swanson was a member of the American Federation of Government Employees while she worked at US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). She is running against the Republican incumbent representative, Pete Stauber.
“Northern Minnesota taught her that unions strengthen our middle class,” Swanson’s campaign website states.
Claire Valdez
Candidate for New York’s seventh congressional district
Claire Valdez won the Democratic primary for New York’s seventh congressional district after the retirement of Nydia Velázquez. Valdez served as an organizer with United Auto Workers Local 2110 at Columbia University.
Mai Vang
Candidate for California’s seventh congressional district
A union member of the California Faculty Association, progressive Mai Vang edged past the 82-year-old Democratic incumbent Doris Matsui in the primary for California’s seventh congressional district. They will face each other again in the November general election.
Randy Villegas
Candidate for California’s 22nd congressional district
Randy Villegas is a former United Auto Workers Local 4811 member, which represents higher-education workers.
Brandon Wade
Candidate for Oklahoma’s second congressional district
Brandon Wade is an official with International Union of Operating Engineers Local 351, where he has held several different roles while working more than 20 years in the oil and gas industry.
Marni von Wilpert
Candidate for California’s 48th congressional district
Marni Von Wilpert is a former NLRB attorney who helped write the comprehensive labor law reform legislation, the Protecting the Right to Organize (Pro) Act, and a member of the Nonprofit Professional Employees Union while working at the Economic Policy Institute.
“One of my biggest priorities for running for Congress myself is to finish this work, to come back as a member of Congress and finally get labor law reform across the finish line,” von Wilpert said.
Her Republican opponent, Jim Desmond, worked as a pilot for Delta Air Lines, where he was a member of the pilots’ union, Air Line Pilots Association, but has opposed unions on project labor agreements.

Title: New laws trigger a fresh legal fight over Nazi-looted art in Los Angeles and Auschwitz museums
Article_Text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Jewish heirs of Holocaust victims and their representatives have filed two lawsuits in California staking their claims to Nazi-looted paintings that still hang on the walls of prominent museums in Los Angeles and Auschwitz.
This pair of lawsuits are the first to be filed after the recent passage of laws by California and Congress, which strengthen U.S.-based claims to artwork that were forcibly taken from Jewish families during World War II.
One lawsuit was filed in Los Angeles Superior Court on Monday by the Jewish Federation of Greater Los Angeles and its board chair Daniel Gryczman against Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena for the return of “Adam and Eve.” These are two life-size oil-on-panel masterpieces created by Lucas Carnach the Elder in 1530.
The other lawsuit was filed in federal court in Los Angeles the same day by the daughters of the late Dinah Gottliebova Babbitt, a Holocaust survivor and California-based animator who was held in Auschwitz. It demanded the return of watercolors of fellow prisoners that the artist was forced to paint for Josef Mengele, a Nazi physician who had earned the nickname the “Angel of Death.”
Spokespersons for both museums say the museums legally hold titles to the works, and intend to continue displaying them to the public. The lawsuits don’t specify the monetary value of the paintings.
Artworks pit Jewish families against museums
The issue of Nazi-looted art is an emotional, legally and ethically charged topic that pits Jewish families that have suffered inter-generational trauma against museums that say they are trying to preserve a painful, yet important, chapter of history. Between 1933 and 1945, the Nazi regime orchestrated the largest art theft in world history, seizing over 600,000 works of art across Europe from Jewish families, collectors and museums. Decades later, many of these masterpieces reside in prominent museums around the world, making the push for their recovery more complex than a simple property dispute.
Rabbi Noah Farkas is president and CEO of the Jewish Federation of Los Angeles, the organization to which Marei von Saher, sole heir of Dutch Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker, has signed over her rights. The paintings were seized from Goudstikker's collection by Hermann Goring, Adolf Hitler’s second-in-command and changed a number of hands before being sold in the 1960s to the Pasadena Museum of Modern Art, which was renamed Norton Simon Museum in honor of its benefactor.
Farkas said the federation plans to use most of the net proceeds from the recovered art to provide much-needed help to the about 2,500 Holocaust survivors living in the Los Angeles area.
“These are incredibly beautiful European masterpieces stolen from a Jewish family to enrich the Nazi party and fund the war and death machine against the people,” he said. “It's our honor to take on this role on behalf of the community and use most of the proceeds to help these elderly survivors live out the last years of their lives in dignity, comfort and peace – something their family members were denied during the Holocaust.”
Marei von Saher, in a statement, said she is grateful to the Jewish organization for taking up her family’s cause.
“This effort represents a meaningful step toward justice for Holocaust survivors and victims of Nazi era atrocities,” she said.
New legislation gives lawsuits second wind
California Assemblyman Jesse Gabriel, D-Woodland Hills, wrote Assembly Bill 2867, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom in September 2024, which requires that the state law must apply in lawsuits brought by California residents or their heirs to recover art seized during the Holocaust or during other acts of persecution. Gabriel, who co-chairs the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, introduced the legislation in response to a federal court ruling, which allowed the state-owned Thyssen-Bornemisza National Museum in Madrid to keep a multimillion-dollar Camille Pissarro impressionist masterpiece.
That painting had been taken by the Nazis from the Cassirer family in 1939. This case, which prompted this new law, is expected to be heard in federal court in California next month.
Gabriel said it’s time for museums to “do some deep introspection on whether they want to be on the right side of history.”
Museums want to preserve paintings for posterity
Norton Simon Museum released a statement pointing out that a federal court in 2018 unanimously determined that the museum had proper title to the Cranach paintings. In May 2019, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to get involved in the case, leaving in place lower court rulings.
They said the Cranach paintings, which originally belonged to the Stroganoff family, were put up for sale in 1931 by the Soviet Union in an illicit auction in Berlin where they were purchased by Goudstikker. After a complicated journey, the paintings were sold to the museum by a Stroganoff family descendant. The museum later restored and preserved the pieces.
“For nearly 50 years, they have been on view at the Norton Simon Museum and will continue to be accessible to the public for years to come,” the statement said.
Pawel Sawicki, a spokesperson for the Auschwitz Memorial, said the watercolors of Roma victims that Gottliebova Babbitt was forced to paint by Mengele to document his horrendous experiments and racial research, “must remain in the Memorial” to document the man's crimes. He said these paintings must not be mischaracterized as “Nazi-looted art” because Gottliebova Babbitt painted them against her will as a prisoner and therefore didn’t have ownership of the watercolors.
While he understands the family’s sentiments, Sawicki said the portraits of Roma and Sinti victims are among the few remaining documents of Mengele’s criminal experiments and should be treated as unique documents related to the history of the Auschwitz concentration camp.
“While fully respecting the rights of people who created some of the documents here, we are of the opinion that any loss in the collections of the Memorial will constitute irreparable harm,” he said. “ … The loss of even the smallest part of the documentation is an irreparable loss and blemish on the memory of the victims of Auschwitz.”
Advocates hope cases will now be heard on their merit
Joel Greenberg, founder of Art Ashes, a Philadelphia-area nonprofit that helps Jewish families track down and recover Nazi-looted art, said in addition to the California law, President Donald Trump signed into law and updated the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025. This new law permanently eliminated the expiration date to allow Holocaust survivors and their heirs to indefinitely pursue the recovery of these works of art.
Greenberg said the new federal law gave families the right to reclaim their art for up to six years from the time they find out in whose possession they are.
“These new laws mean that technical defenses will no longer stick in court,” he said. “Every case will be heard on its merits.”
He said the new legislation also ensures that these Jewish families have their day in court and a fair process to determine ownership of the stolen art.
“It will make sure the stories of what happened to European Jewry is not lost and forgotten,” he said. “The art can still be returned to the rightful owner.”

Title: This swing state Republican keeps distancing himself from Trump. It may not save him in the midterms
Article_Text:
This swing state Republican keeps distancing himself from Trump. It may not save him in the midterms
It’s hard to imagine a Republican who’s done more to draw a sharp contrast with the president than Brian Fitzpatrick
YARDLEY, Pa. -- Mary Ryan may be a registered Republican but she has never voted for President Donald Trump, turned off by his crass style of politics and chaotic approach to governing.
But the 60-year-old medical writer from the Philadelphia suburbs has consistently backed her party's congressman, five-term Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick.
Until now.
This year, Ryan is so fed up with Trump and his grip on Congress that she is planning to vote in November for Fitzpatrick's Democratic opponent in the 1st Congressional District, Bob Harvie, a twice countywide elected commissioner who is a former social studies teacher.
Even though Fitzpatrick has pitched himself as a voice of reason in Washington, Ryan said that “I don't see it happening.”
Defections like this one could sink Fitzpatrick’s reelection chances and cost Republicans their narrow U.S. House majority. As one of the few Republicans representing a congressional district won by Democrat Kamala Harris in the presidential race two years ago, Fitzpatrick has done as much as any House Republican to distance himself from Trump: Fitzpatrick voted against Trump's tariffs, his signature tax legislation and his power to wage war against Iran without congressional approval. The lawmaker even skipped Trump’s recent midterm convention in Dallas.
But that may not be enough to overcome the collateral damage of the president’s sagging approval rating and soaring fuel prices because of the war.
Fitzpatrick, speaking briefly after a Sept. 11 memorial in his district, said he understands this year's political challenges and always considers what is best for his constituents with every vote.
“That’s the job,” he said. Representatives for Fitzpatrick did not respond to requests for a more complete interview.
Harvie describes the race and his decision to run in almost existential terms.
“The lack of trust in our government, the lack of trust in each other and seeing each other as enemies based just on, you know, the color of your skin, the religion you practice, who you voted for,” he said in an interview this summer. “I worry about just the basic foundations of this nation.”
Fitzpatrick has consistently survived challenges in his politically mixed district. He won by 13 percentage points in 2024 when Harris won by less than a single point in the district. In 2022, he won by about 10 points when Democrats were elected to the U.S. Senate and governorship. In 2020, Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden won the district by about 5 points while Fitzpatrick carried it by about 13 points.
“Every two years Democrats in Washington label Congressman Fitzpatrick as vulnerable. Every two years he wins anyway,” said Robert Speel, an associate professor of political science at the Penn State campus in Erie. “It’s, to some extent, possibly like Charlie Brown trying to kick the football and failing each time.”
Harvie pointed to his deep roots in the district as a basis for why he could be different from previous Democrats who ran against Fitzpatrick.
“I’m not somebody who needs to be reintroduced or introduced to people of this district. And that’s very, very different than any race he’s ever run before,” he said.
Jean Dolan, 61, is a Democratic voter from Newtown who has never backed Fitzpatrick and does not plan to this year. She has been frustrated with Trump's immigration crackdown and she worries about how anti-vaccine sentiment in his administration could affect public health. As she sees it, Fitzpatrick is not independent enough from his party's leaders.
“He's a nice guy. I know people like him a lot in the community,” she said. But, she added, “you have to serve everyone in your district."
Fitzpatrick graduated with an MBA and a law degree and worked as a special agent for the FBI and as an assistant U.S. attorney. He also worked in private practice as a lawyer and accountant before running for the seat previously held by his brother, Mike Fitzpatrick, who died of cancer in 2020.
Jim Rachau, a 45-year-old photographer from Doylestown, is a registered independent who plans to vote for Fitzpatrick again this year. Rachau is not thrilled with the war or the economy, but said Fitzpatrick has earned his support with his prior public service as an FBI agent.
“You would think serving for the public good, he would have their best interest at heart,” Rachau said.
In Congress, Fitzpatrick has not shied away from disagreeing with Trump. He criticized the president, for example, in April when Trump called Pope Leo XIV “weak,” and captive to the “Radical Left."
“There’s so many angry voices out there. We all know that's the case,” Fitzpatrick said in an episode of a podcast launched this year with U.S. Rep. Tom Suozzi, a Democrat who represents a battleground district in New York. “People are sick and tired of the noise. They’re sick and tired of elected officials not being focused on the kitchen table issues that people really care about.”
Fitzpatrick also posts online regularly about meeting with groups across the district. He recently showed up to a picket line with striking sheet metal workers; he dropped by a local Catholic church's parish picnic; and he stopped at a community college hosting a maternity coalition.
Fitzpatrick has also unleashed a wave of spending in the race already, disbursing nearly $5 million, according to Federal Election Commission records.
Negative attack ads against Harvie have mushroomed. Many claim Harvie is under FBI investigation, which the Democrat denies. He has filed a federal defamation lawsuit against a super PAC running some of the ads.
According to the suit, local media reported in 2020 with few details that the FBI was investigating local government and that Harvie was called to testify as a witness in the case. His attorneys say he has never been charged.
The FBI did not respond to a request for comment.
No debate has been scheduled between Fitzpatrick and Harvie, but the men appeared at the same Sept. 11 memorial, standing on opposite sides of the speaker’s lectern. They did not appear to speak to each other.
Ryan, the medical writer from the Philadelphia suburbs, said she is thinking less about Fitzpatrick and more about how Republicans in Congress and their reluctance to buck the president.
“Incumbents just feel they can’t cross that line. If they do, they’re not going to get reelected," she said. But she acknowledged that may not matter in the end. "They might not get reelected anyway.”

Title: Gerard Butler's Intense 128-Minute Action Thriller Scores New Free Streaming Home Next Month
Article_Text:
From 300 to Den of Thieves, there's no denying that Gerard Butler has appeared in numerous action hits over the course of his career. However, for every smash he's had, there's been an equal number of flops that might not have made much money, but are still good movies in their own right. Now, 15 years after its release, one of Butler's most underrated films is set to remind audiences how fantastic it is thanks to free streaming.
Gerard Butler Stars as a Man on a Mission
Released in 2011 and based on the true story of a former Pennsylvania gang member turned evangelist, Machine Gun Preacher stars Butler as Sam Childers, who some have referred to as the "Christian Rambo". Once a violent, drug-addicted biker and ex-con, he turns his life around to become a missionary who travels to Africa to do humanitarian work.
Directed by Marc Foster (Quantum of Solace, World War Z), Childers becomes determined to help kids caught in the region's civil wars and eventually establishes an orphanage that comes under constant threat from the LRA. Putting his violent past to good use, he goes so far as to accompany armed groups on missions to rescue children who have been kidnapped, making Machine Gun Preacher as much a story about one man's redemption as it is about faith.
Sadly, Machine Gun Preacher failed to become another box office hit for Butler, but that's mainly due to its limited theatrical release. After debuting at TIFF on Sept. 11, 2011, it went on to earn just $3.3 million at the box office against a budget of $30 million.
Of course, it didn't help matters much that Machine Gun Preacher received bad word of mouth from critics. Earning just a 28% rating on Rotten Tomatoes, they called it everything from "disappointingly ordinary" to "boorishly self-righteous." Audiences were much more forgiving of Butler's efforts, scoring the film a 62% and deeming it "a surprisingly good movie." Your mileage may vary, of course, but if you're hesitant to fork over some cash to watch it, you're in luck since it's returning to free streaming next month.
'Machine Gun Preacher' Lands New Streaming Home
Currently, Machine Gun Preacher is available to stream in the United States with a subscription to Paramount+, where it's been in and out of the Top 10 over the past few weeks. For those without a subscription, though, Butler's action thriller about faith, war and redemption will be making its way back to free streaming very soon.
Per Tubi, Machine Gun Preacher is set to hit the free streaming platform on October 1 along with a host of other great movies, including Butler's best action thriller in years, Plane, Stephen King’s The Green Mile, and Tom Hanks' Forrest Gump. It joins other Butler favorites like Den of Thieves and the first two movies in the Has Fallen series, which are already available free on Tubi.
Next up for Butler is his return as Stoic the Vast in How to Train Your Dragon 2, and the fourth entry in the Has Fallen series, Night Has Fallen. The former is set to premiere on June 11, 2027, and the latter has yet to set a release date.

Title: A&E ROUNDUP: Fundraisers, music festival slated for this weekend
Article_Text:
A&E ROUNDUP: Fundraisers, music festival slated for this weekend
Published 1:30 am Friday, September 18, 2026
|                            Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...                        | 
An new photography exhibit, event fundraisers and a bluegrass festival highlight this weekend’s arts and entertainment options on the North Olympic Peninsula.
• “Being on the Wing” opens at noon today at the The Port Townsend Marine Science Center’s Flagship Landing Gallery, 1001 Water St., Port Townsend.
The free exhibit will feature photography by Mike Kalichman along with text by Nicholas England that grew out of a Pacific Northwest road trip to Seattle, the Skagit River, Fidalgo and Lopez islands in September 2025.
The photographs and text explore both the similarities and differences between human intelligence and that of Salish Sea birds.
“PTMSC is excited to share some of their observations in words and photos,” said Diane Quinn, the center’s executive director. “Like much of the work done at the Port Townsend Marine Science Center, their project inspires us to reflect on our relationship to life in the remarkable Salish Sea, including the birds we might only have seen in passing or at a distance.”
“Being on the Wing” will be on exhibit from noon to 3 p.m. Fridays though Sundays until Nov. 29.
For more information, visit www.ptmsc.org/gallery.
• The Sequim Food Bank will host its second “Everyone at the Table” fundraiser from 3 p.m. to 5 p.m. Saturday.
The annual event will be at the food bank’s distribution center, 144 W. Alder St., Sequim. The free celebration will feature freshly prepared food, live music by Back Pockett, family activities, a raffle and a silent auction.
Donations may be made at www.sequimfoodbank.org/donate.
• “Olympickin’ 2.0” is set for 2 p.m. Saturday at the Quilcene Lantern, 7360 Center Road, Quilcene.
Tickets for the annual bluegrass music festival are $50 per person or $30 for youths, seniors and low income at https://btt.boldtypetickets.com/events/183204409/olympickin-2026.
Onsite camping is available for $20.
Music performers will include Broken Compass Bluegrass from Northern California; Dadweed from Portland, Ore.; the Sweater Weather Stringband from the North Olympic Peninsula; Claire Willow and Elise Snoey from Bellingham and Seattle; Georgia Strait Bluegrass, a bluegrass supergroup with members from around the Pacific Northwest; and Union City Council from the south Hood Canal. Dave Thielk also will call for a square dance.
The festival will kick off with a gravel bike ride at 10 a.m. Saturday and close with a bluegrass set on Sunday morning. The nonprofit festival is partnering with the Andy Mackie Music Foundation to bring musical instruments and education to Olympic Peninsula youth.
For more information, visit www.sweaterweatherstringband.com/olympickin-bluegrass-festival.
• The fifth Forever StreamFest: Tending Our Gardens Beyond Our Backyards will be from 10 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. Saturday at Pebble Beach Park, 301 Marine Drive, Port Angeles. The free conservation education program is sponsored by Port Angeles Garden Club.
Attendees will be able to learn ways to join efforts to protect, restore and preserve streams and natural resources throughout the North Olympic Peninsula.
The family-friendly festival will feature food, a beer and cider garden, face painting, a poster contest, music and environmental exhibits.
For more information, visit www.portangelesgardenclub.org.
• Tracy Grammer will perform at 7 p.m. Saturday during the Rainshadow Concerts series in Building 315 at Fort Worden Historical State Park, 200 Battery Way, Port Townsend.
Tickets are $25 per person at www.ticketstorm.com/c/17038/rainshadow recording or $30 at the door.
Grammer has recorded and performed with Joan Baez and Mary Chapin Carpenter and has headlined at the Philadelphia Folk Festival and the Falcon Ridge Folk Festival.
• The 30th Quilcene Fair and Parade is set for Saturday at Quilcene School, 294715 U.S. Highway 101.
Booths and vendors will be open from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. The parade will begin at 11 a.m. Other features will include a car show at 10 a.m., Strait Up Foam Fun, live music and arts and crafts.
For more information, visit www.quilcenefair.org.
• Clallam County Parks will host Community in the Parks from noon to 3 p.m. Saturday in the group shelter at Salt Creek Recreation Area, 3506 Camp Hayden Road, Port Angeles.
The free open house is designed to promote the county’s parklands to both residents and visitors.
Participants will receive information about various parks in Clallam County, have an opportunity to try new activities and meet representatives from outdoor recreation businesses and organizations.
The program will offer mini-kayaking sessions, walking tours of historic Camp Hayden and hands-on crafts and games.
The program is outdoors, so attendees should dress for fall weather conditions.
Participating businesses and organizations include Elevate Outdoors, the Peninsula Trails Coalition, Feiro Marine Life Center, the Elwha Klallam Museum at the Carnegie and Clallam County Parks’ Weekday Wonders volunteers.
Additional programs are planned for the Dungeness Recreation Area, Clallam Bay Spit Community Beach Park and Robin Hill Farm Park during 2027.
For more information, call county parks at 360-417-2291 or visit www. clallamcountywa.gov/294/parks-fair-facilities.
• The Production Alliance will host the Jefferson County Farm Tour from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Saturday and Sunday at 17 sites across East Jefferson County.
Farm Tour Central, located at the Chimacum Corner Farmstand, 9122 Rhody Drive in Chimacum, will be the main information hub, where visitors and get maps, brochures, route recommendations, up-to-date details and merchandise.
The tour is free and open to all. A donation of $10 per car can be made at any farm on the tour or at Farm Tour Central.
Pets are not allowed on the tour due to concerns about biosecurity and the safety of livestock. Trained service animals are welcome.
The tour is conducted in partnership with Washington State University’s Jefferson County Extension, local farmers, Jefferson County Farmers Markets, Jefferson Land Trust, the Food Co-op, the Port of Port Townsend and the Chimacum Corner Farmstand.
For more information, visit www.theproductionalliance.org/farmtour.
The Mod Lounge will host a mid-century soirée at 6 p.m. Saturday at the Port Angeles Fine Arts Center, 1203 E. Lauridsen Blvd., Port Angeles.
Tickets for the fundraiser are $50 per person at www.pafac.org/the-mod-lounge.
The center will celebrate its mid-century roots by transforming into a 1950s-inspired indoor and outdoor lounge.
The lounge will include a silent auction, art-making stations, food and drinks as well as dancing in the center’s courtyard.
Guests are encouraged to don 1950s mod- inspired attire.
• Black Diamond Junction will perform from 6 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. Saturday at Elks Lodge #2642, 143 Port Williams Road, Sequim.
Admission is $12 per person, $10 for lodge members.
• Luca Stricagnoli will perform a Candlelight Concert at 6:30 p.m. Sunday in the Donna M. Morris Auditorium at Field Arts & Events Hall, 201 W. Front St., Port Angeles.
Tickets are $30 to $50 per person, $15 for youths, at www.fieldhallevents.org/tickets.
• Laurovia Jazz and Soul, with special guest Maram Sarifi, will perform a benefit concert for Dove House from 5 p.m. to 7 p.m. Sunday at Grace Lutheran Church, 1120 Walker St., Port Townsend.
Admission is by $25 donation at https://www.dovehousejc.org/online-store-888320.html or at the door.
• The Buck Ellard Band will perform during a Dinner and Dance from 5 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. at the Sequim Prairie Grange, 291 Macleay Road, Sequim.
Admission is $15 per person. Youths younger than 12 will be admitted for free.
The meal will be served at 5 p.m. and music will start at 6 p.m.
• Lindsey Dono will call for the first contra dance of the 2026-27 season at 7:30 tonight at the Black Diamond Community Hall, 1942 Black Diamond Road, Port Angeles.
Music will be provided by the New England-based Dawn Chorus featuring Grace Henderson-Jones on flute, Cedar Stanistreet on fiddle and Rosie O’Neill on guitar.
Dono will teach a free lesson at 7 p.m. to those who have paid admission. The requested donation is $20 per person.
The dance will be preceded by a season-opening potluck dinner at 5:30 p.m.
• Sue Mendenhall will present “What is the Importance of Planning and Creating a Genealogical Research Paper for Publication and How to Succeed?” at 9:30 a.m. Saturday in the community room at KSQM-FM, 609 W. Washington St., Sequim.
Mendenhall will discuss the process of preparing a research paper for publication during a hybrid meeting of the Clallam County Genealogical Society. She will discuss the application of the Genealogical Standard of proof, proper citation and other things that an editor may require for publication.
The public is invited to attend the free presentation. A Zoom link is available by calling the society at 360-417-5000 or emailing askus@ clallamcogs.org.
For more information, visit www.clallamcogs.org.
• CeCe Fitton, Nancy Kohn, Lorraine Eckard and Niki Kobes will present “Planting and Care of a Wildflower Meadow” at 10 a.m. Saturday at the Woodcock Demonstration Garden, 2711 Woodcock Road, Sequim.
The free workshop is part of the Digging Deeper gardening series sponsored by the Clallam County Master Gardeners. The master gardeners will discuss the creation and management of wildflower meadows.
For more information, call 360-565-2679 or visit https://extension.wsu.edu/clallam.
• Paul Loubere will present “Advancing Ocean, Retreating Bluffs around Port Townsend” at 4 p.m. Saturday during a meeting of the Quimper Geological Society at the First Baptist Church, 1202 Lawrence St., Port Townsend.
Loubere, a retired research professor, will describe what the mapping of seabed environments in Port Townsend Bay reveals in slope failures.
For more information, visit www.quimpergeology.org.

Title: 4 Rare Coins From the '90s That Only Collectors Know About
Article_Text:
4 Rare Coins From the ’90s That Only Collectors Know About
The last decade of the 20th century produced coins that modern numismatic enthusiasts spend three-, four- and even five-figure sums to get their hands on today. The U.S. Mint produced collector coins and error strikes that turned gold coins, silver proofs and even garden-variety pocket change into treasured collectibles.
For You: 8 Wealth-Building Shortcuts Proven To Add $1K to Your Wallet This Month
Learn More: 9 Unusual Ways To Make Extra Money (That Actually Work)
Here are some of the rarest and most valuable coins from the 1990s.
1990-99 Double-Denomination Coins
Double-denomination coins are among the most coveted curiosities in the numismatic world. As the name implies, this minting error occurs when two denominations are accidentally struck on the same coin.
According to the Professional Coin Grading Service (PCGS), this mistake affected nearly every 20th-century coin series — including those from the 1990s. The most common pairs by far are:
- The Lincoln cent on the Roosevelt dime, known as the 11c (11 cents)
- The Jefferson nickel on Lincoln cent, or 6c
The big two combos are rarities that can be valuable. All others are extremely scarce, with only 25 to 50 known examples for each entire coin series.
One 1990 example from the more common, but still rare, 11c pairing is being auctioned on eBay for $2,400.
Explore Next: 10 Things You Must Do When Your Savings Reach $50,000
Advertisement
1992 Close AM Lincoln Cents
The 1992 Close AM and 1992-D Close AM (the “D” is for Denver) are some of the rarest and most valuable coins from the 1990s. According to the PCGS, the U.S. Mint adjusted the penny’s design slightly in ’92 to enable a higher-quality strike. They were supposed to be released in 1993, and most were — most, but not all.
A handful were accidentally scattered among the more than 4 billion Lincoln pennies the Philadelphia and Denver mints struck in 1992. These highly elusive “transitional” coins can easily fetch four figures, even in worn condition, with pristine examples commanding five figures.
1995-W $1 Silver Eagle Proof
The U.S. Mint launched the American Eagle Coin program in 1986, including a special proof version for collectors. The $1 silver proof has since become an icon, and according to PCGS — which ranks it at No. 13 on its list of the top 100 modern coins — 1995 is the most coveted year of all. That’s because it was the first year to bear the “W” mint mark, indicating its production in the West Point Mint, and because of its low mintage — just 30,125 were ever produced.
In 2013, one sold for $86,655 and another fetched $55,550.
1997-W Jackie Robinson $5 Gold Coin
In 1997, the U.S. Mint authorized the West Point Mint (W) to produce up to 100,000 gold half eagles commemorating the 50th anniversary of the Brooklyn Dodgers’ signing of Jackie Robinson in 1947.
Nowhere near that amount would ever be produced.
According to the Numismatic Guaranty Company, demand for the coin was “shockingly low” despite the enduring popularity of the man who broke the baseball color barrier and paved the way for the integration of professional sports. It performed the worst by far among the several commemorative coins produced that year. That low demand, however, has since turned it into an in-demand collector coin. The PCGS ranked it as the No. 24 best modern coin because only 5,174 were ever minted. Originally selling for $180, they commonly command four-figure sale prices today.

LOS ANGELES (AP) — Jewish heirs of Holocaust victims and their representatives have filed two lawsuits in California staking their claims to Nazi-looted paintings that still hang on the walls of prominent museums in Los Angeles and Auschwitz.
This pair of lawsuits are the first to be filed after the recent passage of laws by California and Congress, which strengthen U.S.-based claims to artwork that were forcibly taken from Jewish families during World War II.
One lawsuit was filed in Los Angeles Superior Court on Monday by the Jewish Federation of Greater Los Angeles and its board chair Daniel Gryczman against Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena for the return of “Adam and Eve.” These are two life-size oil-on-panel masterpieces created by Lucas Carnach the Elder in 1530.
The other lawsuit was filed in federal court in Los Angeles the same day by the daughters of the late Dinah Gottliebova Babbitt, a Holocaust survivor and California-based animator who was held in Auschwitz. It demanded the return of watercolors of fellow prisoners that the artist was forced to paint for Josef Mengele, a Nazi physician who had earned the nickname the “Angel of Death.”
Spokespersons for both museums say the museums legally hold titles to the works, and intend to continue displaying them to the public. The lawsuits don’t specify the monetary value of the paintings.
Artworks pit Jewish families against museums
The issue of Nazi-looted art is an emotional, legally and ethically charged topic that pits Jewish families that have suffered inter-generational trauma against museums that say they are trying to preserve a painful, yet important, chapter of history. Between 1933 and 1945, the Nazi regime orchestrated the largest art theft in world history, seizing over 600,000 works of art across Europe from Jewish families, collectors and museums. Decades later, many of these masterpieces reside in prominent museums around the world, making the push for their recovery more complex than a simple property dispute.
Rabbi Noah Farkas is president and CEO of the Jewish Federation of Los Angeles, the organization to which Marei von Saher, sole heir of Dutch Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker, has signed over her rights. The paintings were seized from Goudstikker’s collection by Hermann Goring, Adolf Hitler’s second-in-command and changed a number of hands before being sold in the 1960s to the Pasadena Museum of Modern Art, which was renamed Norton Simon Museum in honor of its benefactor.
Farkas said the federation plans to use most of the net proceeds from the recovered art to provide much-needed help to the about 2,500 Holocaust survivors living in the Los Angeles area.
“These are incredibly beautiful European masterpieces stolen from a Jewish family to enrich the Nazi party and fund the war and death machine against the people,” he said. “It’s our honor to take on this role on behalf of the community and use most of the proceeds to help these elderly survivors live out the last years of their lives in dignity, comfort and peace – something their family members were denied during the Holocaust.”
Marei von Saher, in a statement, said she is grateful to the Jewish organization for taking up her family’s cause.
“This effort represents a meaningful step toward justice for Holocaust survivors and victims of Nazi era atrocities,” she said.
New legislation gives lawsuits second wind
California Assemblyman Jesse Gabriel, D-Woodland Hills, wrote Assembly Bill 2867, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom in September 2024, which requires that the state law must apply in lawsuits brought by California residents or their heirs to recover art seized during the Holocaust or during other acts of persecution. Gabriel, who co-chairs the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, introduced the legislation in response to a federal court ruling, which allowed the state-owned Thyssen-Bornemisza National Museum in Madrid to keep a multimillion-dollar Camille Pissarro impressionist masterpiece.
That painting had been taken by the Nazis from the Cassirer family in 1939. This case, which prompted this new law, is expected to be heard in federal court in California next month.
Gabriel said it’s time for museums to “do some deep introspection on whether they want to be on the right side of history.”
Museums want to preserve paintings for posterity
Norton Simon Museum released a statement pointing out that a federal court in 2018 unanimously determined that the museum had proper title to the Cranach paintings. In May 2019, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to get involved in the case, leaving in place lower court rulings.
They said the Cranach paintings, which originally belonged to the Stroganoff family, were put up for sale in 1931 by the Soviet Union in an illicit auction in Berlin where they were purchased by Goudstikker. After a complicated journey, the paintings were sold to the museum by a Stroganoff family descendant. The museum later restored and preserved the pieces.
“For nearly 50 years, they have been on view at the Norton Simon Museum and will continue to be accessible to the public for years to come,” the statement said.
Pawel Sawicki, a spokesperson for the Auschwitz Memorial, said the watercolors of Roma victims that Gottliebova Babbitt was forced to paint by Mengele to document his horrendous experiments and racial research, “must remain in the Memorial” to document the man’s crimes. He said these paintings must not be mischaracterized as “Nazi-looted art” because Gottliebova Babbitt painted them against her will as a prisoner and therefore didn’t have ownership of the watercolors.
While he understands the family’s sentiments, Sawicki said the portraits of Roma and Sinti victims are among the few remaining documents of Mengele’s criminal experiments and should be treated as unique documents related to the history of the Auschwitz concentration camp.
“While fully respecting the rights of people who created some of the documents here, we are of the opinion that any loss in the collections of the Memorial will constitute irreparable harm,” he said. “ … The loss of even the smallest part of the documentation is an irreparable loss and blemish on the memory of the victims of Auschwitz.”
Advocates hope cases will now be heard on their merit
Joel Greenberg, founder of Art Ashes, a Philadelphia-area nonprofit that helps Jewish families track down and recover Nazi-looted art, said in addition to the California law, President Donald Trump signed into law and updated the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025. This new law permanently eliminated the expiration date to allow Holocaust survivors and their heirs to indefinitely pursue the recovery of these works of art.
Greenberg said the new federal law gave families the right to reclaim their art for up to six years from the time they find out in whose possession they are.
“These new laws mean that technical defenses will no longer stick in court,” he said. “Every case will be heard on its merits.”
He said the new legislation also ensures that these Jewish families have their day in court and a fair process to determine ownership of the stolen art.
“It will make sure the stories of what happened to European Jewry is not lost and forgotten,” he said. “The art can still be returned to the rightful owner.”

Title: MLB roundup: Braves top Astros, wrap up postseason berth
Article_Text:
Field Level Media
                
19 Sep 2026, 13:25 GMT+10
            
(Photo credit: Troy Taormina)
Michael Harris II, Ronald Acuna Jr. and Matt Olson slugged two-run home runs and deadline acquisition Tyler Mahle continued his exceptional pitching for the visiting Atlanta Braves, who secured a postseason berth with a 6-2 victory over the Houston Astros on Friday.
Atlanta qualified for the postseason for the eighth time in nine seasons. The Braves lowered their magic number to clinch the National League East to three over the Philadelphia Phillies.
Harris provided Mahle a 2-0 lead when he followed a one-out single by Matt Olson with an opposite-field blast to left off Astros starter Peter Lambert (8-10) in the fourth inning. Harris (3-for-5) drove a first-pitch slurve from Lambert 367 feet for his 26th homer of the year.
Mahle (7-10) improved to 4-1 with a 1.28 ERA over eight starts since his acquisition from the Giants. He allowed one run on three hits and one walk with six strikeouts over six innings.
Guardians 5, Athletics 3
Jose Ramirez hit a solo homer in the sixth inning for his 1,000th career RBI after rookie Travis Bazzana went deep in the fifth, fueling host Cleveland to a victory over the Athletics.
The Guardians have won three in a row to move a game ahead of the second-place Chicago White Sox in the American League Central. Joey Cantillo (10-9) threw six scoreless innings in relief, and Cade Smith handled the ninth for his 38th save.
Zack Gelof belted a three-run homer in the first inning for the Athletics, whose losing skid reached four games. Reliever Scott Blewett (2-1) permitted one run on one hit in 1 2/3 innings.
Padres 8, Marlins 2
Ty France clouted a three-run homer to cap a six-run fifth inning as San Diego stopped visiting Miami to forge a three-way tie atop the National League wild-card standings.
Winning for the 11th time in 12 games, the Padres pulled even with the Chicago Cubs and Philadelphia Phillies, who both lost. San Diego's magic number for clinching a playoff spot dropped to four.
San Diego starter Nick Pivetta (3-2) worked five innings, yielding four hits and a run. Marlins reliever Cade Gibson (5-2) was charged with the first two runs in the game-changing fifth. The Padres' Jackson Merrill and the Marlins' Agustin Ramirez homered.
Mets 6, Phillies 3
Zac Thornton tossed six solid innings, Juan Soto homered among his three hits and host New York beat Philadelphia.
Soto went 3-for-5 for the Mets, while Francisco Lindor and Carson Benge each collected two hits. Thornton (5-5) gave up two runs on five hits.
Edmundo Sosa finished 3-for-3 with a homer and Derek Hill also went deep for the Phillies, who fell to 7-9 this month. Newly acquired Jose Urquidy threw 4 2/3 shutout innings after opener Tim Mayza (3-4) surrendered three runs while getting just one out.
Reds 6, Cubs 4
Cincinnati scored three times in the sixth inning in a back-and-forth win over visiting Chicago.
Elly De La Cruz had two hits, two walks and two runs for the Reds. Cincinnati starter Chase Burns and reliever Julian Aguiar (1-0) each allowed two runs on four hits in three innings.
Cubs starter Clay Holmes (6-8) surrendered six runs on three hits in 5 1/3 innings. Ian Happ homered for Chicago, and Michael Conforto amassed three hits.
Twins 3, Angels 0
Connor Prielipp allowed two hits over a career-high seven innings and fellow rookie Walker Jenkins went 3-for-4 with a home run as Minnesota topped Los Angeles in Anaheim, Calif.
Travis Adams pitched a 1-2-3 ninth inning to pick up his third save. Jenkins, who began his career going 4-for-45, homered for the second straight game on his sixth consecutive hit in the series.
Jose Siri had two hits for the Angels. Grayson Rodriguez (4-8) gave up three runs on eight hits in 6 2/3 innings.
Brewers 6, Orioles 5 (10 innings)
Sal Frelick singled home a 10th-inning run and visiting Milwaukee pulled out a victory against Baltimore.
Trevor Megill (3-3) was the winning pitcher despite a blown save. Chad Patrick retired the Orioles in order in the bottom of the 10th for his sixth save.
Milwaukee's Jackson Chourio and Baltimore's Pete Alonso hit three-run homers early in the game. Gunnar Henderson and Coby Mayo both collected three hits for the Orioles.
Dodgers 8, Giants 2
Mookie Betts homered twice, including his 53rd career leadoff homer, and Josue De Paula hit a tiebreaking double to help Los Angeles produce a victory over visiting San Francisco.
The Dodgers socked five home runs while winning for the 12th time in the last 15 games. Max Muncy and Kyle Tucker hit back-to-back homers in the eighth, and Betts and Will Smith repeated the feat later in the frame. Tyler Glasnow (5-1) gave up two runs and three hits while striking out a season-high 10 in six innings.
Jung Hoo Lee homered and Jonah Cox had an RBI single as the Giants fell for the fifth time in seven games.
Yankees 9, Diamondbacks 2
George Lombard Jr. had two hits and three RBIs, and his two-run single capped a five-run first-inning outburst as New York cruised past Arizona in Phoenix.
Ben Rice and Lombard homered and Rice added a triple as the Yankees won for the fourth time in five games. Gerrit Cole (9-9) gave up two runs on four hits in six innings.
Corbin Carroll homered and doubled for the Diamondbacks, who have lost five of six to see their NL wild-card chances fade. Eduardo Rodriguez (15-7) yielded seven runs in 5 1/3 innings.
Red Sox 4, Rays 2
Roman Anthony homered and had three RBIs, Jahmai Jones went deep and Boston cooled off first-place Tampa Bay in St. Petersburg, Fla.
Anthony went 2-for-5 while Caleb Durbin was 2-for-3 for the Red Sox. Boston starter Ranger Suarez (8-4) fought control issues but allowed one run on three hits in 5 2/3 innings.
Junior Caminero doubled, walked twice and drove in a run for the Rays, who had only five hits as their six-game winning streak ended. Ian Seymour (9-7) allowed four runs on seven hits in five innings.
Rangers 7, Blue Jays 1
Corey Seager capped a four-run second inning with an RBI double as Texas topped Toronto in Arlington, Texas.
The Rangers drew 10 walks and moved into a first-place tie with Houston in the American League West. Jake Burger had two RBIs for Texas, which won for the fifth time in six games. Texas took a 4-0 lead in the second inning against Dylan Cease (11-6), who allowed four runs (one earned) on three hits over 2 2/3 innings.
The Blue Jays fell two games back of the White Sox for the final AL wild-card spot. Myles Straw had two hits with an RBI for Toronto, which committed three errors and lost for the third time in four games.
Tigers 11, White Sox 8
Dillon Dingler delivered the go-ahead single and Riley Greene followed with a two-run homer in a five-run eighth inning as visiting Detroit stormed back from six runs down to beat Chicago.
Hao-Yu Lee went 4-for-5 with a homer, three RBIs and two runs for the Tigers. Kevin McGonigle finished 2-for-5 with four RBIs. Drew Sommers (2-4) threw two shutout innings, fanning five, and Kenley Jansen blanked the White Sox in the ninth for his 21st save.
Colson Montgomery and Miguel Vargas each had two hits and three RBIs for the White Sox, who have lost three out of four. Sean Newcomb (2-5) got only two outs in relief while allowing three runs.
Pirates 8, Royals 5
Konnor Griffin had four hits and two RBIs and Spencer Horwitz delivered a tiebreaking two-run single in the seventh as Pittsburgh rallied to beat visiting Kansas City.
Pittsburgh trailed 4-0 after the top of the third inning and 5-2 entering the bottom of the fourth. The Pirates won their second straight after losing four of their previous five.
Vinnie Pasquantino and Michael Massey each homered as the Royals scored five runs against Pittsburgh ace Paul Skenes, who scattered six hits in his six innings. Royals starter Randy Dobnak allowed four runs on seven hits over 3 2/3 innings.
Nationals 9, Cardinals 1
Cade Cavalli pitched five scoreless innings and recorded the 200th strikeout of his first full major league season, leading Washington to a victory at St. Louis.
Cavalli (13-5), who agreed with the Nationals earlier in the day on a four-year, $47 million contract extension, allowed four hits and struck out six. Dylan Crews hit a two-run homer and Yohandy Morales added a two-run double for Washington.
Cardinals starter Kyle Leahy (10-5) allowed seven runs, six earned, on five hits over three innings. Leo Bernal went 3-for-4.
Mariners 5, Rockies 4
Lazaro Montes homered leading off the top of the ninth, J.P. Crawford went deep to open the game, and Seattle beat Colorado in Denver.
Randy Arozarena finished with three hits as the Mariners logged their second win in a row. Carlos Vargas (2-0) recorded one out in relief, and Andres Munoz earned his 28th save with a scoreless ninth inning.
Cole Carrigg, Connor Norby and Jake McCarthy had three hits apiece and Ezequiel Tovar contributed two hits for the Rockies, who have lost three in a row and 11 of 12. Jordan Romano (0-4) served up Montes' homer.
--Field Level Media

Title: Phillies turn to improving Andrew Painter in clash vs. Mets
Article_Text:
Phillies turn to improving Andrew Painter in clash vs. Mets
(Photo credit: Dale Zanine)
Christian Scott, Zac Thornton and Nolan McLean are providing the New York Mets hope that they eventually will be part of a rotation for a playoff contender.
The Philadelphia Phillies need rookie Andrew Painter to continue proving that now.
Painter will take the mound for the Phillies on Saturday afternoon when they visit the Mets in the third contest of a four-game series between the National League East rivals.
Painter (3-9, 5.54 ERA) will oppose Scott (4-5, 3.76) in a battle of right-handers.
The Phillies missed a chance to take over sole possession of the top wild-card spot in the NL on Friday night, when Thornton and two relievers combined on a six-hitter in the Mets' 6-3 win.
The Phillies, Chicago Cubs and San Diego Padres are tied for the NL's three wild-card spots at 85-69. The Cubs lost to the Cincinnati Reds 6-4 before the Padres created the three-way tie hours later with an 8-2 win over the Miami Marlins.
The Arizona Diamondbacks reside five games behind the Phillies, Cubs and Padres.
The importance of Painter was further magnified Friday, when Philadelphia fell to 0-2 in bullpen games necessitated by the absence of left-hander Jesus Luzardo (shoulder, 15-day injured list).
The All-Star was scratched from his scheduled start against the Atlanta Braves last Saturday, when the Phillies used six pitchers as the Braves rolled to a 12-2 win. On Friday, opener Tim Mayza got just one out and allowed three runs while pitching in Luzardo's spot.
The Phillies' bullpen also is being taxed by injury and ineffectiveness.
Right-hander Jonathan Bowlan departed Thursday's game vs. the Mets with a tight right groin. On Friday, Orion Kerkering gave up Juan Soto's three-run blast in the sixth inning -- the second homer surrendered by Kerkering in his last three outings, during which he has a 13.50 ERA.
'Anybody that gives up runs, when things aren't going good, your confidence is not sky high like when you're getting all your outs and everything's going smoothly,' Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said. 'But we've got to get past that at this point.'
Painter is 2-1 with a 3.58 ERA in nine starts since being recalled from Triple-A Lehigh Valley on July 31. He didn't factor into the decision in his most recent start last Sunday, when he gave up one run over five innings as the Phillies beat the Braves 9-4. He has yet to face the Mets in his career.
The Mets (70-84) have been under .500 since April and officially were eliminated from playoff contention earlier this week. But McLean and Thornton continued to provide optimism for 2027 by combining to allow just three runs over 12 innings in the first two games of the series.
McLean took the hard-luck loss Thursday, when he gave up one run in six innings in the Phillies' 3-0 win.
Thornton, McLean and Scott have a combined 3.40 ERA in 66 starts. Thornton and McLean are rookies while Scott is in his second big-league season after Tommy John surgery cut his 2024 campaign short.
'I think you have to train like you've never won anything and compete like you've never lost,' Mets interim manager Andy Green said Friday night about Thornton. 'I think you have to live in that space constantly.'
Scott took the defeat Sunday after allowing two runs over six innings in the Mets' 2-0 loss to the New York Yankees. He is 1-0 with a 1.80 ERA in two career starts against the Phillies.
--Field Level Media

Title: A voter enthusiasm gap is steering the midterms (Opinion)
Article_Text:
By Mary Ellen Klas
With the 2026 primary election season over, the state of American democracy is looking — sigh of relief — better than expected.
As the Trump administration has trampled on the rule of law, tried to undermine elections and pursued a self-enriching agenda, Americans are pushing back and demanding change — from both parties. Democracy depends on trusting ordinary people to make consequential decisions and, this election cycle, voters have reminded us they’re doing just that.
Democratic voters have been especially engaged. In primaries and special elections in the last 18 months, they voted in numbers the party hasn’t seen in decades. Democrats broke voter turnout records in the key states of Wisconsin, Michigan, Texas and Georgia. They’ve made 37 safe Republican seats competitive and signaled a blue wave may be coming in November.
As of late June, about 12.6 million votes had been cast in Democratic House primaries, compared with 8.6 million in Republican primaries, according to a Washington Post analysis.
The reasons are many. Midterm elections always favor the party out of power. Highly educated voters are more reliable voters in primary and special elections than the rest of the electorate and, in the Trump era, these voters are more Democratic-leaning than the electorate at large. And perhaps the most obvious reason: Trump’s poll numbers are so low, his war with Iran is so unpopular and his handling of the economy is so disappointing that Republican voters are staying home.
But Trumpism — by which I mean the personalized, transactional, strongman way Trump governs — is also playing a role. While Democrats can run hyper-local campaigns, focused on their plans to address housing costs and gas prices, Republicans are yoked to a domineering president with unpopular policies. If they step out of the circle and criticize Trump, his war, or his policies, they get shamed by his shrinking base, called out by the president on social media, or confronted with a primary opponent backed by the president.
That’s all led highly motivated voters to support Democrats over Republicans 53% to 45% in recent polls.
This Democratic overperformance has already had results. The Down Ballot, an election analysis website, examined the results of 110 special elections since January of 2025 and determined that Democrats have done better than their 2024 margins by an average of 12.5 points.Of course, voter turnout in primary elections is not a perfect predictor of general election results, especially in key states like Pennsylvania, Iowa, Ohio and Florida, which have closed primary systems that strand millions of independent voters. In 10 states with semi-closed primaries, like North Carolina, unaffiliated voters can vote if they meet certain criteria. These independent or no-party-affiliated voters are likely to determine the outcome of key races across the country, and 47% of all Americans say they don’t consider themselves a part of either major political party.
“The big unknown moving forward is: To what degree are disaffected Trump voters going to show up and vote, and who will they vote for?” said Michael McDonald, a political science professor at the University of Florida who studies voter turnout. “We know that Republicans are less enthusiastic. We suspect that they’re not going to show up.”
And if that happens, he told me, it could be like the midterms of 2018 when Democrats had an 8.5-percentage-point margin in the national vote for Congress and picked up over 40 seats. (To clinch control of Congress in November, Democrats need to flip four House seats and four Senate seats. They’ll need those margins to hold.)
Aware of this, Republicans have attempted to mitigate some of the backlash. At Trump’s urging, they launched a national redistricting war that netted them, on paper, a six- to nine-seat advantage in the U.S. House. But by creating more competitive districts, Republicans may have also inadvertently contributed to the turnout surge by giving Democrats more reason to participate.In Texas, for example, where Republicans redrew the map to give themselves five additional seats, more votes were cast for Democrats than Republicans in primaries for three of the five redrawn districts.
Meanwhile, Democratic candidates have made some calculated overtures to Republicans to demonstrate to swing voters they can straddle party differences. In Georgia, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff was endorsed by the GOP mayors of Valdosta and Tifton. In Arizona, Democratic Governor Katie Hobbs named former Republican and Mesa Mayor John Giles as her running mate in her re-election bid. And in Texas, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico hired a staffer from Republican Senator John Cornyn’s Senate office to serve as deputy policy director.
The 2026 field of Democratic nominees also reflects these pluralistic sensibilities. Voters have elevated Democratic candidates with a variety of views — from pro-Israel centrists to members of the Democratic Socialists of America. There may be risks to this for the party — as I’ve noted before, big tents can get big rips — but it’s surely better for elected officials to reflect Americans’ diversity of views than to merely repeat the talking points of one retributive president.
Republicans have already started to portray this election as a choice between the status quo and communism, labeling a socialist every Democrat who demands better health care, lower housing costs and affordable groceries. But to get people to turn out to vote, you’ve got to give them something to vote for. If Democrats listen to voters, they’ll conclude that voters don’t want the status quo. They want results.
Mary Ellen Klas is a politics and policy columnist for Bloomberg Opinion. A former capital bureau chief for the Miami Herald, she has covered politics and government for more than three decades.
