Title: New laws trigger fresh legal fight over Nazi-looted art in LA and Auschwitz museums
Article_Text:
New laws trigger fresh legal fight over Nazi-looted art in LA and Auschwitz museums
Jewish heirs of Holocaust victims have filed lawsuits in California to reclaim Nazi-looted paintings from museums in Los Angeles and Poland
LOS ANGELES -- Jewish heirs of Holocaust victims and their representatives have filed two lawsuits in California staking their claims to Nazi-looted paintings that still hang on the walls of prominent museums in Los Angeles and Auschwitz.
This pair of lawsuits are the first to be filed after the recent passage of laws by California and Congress, which strengthen U.S.-based claims to artwork that were forcibly taken from Jewish families during World War II.
One lawsuit was filed in Los Angeles Superior Court on Monday by the Jewish Federation of Greater Los Angeles and its board chair Daniel Gryczman against Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena for the return of “Adam and Eve.” These are two life-size oil-on-panel masterpieces created by Lucas Carnach the Elder in 1530.
The other lawsuit was filed in federal court in Los Angeles the same day by the daughters of the late Dinah Gottliebova Babbitt, a Holocaust survivor and California-based animator who was held in Auschwitz. It demanded the return of watercolors of fellow prisoners that the artist was forced to paint for Josef Mengele, a Nazi physician who had earned the nickname the “Angel of Death.”
Spokespersons for both museums say the museums legally hold titles to the works, and intend to continue displaying them to the public. The lawsuits don’t specify the monetary value of the paintings.
The issue of Nazi-looted art is an emotional, legally and ethically charged topic that pits Jewish families that have suffered inter-generational trauma against museums that say they are trying to preserve a painful, yet important, chapter of history. Between 1933 and 1945, the Nazi regime orchestrated the largest art theft in world history, seizing over 600,000 works of art across Europe from Jewish families, collectors and museums. Decades later, many of these masterpieces reside in prominent museums around the world, making the push for their recovery more complex than a simple property dispute.
Rabbi Noah Farkas is president and CEO of the Jewish Federation of Los Angeles, the organization to which Marei von Saher, sole heir of Dutch Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker, has signed over her rights. The paintings were seized from Goudstikker's collection by Hermann Goring, Adolf Hitler’s second-in-command and changed a number of hands before being sold in the 1960s to the Pasadena Museum of Modern Art, which was renamed Norton Simon Museum in honor of its benefactor.
Farkas said the federation plans to use most of the net proceeds from the recovered art to provide much-needed help to the about 2,500 Holocaust survivors living in the Los Angeles area.
“These are incredibly beautiful European masterpieces stolen from a Jewish family to enrich the Nazi party and fund the war and death machine against the people,” he said. “It's our honor to take on this role on behalf of the community and use most of the proceeds to help these elderly survivors live out the last years of their lives in dignity, comfort and peace – something their family members were denied during the Holocaust.”
Marei von Saher, in a statement, said she is grateful to the Jewish organization for taking up her family’s cause.
“This effort represents a meaningful step toward justice for Holocaust survivors and victims of Nazi era atrocities,” she said.
California Assemblyman Jesse Gabriel, D-Woodland Hills, wrote Assembly Bill 2867, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom in September 2024, which requires that the state law must apply in lawsuits brought by California residents or their heirs to recover art seized during the Holocaust or during other acts of persecution. Gabriel, who co-chairs the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, introduced the legislation in response to a federal court ruling, which allowed the state-owned Thyssen-Bornemisza National Museum in Madrid to keep a multimillion-dollar Camille Pissarro impressionist masterpiece.
That painting had been taken by the Nazis from the Cassirer family in 1939. This case, which prompted this new law, is expected to be heard in federal court in California next month.
Gabriel said it’s time for museums to “do some deep introspection on whether they want to be on the right side of history.”
Norton Simon Museum released a statement pointing out that a federal court in 2018 unanimously determined that the museum had proper title to the Cranach paintings. In May 2019, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to get involved in the case, leaving in place lower court rulings.
They said the Cranach paintings, which originally belonged to the Stroganoff family, were put up for sale in 1931 by the Soviet Union in an illicit auction in Berlin where they were purchased by Goudstikker. After a complicated journey, the paintings were sold to the museum by a Stroganoff family descendant. The museum later restored and preserved the pieces.
“For nearly 50 years, they have been on view at the Norton Simon Museum and will continue to be accessible to the public for years to come,” the statement said.
Pawel Sawicki, a spokesperson for the Auschwitz Memorial, said the watercolors of Roma victims that Gottliebova Babbitt was forced to paint by Mengele to document his horrendous experiments and racial research, “must remain in the Memorial” to document the man's crimes. He said these paintings must not be mischaracterized as “Nazi-looted art” because Gottliebova Babbitt painted them against her will as a prisoner and therefore didn’t have ownership of the watercolors.
While he understands the family’s sentiments, Sawicki said the portraits of Roma and Sinti victims are among the few remaining documents of Mengele’s criminal experiments and should be treated as unique documents related to the history of the Auschwitz concentration camp.
“While fully respecting the rights of people who created some of the documents here, we are of the opinion that any loss in the collections of the Memorial will constitute irreparable harm,” he said. “ … The loss of even the smallest part of the documentation is an irreparable loss and blemish on the memory of the victims of Auschwitz.”
Joel Greenberg, founder of Art Ashes, a Philadelphia-area nonprofit that helps Jewish families track down and recover Nazi-looted art, said in addition to the California law, President Donald Trump signed into law and updated the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025. This new law permanently eliminated the expiration date to allow Holocaust survivors and their heirs to indefinitely pursue the recovery of these works of art.
Greenberg said the new federal law gave families the right to reclaim their art for up to six years from the time they find out in whose possession they are.
“These new laws mean that technical defenses will no longer stick in court,” he said. “Every case will be heard on its merits.”
He said the new legislation also ensures that these Jewish families have their day in court and a fair process to determine ownership of the stolen art.
“It will make sure the stories of what happened to European Jewry is not lost and forgotten,” he said. “The art can still be returned to the rightful owner.”

Title: 10 things to know about famed TV host and evangelist Fulton Sheen ahead of the Illinois native's historic beatification
Article_Text:
The priest rose from humble beginnings on a central Illinois farm to commanding the airwaves of national radio broadcasts and primetime television shows that enthralled millions — including one little boy in the same state who would become pope.
Catholic Archbishop Fulton J. Sheen’s Emmy Award-winning 1950s program “Life Is Worth Living” offered a unique blend of scripture, catechism and humor on a secular network, drawing spectators of all faiths and backgrounds.
Donning an iconic pectoral cross and ferraiolo, the American prelate lectured from a simple chalk board, often tackling some of the common challenges of daily life: Anxiety. Love. Charity. Suffering. Loss and grief.
His pioneering televangelism continued to garner massive audiences in the 1960s with a similar series, the syndicated TV show “The Fulton Sheen Program.” He authored more than five dozen books, including “Peace of Soul,” which ranked sixth on the New York Times bestseller list.
Sheen later this month will make history as the first Illinois native to be beatified, the last major step before sainthood in the Catholic Church.
Tens of thousands of worshippers are expected to gather for his beatification Mass on Sept. 24 in St. Louis at the Dome at America’s Center, where the renowned evangelist will be designated as “Blessed Fulton Sheen.”
Chicago-born Pope Leo XIV noted during a June address that he had been moved by Sheen’s words as a child, calling the famed broadcaster “a light of faith, hope and love that shone through the radio and television media for decades.”
“I myself am a witness of his evangelization when I was growing up,” the pontiff said during a Vatican audience with the Pontifical Mission Societies. “His broadcasts touched millions with the hope of the Gospel.”
The Vatican gave the green light for Sheen’s beatification in February, after years of delays during an often turbulent canonization process.
A beatification ceremony was originally scheduled in 2019. But in an unusual move, the event was postponed by the Vatican amid legal investigation of clergy accused of sexual abuse throughout the state of New York. Although no accusations of abuse were made against Sheen personally, a bishop in Rochester, New York, raised concerns that further examination was needed to determine if Sheen had mishandled allegations of abuse or misconduct during his service as bishop there in the late 1960s.
Church officials later decided Sheen’s record wasn’t a cause for further postponement, and the Vatican earlier this year approved resuming plans for the beatification ceremony.
Catholic faithful around the world continued to be influenced by Sheen’s message for years after his 1979 death, spurring calls for his canonization.
Then a miracle — the healing of a Peoria-area baby reportedly born unresponsive and without a pulse for 61 minutes — was attributed to Sheen’s intercession and recognized by Pope Francis in 2019, fulfilling a requirement for the path to sainthood.
The infant’s mother, Bonnie Engstrom of Washington, Illinois, said she had invoked Sheen’s prayers during that fateful hour. She and her family plan to attend the upcoming beatification in St. Louis.
The baby — James Fulton Engstrom, who is now a teenager — will present a relic of Sheen during the ceremony.
“All of Illinois can be proud that one of our own is going to be raised to the level of blessed,” Bonnie Engstrom said during a recent interview with the Tribune.
Numerous services and events leading up to the beatification Mass will also be held in Peoria, where Sheen was ordained a priest on Sept. 20, 1919, at the Cathedral of St. Mary of the Immaculate Conception; there will be a special Mass there commemorating the anniversary of that ordination this Sunday.
“There’s just going to be a tremendous grace poured upon the church in this moment,” said Diocese of Peoria Bishop Louis Tylka during a virtual pre-beatification kickoff celebration in late August. “Seeing so many people excited … my hope is that it’s a moment of inspiration.”
As Sheen’s historic beatification approaches, here are 10 noteworthy facts about his life, ministry and legacy:
1. His religious TV shows competed — and even beat out — major stars of the day. Airing in black and white, the weekly episodes of “A Life Worth Living” vied for viewership with “The Frank Sinatra Show” and comedian Milton Berle, dubbed “Mr. Television,” who famously quipped, “At least I’m losing my ratings to God.”
Sheen won the 1953 Emmy for Most Outstanding Television Personality over actor Lucille Ball, broadcaster Edward R. Murrow, comedian Jimmy Durante and former Illinois Gov. Adlai Stevenson, who had just lost the presidency to Dwight D. Eisenhower.
The clergyman had credited the achievement to his TV show’s four writers: Gospel authors Matthew, Mark, Luke and John.
“(Sheen) was a really important figure in American media in the 20th century, first in radio and then in television,” said Kathleen Sprows Cummings, professor of history at the University of Notre Dame and author of the book “A Saint of Our Own: How the Quest for a Holy Hero Helped Catholics Become American.” “He helped Catholicism become more understood and accepted by becoming a celebrity on his TV shows.”
2. He was born on a farm in the small town of El Paso, Illinois, on May 8, 1895.
Yet Sheen was never much good at farmwork, preferring reading to shucking corn, cleaning horse stalls and baling hay. He recalled that a neighbor once told his dad he would never amount to much because, “He’s always got his nose in a book,” according to “Treasure in Clay: The Autobiography of Fulton J. Sheen.”
3. His original name was Peter John Sheen — and he was sometimes called P.J. as a boy. Yet he grew to prefer his mother’s maiden name, Fulton, “and used it until it stuck,” according to a 1952 Time Magazine article that featured Sheen on the cover.
4. A clumsy childhood faux pas turned into a formative prophecy. While serving as an altar boy during Mass at the cathedral in Peoria, a young Sheen accidentally dropped and shattered a wine cruet in the sanctuary.
He was terrified that presiding Bishop John L. Spalding would reprimand him.
“There is no atomic explosion that can equal in intensity of decibels the noise and explosive force of a wine cruet falling on the marble floor of a cathedral in the presence of a bishop,” Sheen recounted in “Treasure in Clay.”
Instead, the bishop comforted the young boy and offered two predictions: that Sheen would one day study at the University of Louvain in Belgium and that he would go on to become a bishop, saying, “Someday you will be just as I am,” according to the autobiography.
Both predictions came true.
5. He was an ardent anti-communist. Sheen professed a particular spiritual closeness with Christians oppressed in Eastern Bloc countries during the height of the Cold War.
He was given special biritual faculties by the pope allowing him to celebrate the liturgy in the Byzantine Rite, to help show solidarity with the many Byzantine Rite Catholics who lived in parts of Eastern Europe under communist rule.
“He wanted to connect with the Byzantine Catholic Church in order to be close to people in Eastern Europe who were being persecuted,” the Archbishop Fulton Sheen Museum in Peoria said on its Facebook page.
In 1955, Sheen celebrated a large outdoor Byzantine Divine Liturgy in Pennsylvania and arranged for it to be broadcast in countries behind the Iron Curtain via Voice of America and Radio Free Europe.
“We are praying for your freedom!” Sheen declared during the homily.
6. He’s often credited with predicting the demise of communist dictator Joseph Stalin on-air.
In an uncanny February 1953 episode titled “The Death of Stalin,” Sheen read the monologue from the burial scene of “Julius Caesar” by Shakespeare but subbed the Roman characters with the names of major Soviet leaders; the role of star-crossed Caesar was assigned to Stalin.
“Stalin must one day meet his judgment,” Sheen declared, his eyes piercing the camera.
Stalin suffered a stroke roughly a week later. On March 5, 1953, he was dead.
7. Sheen oversaw the raising of millions of dollars for global Catholic missions, according to The Pontifical Mission Societies USA.
His niece, the late Joan Sheen Cunningham of Peoria, recalled that Sheen also donated his earnings from his television shows, according to her book “My Uncle Fulton Sheen.”
“Though he was contracted for $26,000 an episode, Bishop Sheen never saw the money. It went straight to Rome to be distributed to missionaries throughout the world,” she wrote. “Bishop Sheen derived great satisfaction knowing that his salary provided a regular means of support for the missions and that he had earned the money in such a positive manner — the edification of his viewers.”
8. He devoted one continuous hour to prayer each day, called his “holy hour.”
“Over time he came to rely on the Holy Hour, craving its benefits and seeing his time spent before the Eucharist as akin to breathing with the help of an oxygen tank,” Cunningham recalled in her book.
On Dec. 9, 1979, at the age of 84, Sheen died at his home chapel in Manhattan, New York, while praying during this “holy hour” period.
9. His canonization process has been tumultuous, including a lengthy — and highly publicized — court battle over his final resting place.
This ended in 2019 when his remains were moved from New York and interred in a tomb at the cathedral in the Diocese of Peoria, which had opened Sheen’s cause for canonization in 2002.
“Battles over saints’ bodies are ubiquitous in the Catholic church,” Cummings noted. “But they don’t usually play out on the front page of the New York Times.”
10. A second miracle will likely have to be attributed to Sheen’s intercession by the Catholic Church before he can become a saint.
Once someone is beatified, another miracle is typically needed before the candidate is canonized, though popes in the past have sometimes waived that step in special circumstances.
“We will pray for one more miracle to be verified through his intercession and then, God willing, he will be declared a saint,” Tylka said during the August pre-beatification event. “I like to say he is already a saint — we’re just trying to catch up.”

Title: PNC Financial Reaffirms Outlook as Loans, Fees and AI Investments Gain Momentum
Article_Text:
Key Points  
    -       Interested in The PNC Financial Services Group, Inc? Here are five stocks we like better.  
-       PNC reaffirmed its third-quarter and full-year outlook, citing resilient consumer spending, broad commercial-lending demand and improving credit indicators. It expects net interest margin to exceed 3% by year-end.  
-       Loan and fee growth remain key drivers: commercial lending and commercial real estate have resumed growing, while capital markets, Harris Williams, cards and treasury management are reporting strong momentum.  
-       PNC is investing in AI, technology and branch expansion, including 300 planned additional branches, while integrating FirstBank ahead of schedule and maintaining a roughly 10% common equity tier 1 ratio.  
The PNC Financial Services Group (NYSE:PNC) said it remains on track to meet its previously issued third-quarter and full-year guidance, citing resilient consumer spending, broad commercial lending demand and continued momentum in its expansion markets.  
        Speaking at an investor conference, President Mark Wiedman and Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer Rob Reilly outlined priorities including deeper customer relationships, expanded international capabilities, investment in artificial intelligence and continued branch expansion.  
        → IonQ and NVIDIA Just Cracked a Major Quantum Computing Bottleneck  
            Reilly said PNC's outlook for interest rates includes a likely rate increase, followed by potential additional 25-basis-point hikes in December and March. He said the company is positioned neutrally for 2026, with potentially greater benefits in later years if the yield curve steepens.  
            Consumer, Commercial Credit Remain Strong  
        Wiedman said the economy has been stronger than expected, pointing to broad-based earnings growth, consumer spending and improving customer balance sheets. He said spending among PNC customers was up 4% year over year across income cohorts, including lower-income customers.  
        → 2 Stocks Breaking Out Post-FOMC With One Thing in Common  
            He added that customer current-account balances at PNC were 20% higher than in 2019 after inflation. Spending growth has been particularly notable in gambling, higher-end travel and entertainment, while home-improvement spending has been less prominent, Wiedman said.  
         Reilly said consumer delinquencies have declined and commercial credit conditions remain favorable. He said PNC's criticized assets, nonperforming loans and other leading credit indicators have improved.  
            → Generac Plugs into Amazon for an $8B AI-Powered Deal  
       While management did not identify broad credit problems, Reilly cited pressure in healthcare related to changes in the Affordable Care Act, distilleries amid changing alcohol-consumption trends, and some transportation-related borrowers. Wiedman said PNC has also been selective in financing AI infrastructure and data centers, favoring projects backed by high-credit-quality hyperscalers and strong contracts.  
          Loan, Deposit and Revenue Outlook  
       PNC reported strong loan growth in the first half of 2026, excluding the contribution from its FirstBank acquisition, which closed in January. Reilly said commercial lending continues to grow, although at a slower pace than during the first half and more in line with historical growth in a strong economy. Commercial real estate lending has returned to growth after a lengthy period of declines, he said.  
       On the consumer side, PNC is emphasizing credit cards as an opportunity to deepen customer relationships. Wiedman said the company believes it can at least double its penetration among existing customers relative to pure-play banks. PNC is less aggressively retaining originated mortgages on its balance sheet and is not currently emphasizing auto lending.  
       Reilly said spot deposits are growing faster than loans in the third quarter, driven primarily by commercial deposits. Deposit costs are expected to rise by about 5 basis points because of mix, he said, while the company expects deposit betas near their historical level of roughly 50% if rates increase.  
          PNC expects its net interest margin to exceed 3% by year-end. Reilly said the bank prioritizes total revenue, net interest income, earnings per share and return on assets over maximizing margin on individual loans. Lower-spread, high-credit-quality loans can generate additional capital-markets or treasury-management revenue, he said.  
       Fee Growth, AI and Expansion Strategy  
       Wiedman said fee-income opportunities include capital markets, debt and derivatives, Harris Williams M&A advisory services, treasury management and card products. Reilly said capital markets and Harris Williams are having record years, while card and cash-management businesses continue to grow. Mortgage-related fees remain flat, as expected.  
       The company also plans to maintain positive operating leverage while investing in technology, cards, international payments and expansion markets. Wiedman said PNC's AI initiatives are focused on five major areas, including retail operations, commercial loan servicing and fraud.  
          In software development, PNC has implemented developer assistance tools that helped it deliver certain offerings about 40% more efficiently, Wiedman said. The company sees the potential for larger productivity gains as it expands the use of AI agents, while also emphasizing controls over cyber and operational risks. Reilly said PNC is increasingly developing AI capabilities in-house, including its own computing infrastructure and models, rather than relying solely on vendors.  
       PNC has committed to build 300 additional branches on top of its existing network of roughly 2,300 branches. Reilly said the company is targeting higher-growth markets where it has already established a presence and believes reaching approximately 7% branch market share can produce an "exponential lift" in business activity.  
       Wiedman said PNC opened about 25 branches last year and expects to open about 55 this year. He added that branch revenue has met or exceeded internal targets and that nearby branches make the company's digital marketing more effective.  
          FirstBank Integration and Capital  
       Management said the FirstBank integration has progressed faster than anticipated. Reilly said PNC has met or exceeded the financial measures it expected when the deal was announced, while demand for products not previously offered by FirstBank, including commercial and asset-management services, has been strong in Colorado.  
       Reilly said PNC's common equity tier 1 ratio of about 10% is appropriate currently. He expects the company could add roughly one percentage point of capital under expected Basel changes, though the bank would seek to work that level down through loan growth and, beyond that, capital returns.  
       PNC expects to exit 2026 with an approximately 18% return on tangible common equity, Reilly said. He added that organic growth remains sufficient for the company's objectives, while potential acquisitions would face a high hurdle because current valuations are elevated and a major transaction could distract from PNC's AI priorities.

Title: Ed Sheeran is set to return to stage for 1st time since Macklemore was cut and other acts withdrew
Article_Text:
Ed Sheeran is set to take the stage – possibly without an opening act – Saturday night at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field, his first stop since Macklemore was dropped from the tour’s US dates over his pro-Palestinian remarks onstage, leading Sheeran’s other opening acts to resign.
The controversy has some ticketholders reconsidering whether to attend the English superstar’s concert, while others remain committed to seeing Sheeran perform.
Karen DeAngelis, who lives in Virginia, said she and her 10-year-old daughter are still planning to spend the weekend in Philadelphia, but after Sheeran didn’t defend Macklemore, she is no longer sure if they’ll attend the concert.
Macklemore, best known for 2012’s “Thrift Shop,” has publicly advocated for Palestinian rights since Israel began its yearslong bombing campaign in Gaza after the October 7 attacks.
Opening for Sheeran earlier this month at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, the rapper wore a black-and-white keffiyeh tied around his neck.
“A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place, was so I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: Free Palestine,” he said, according to video of the event. He added that “to all of my Jewish brothers and sisters, criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you.”
On Monday, days after the shows in New Jersey, Macklemore said on Instagram he’d been dropped from Sheeran’s remaining US tour dates.
Macklemore has pointed the blame squarely at Robert Kraft, who owns Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts, where Sheeran and Macklemore were scheduled to perform later this month. Kraft, Macklemore said, had “rallied some of the other stadium owners” and given Sheeran an ultimatum: “if Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play in our venues.”
Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots, said this week he would bar Macklemore from performing at Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts this month.
“Based on Macklemore’s recent actions, material shared from the stage during Ed Sheeran’s shows in New Jersey, and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community, we determined that his participation in the September 25th and 26th concerts at Gillette Stadium would cross that line,” Kraft said in a statement.
DeAngelis said she read Sheeran’s statement in response to Macklemore being dropped from the tour, in which he explained it had been the promoter’s decision, not his own.
Sheeran wrote that he “spoke with the venues at length all week to try to build a bridge” before Macklemore was dropped.
The mother said she wasn’t pleased with the singer’s response.
“It was very disappointing, to be quite honest, because we had followed along with what was said, and we thought, this is a message of peace. This is a message of hope. This is a message of a call to action,” DeAngelis said, adding, “Macklemore has been someone who’s spoken out for a bit now, so it certainly couldn’t have been a surprise, you know.”
“I thought, ‘you can’t stand up for free speech. You don’t want to stand up against something that’s so terrible,’” she said.
DeAngelis said she was also concerned by “the second side” to the controversy.
“Now I’m hearing about security concerns and about increased police force and protesting, and I think that’s fine for me, but I have a 10-year-old, so I don’t know,” she said.
A coalition of pro-Palestinian organizations said they would demonstrate near the concert venue Saturday afternoon to “return the conversation to Palestine, and return Philadelphia to action.”
The Philadelphia Police Department said it will continue to monitor the event and make “any necessary adjustments based on public safety needs.”
“As with all large events at the stadium complex, the Philadelphia Police Department is working closely with venue and event organizers to help ensure the safety of concertgoers, employees, and neighborhood residents,” the department said in a statement Saturday.
Heather Park said she was concerned the concert would be canceled due to a lack of support for the event.
Park, who has been waiting to see Sheeran in concert since the last time he came to Philadelphia, said the controversy that erupted surrounding Macklemore’s statement “is just ridiculous.”
“I’m still going,” Park told CNN. “Even if Macklemore was still opening up, I would still go. Like, he’s allowed to have his opinion. I’m allowed to have mine.”
The price tracking site TicketData noted while it is normal for many concert resale ticket prices to drop closer to the show date, resale prices for Saturday’s Sheeran show have fallen by a significant amount.
Notably, TicketData said, the promoter started allowing refunds for the show when ticketholders requested them through Ticketmaster’s chat support. The move effectively puts “a floor under the resale market,” Keith Pagello, founder of TicketData, told CNN, adding that an opening act dropping off is not typically a circumstance where a promoter would offer refunds, “so they are going above and beyond here.”
Debate continues ahead of curtain time
The concert, which was originally advertised as 5:30 p.m., is now slated to start at 8:00 p.m. CNN has reached out to the touring company, Messina Touring Group, for comment but did not immediately hear back.
It’s not clear whether the superstar will address the lack of opening acts during the concert, but British singer-songwriter Billy Bragg called on Sheeran to say “Free Palestine” from the stage.
“If Sheeran truly wants to regain his credibility, then he has an opportunity to begin that process tonight, when he takes to the stage at Lincoln Field in Philadelphia,” Bragg wrote in a post on Instagram.
Sheeran has not addressed the controversy since his Instagram post on Tuesday, when he said, “There is a reason I do not use my professional platform for politics — my audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds. Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum. I respect Macklemore’s strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes. However, there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: peace.”
Irish singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe, who along with Finneas, the Irish band Beoga and the Danish band Lukas Graham all withdrew from their opening slots and as Sheeran’s support band on the tour, called for the focus to be put on the stadium owner rather than Sheeran.
“All I keep hearing is Ed Sheeran this, Ed Sheeran that. When you really should be focusing on the likes of Robert Kraft,” Rowe said in a video posted on TikTok. “You should be using this opportunity to plaster Robert Kraft’s face everywhere. Someone who tried to shut down free speech. Someone who tried to silence the voices of people who are shouting about genocide.”
Palestine Legal litigation director Radhika Sainath said Sheeran should “have called Kraft’s bluff” in a statement. The organization says it aims to protect “the civil and constitutional rights of people in the U.S. who speak out for Palestinian freedom.”
“If Sheeran had fought back instead of giving in to censorship and bullying, not only would he have retained the moral high ground with his millions of fans – and been on the right side of history – he would likely have a strong case for hundreds of thousands of dollars in damages for whatever losses he incurred over Kraft’s threatened cancellation,” Sainath said.
But prior to his removal from the tour, Macklemore’s comments at the concert also prompted criticism from the singer Pink and a petition against his appearances.
The Jewish Federation of Greater Philadelphia said in a statement it “believes in strong public debate and civil discourse, including on Israel and the Palestinians, and artists have every right to take part in it. Our concern is with the problematic history of the messenger and the specific message, as well as the venue he chose to deliver it in.”
The group referenced Macklemore’s 2014 performance – which he has publicly apologized for – when he wore what he called “a random costume” of a hooked false nose, wig and fake beard, but which observers widely read as an antisemitic caricature.
“Our position remains unambiguous: we are unwavering in our commitment to Israel as a free, prosperous, Jewish and democratic state, and we believe that Palestinians deserve to live in peace and prosperity as well. At a moment of extraordinary pain and polarization, we should be working to create spaces that recognize the humanity and dignity of Palestinians and Israelis alike,” the Jewish Federation of Greater Philadelphia said. “A concert attended by tens of thousands of people from different backgrounds should be an opportunity to bring people together, not deepen the divisions between them.”
CNN’s Danny Freeman, Sarah Boxer, Zoe Sottile, Miriam Elder, Maria Sole Campinoti and Choire Sicha contributed to this report.

Title: Staffing shortages, traffic jams and a culture war: Inside the fight over America's national parks
Article_Text:
For Sam Peterson, it was love at first sight: the sweeping views of densely forested valleys and sun gleaming through snow-tipped mountain peaks.
After navigating Glacier National Park’s iconic Going-to-the-Sun Road, a 52-mile highway crossing the Continental Divide in Montana, Peterson spotted a park ranger, sporting the iconic grey and green uniform, and knew instantly what he wanted to do with his life.
He left his job as a history teacher in Oregon to become a ranger in northeast Washington state at the Lake Roosevelt National Recreation Area. After being promoted to a permanent position, Peterson had a two-month gap before his new role began. Eager to keep working, he volunteered for a temporary assignment at the Jimmy Carter National Historical Park in Plains, Georgia.
Then came the call: former President Jimmy Carter had died. Peterson agreed without hesitation to stay on and help with the funeral, delaying the start of his new position by two weeks.
But the decision cost him his career.
The Trump administration imposed a government-wide hiring freeze, halting his promotion. A month later, on February 14, he was notified, along with tens of thousands of other park rangers and civil servants across multiple agencies, that his new position has been terminated - a day employees have since coined the “Valentine’s Day massacre.”
“There were some tears, there was shock. There was just this fear, this feeling of failure,” Peterson said, describing how he and his wife were given 60 days to move out of the National Park housing they’d settled into.
CNN spoke to more than a dozen current and former employees of the National Park Service, advocates and former officials who described an agency that has been gutted over the last 18 months, with permanent staff pushed out, vacancies left unfilled, funds redirected and educational material altered – all while visitations to dozens of parks reach record-highs and as extreme weather fuels dangerous conditions.
The challenges, some fear, are overwhelming for a system beloved by the American public and monumental for preserving America’s legacy and natural beauty.
‘It all blew up’
Overall, roughly 1,000 NPS employees were fired that February 14, as part of an effort led by President Donald Trump and Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency to drastically reduce the number of people working for the federal government.
Peterson, who said he was making $39,000 a year at the time, had just returned from buying his wife flowers when he was notified his position had been terminated. “It has been determined that you are not effective at your job,” the email read.
“We’d put everything out there to do this really cool thing and serve our community,” his wife, Ashley St. Aubin-Clark, told CNN. “It just felt like it all blew up.”
Multiple legal actions were taken against the mass layoffs, and in March 2025, a judge issued a preliminary injunction ordering federal agencies to reinstate probationary employees that had been fired, finding the government dismissed the employees for performance reasons it knew “good and well” were a lie.
Peterson was offered his old job back, but by then he was already in a new position at a museum in Astoria, Oregon. “I had already signed a lease for an apartment… My wife had already resigned her teaching position in the community we had been living in.”
In September last year, the same judge issued his final ruling, calling the firings illegal but declining to order reinstatement, noting the terminated employees had “moved on with their lives.” The government has appealed the ruling.
Since Trump’s return to office, the NPS has lost approximately 4,000 permanent employees, a drop of about 24%, through layoffs, buyouts, early retirements, and a nine-month hiring freeze, according to the National Parks Conservation Association.
The decline builds on a longer slide: The NPS had already lost some 2,000 permanent staff between 2011 and 2024, according to Emily Douce, deputy vice-president for government affairs at the NPCA.
Despite the hiring freeze being lifted in October 2025, separate policies set by the Office of Personnel Management and the Office of Management and Budget have capped federal hiring at no more than one new employee for every four who leave, with exceptions for public safety roles. This means most vacancies at national parks remain unfilled.
Packed parks and low morale
The staffing strain comes as many national parks tally record-high visitation numbers, leading to standstill traffic on park roads, packed parking lots and overcrowded visitor centers – all of which raise concerns about damage to the wildlife and landscapes the parks aim to preserve.
At Yosemite National Park, the reservation system was eliminated and visitation surged 45 percent, according to government data. Douce said the result has been “devastating.”
“Almost like a Disneyland or Disney World, rather than enjoying a peaceful place in a park,” she told CNN.
In the midst of America’s 250th anniversary this summer, park rangers were responsible for managing sites in Philadelphia, New York, and across the West that were expected to see huge visitation numbers. “It’s really sad because these poor Park Service employees want to protect these places, but it’s really difficult with this huge reduction in staffing,” Douce said.
The situation is stressful for the park employees who remain and are left doing extra work while dealing with “uncertainty and fear about whether or not they’re going to be next,” said Bill Wade, a former ranger who now leads the Association of National Park Rangers. “Morale is the lowest it’s ever been that anybody can remember,” he told CNN.
They’re also facing pressure as the consequences of the climate crisis wreak ecological havoc on the country’s national parks, with a historic drought dwindling water resources and fueling wildfires across the West.
As the world continues to burn more fossil fuel, warming Earth’s atmosphere, extreme weather events are becoming more frequent and deadly, as seen by relentless heat waves, rampant wildfires and catastrophic flooding – posing a greater challenge to land preservation.
Congress, for its part, has tried to hold the line – with bipartisan support on park preservation. The administration’s fiscal year 2026 budget proposal for discretionary spending included $1.2 billion in NPS cuts – a 37% decrease – the largest in the agency’s 110-year history. Congress rejected it and passed a budget with just a 2% decrease. For the 2027 fiscal year, the administration again asked for more than $1 billion to be cut from NPS funding. While the budget hasn’t been finalized, the House Appropriations Subcommittee approved just a 1% funding cut.
But Congress’s spending decisions have not translated into staffing. John Garder, who has tracked NPS budgets for the NPCA for 15 years, told CNN parks are being told not to use the money on staffing, as lawmakers directed, but to instead use it for things like repair projects, wildlife monitoring equipment or landscaping equipment.
“It’s an affront to Congress when both parties provided sufficient funding for the level of staff that they used to have and gave specific direction to have sufficient staff to meet the Park Service mission,” Garder said. “And it’s an affront to the American people who treasure these places and expect their parks to be staffed and cared for.”
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, testifying before the House Natural Resources Committee in May, defended the administration’s approach. He said the department had “hired thousands and thousands of people into the national parks system,” and the budget focused on visitor-facing operations.
But Garder said the “thousands” Burgum cited were seasonal employees, not permanent replacements for the career scientists and resource managers the agency has lost. The number of permanent hires is between 500 and 600, Garder said.
In a statement to CNN, a spokesperson for the Department of the Interior did not respond to questions about how many permanent hires had been made, but said the department was “modernizing to eliminate unnecessary duplication, improve efficiency, strengthen coordination, and better align resources with mission-critical work.”
In June, Maine independent Sen. Angus King, the ranking member of the Senate subcommittee on national parks, and other senators wrote to Burgum demanding transparency about the redirection of park funds toward what King called “vanity projects” in Washington, DC, including ornamental fountains, the renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, and covering statues in gold leaf, none of which were among the Park Service’s top construction priorities.
The Department of the Interior also did not respond to questions about the redirection of funds, but said it has been working on “many deferred maintenance projects throughout the country.”
A fight over what the parks can say
The staffing collapse is one piece of a broader effort. The administration has also moved to reshape how America’s public lands tell the nation’s history – and who gets to decide what stories are told.
In spring 2025, Trump signed an executive order titled “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History,” directing federal agencies to remove descriptions, depictions and other content that “inappropriately disparage Americans past or living, including persons living in colonial times.”
The order set in motion efforts to revise or remove interpretive signs and other materials across national parks and federal sites, touching on subjects ranging from slavery and Indigenous history to climate change.
Within weeks, QR codes were displayed in parks nationwide, inviting the public to report anything they found objectionable. Some critics called them snitch signs.
A seasonal ranger who worked at Mount Rushmore last summer described the process to CNN: A visitor scans the code and the complaint goes to Washington. If the complaint is deemed credible, an assessor is dispatched and staff are told to remove the material or be fired.
“If my site superintendent, who’s been in the park service for over 20 years, said, ‘I’m not going to do that. You can kick rocks,’ they would be fired on the spot,” the ranger said. “This level of censorship threatens everyone’s jobs.” He spoke on condition of anonymity while working at a national historical park that focuses on Indigenous history, exactly the kind of content the order targets.
Under the directive, at least 45 signs that covered topics ranging from climate change to Native American history were altered, according to Save Our Signs, an advocacy group that tracks changes to NPS displays.
At Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming, a former ranger said staff were ordered to take down part of an exhibit that asked visitors to consider the complicated legacy of Gustavus Cheyney Doane, an explorer and soldier who was involved in the massacre of members of the Piegan Blackfeet tribe in 1870. The order came by phone, the ranger said, noting “there’s no trace” of the order if someone were to file a Freedom of Information Act request to see it.
Another flashpoint in the controversy has been the iconic photograph, “Scourged Back,” depicting welts and scars across the body of a formerly enslaved Louisiana man, one of the 19th century’s defining photographs. The Washington Post reported that officials at an unidentified national park had ordered that the photo be taken down, along with other signs and exhibits related to slavery. The National Park Service denied the report and said no such order was given, but by then, it had already sparked concern over historical censorship.
In May, the National Park Service released its database of 35,700 public submissions received between June 2025 and January 2026. About two-thirds were used not to flag exhibits but to defend them or to criticize the policy, express support for park rangers, or demand the signs be taken down. Fewer than 2 percent used the tool for its intended purpose.
The administration’s censorship seems to extend beyond signs and exhibits, one former ranger told CNN. SJ Joslin, a wildlife biologist who ran the bat program at Yosemite and managed the park’s terrestrial wildlife data, was fired in August 2025 after hanging a transgender pride flag from El Capitan while off-duty.
There’s a long history of people temporarily hanging flags from El Capitan, Joslin said. “As long as people have been climbing El Cap, it’s been this canvas for First Amendment speech, and there’s never been any repercussions from anyone flying flags.”
Joslin, who is nonbinary and uses they/them pronouns, told CNN the flag hung from a naturally formed heart-shaped feature 800 feet up the rock face for about two-and-a-half hours in May 2025 before Joslin and others they were with took it down.
“The whole point was, like, it’s this heart feature on an iconic granite monolith, and we’re hanging the symbol of love in a heart,” Joslin said.
The next day, Yosemite’s acting superintendent signed a new rule prohibiting people from hanging large banners and flags in areas designated as wilderness, which would include El Capitan.
Other high-profile instances of a banner or flag being hoisted on the rock face were seen in the prior year. In February 2025, a group of Yosemite employees hung an American flag upside down – a symbolic distress call – in response to the staffing cuts. And in June 2024, a banner reading “Stop the genocide” was displayed to bring attention to the Israeli offensive in Gaza, The San Francisco Chronicle reported.
In response to inquiries, a spokesperson for the National Park Service did not comment on Joslin’s termination, but said the agency “will not tolerate violations of laws and regulations” affecting park resources or the visitors experience, and that demonstrations outside designated First Amendment areas require a permit.
Today, Joslin still lives near Yosemite and has yet to find another job. On Memorial Day weekend, they went into the park and picked up trash. When they tried to volunteer at the park, they say they were unofficially told their name was “untouchable.”
A legacy at risk of being lost
What worries those CNN spoke to who have spent their lives in the parks is not just what has happened, but what cannot easily be rebuilt.
Adam Auerbach, a former seasonal ranger at Rocky Mountain National Park in Colorado, spent months working toward a Presidential Management Fellowship, a nearly 50-year-old federal leadership pipeline. The administration killed the program before he reached the final round of the application process.
Auerbach now watches as positions that once went to people with five years of experience go to applicants with 15 years of experience and a PhD, because the market is flooded with displaced federal workers
“They’re cutting today’s civil servants,” he told CNN, “but they’re also cutting out the pathway so that there can be qualified people to follow in their footsteps.”
Garder, the NPCA budget director, put it plainly. “You can systematically destroy the park service in the span of a year or two or four. … But you can’t rebuild it in such a short amount of time.”
Peterson said he would like to return someday, likening the excitement he used to feel about the job to “the night before a big school field trip when you’re 13 years old.” But his wife has already given up a lot.
“I have those positive memories of being a park ranger,” Peterson said. “But she only has the negative side of it. She only has the part where her husband got fired from his dream job, we had to move, and all these terrible things happened.”
Meanwhile, Peterson still volunteers at a park site. He lobbies Congress to keep the parks funded and he still has his ranger hat. Someday, he hopes to give his wife the good experience of being married to a park ranger: the hikes after work, the wildlife, the house in a park.

Title: MLB roundup: Braves top Astros, wrap up postseason berth
Article_Text:
Field Level Media
                
19 Sep 2026, 13:25 GMT+10
            
(Photo credit: Troy Taormina)
Michael Harris II, Ronald Acuna Jr. and Matt Olson slugged two-run home runs and deadline acquisition Tyler Mahle continued his exceptional pitching for the visiting Atlanta Braves, who secured a postseason berth with a 6-2 victory over the Houston Astros on Friday.
Atlanta qualified for the postseason for the eighth time in nine seasons. The Braves lowered their magic number to clinch the National League East to three over the Philadelphia Phillies.
Harris provided Mahle a 2-0 lead when he followed a one-out single by Matt Olson with an opposite-field blast to left off Astros starter Peter Lambert (8-10) in the fourth inning. Harris (3-for-5) drove a first-pitch slurve from Lambert 367 feet for his 26th homer of the year.
Mahle (7-10) improved to 4-1 with a 1.28 ERA over eight starts since his acquisition from the Giants. He allowed one run on three hits and one walk with six strikeouts over six innings.
Guardians 5, Athletics 3
Jose Ramirez hit a solo homer in the sixth inning for his 1,000th career RBI after rookie Travis Bazzana went deep in the fifth, fueling host Cleveland to a victory over the Athletics.
The Guardians have won three in a row to move a game ahead of the second-place Chicago White Sox in the American League Central. Joey Cantillo (10-9) threw six scoreless innings in relief, and Cade Smith handled the ninth for his 38th save.
Zack Gelof belted a three-run homer in the first inning for the Athletics, whose losing skid reached four games. Reliever Scott Blewett (2-1) permitted one run on one hit in 1 2/3 innings.
Padres 8, Marlins 2
Ty France clouted a three-run homer to cap a six-run fifth inning as San Diego stopped visiting Miami to forge a three-way tie atop the National League wild-card standings.
Winning for the 11th time in 12 games, the Padres pulled even with the Chicago Cubs and Philadelphia Phillies, who both lost. San Diego's magic number for clinching a playoff spot dropped to four.
San Diego starter Nick Pivetta (3-2) worked five innings, yielding four hits and a run. Marlins reliever Cade Gibson (5-2) was charged with the first two runs in the game-changing fifth. The Padres' Jackson Merrill and the Marlins' Agustin Ramirez homered.
Mets 6, Phillies 3
Zac Thornton tossed six solid innings, Juan Soto homered among his three hits and host New York beat Philadelphia.
Soto went 3-for-5 for the Mets, while Francisco Lindor and Carson Benge each collected two hits. Thornton (5-5) gave up two runs on five hits.
Edmundo Sosa finished 3-for-3 with a homer and Derek Hill also went deep for the Phillies, who fell to 7-9 this month. Newly acquired Jose Urquidy threw 4 2/3 shutout innings after opener Tim Mayza (3-4) surrendered three runs while getting just one out.
Reds 6, Cubs 4
Cincinnati scored three times in the sixth inning in a back-and-forth win over visiting Chicago.
Elly De La Cruz had two hits, two walks and two runs for the Reds. Cincinnati starter Chase Burns and reliever Julian Aguiar (1-0) each allowed two runs on four hits in three innings.
Cubs starter Clay Holmes (6-8) surrendered six runs on three hits in 5 1/3 innings. Ian Happ homered for Chicago, and Michael Conforto amassed three hits.
Twins 3, Angels 0
Connor Prielipp allowed two hits over a career-high seven innings and fellow rookie Walker Jenkins went 3-for-4 with a home run as Minnesota topped Los Angeles in Anaheim, Calif.
Travis Adams pitched a 1-2-3 ninth inning to pick up his third save. Jenkins, who began his career going 4-for-45, homered for the second straight game on his sixth consecutive hit in the series.
Jose Siri had two hits for the Angels. Grayson Rodriguez (4-8) gave up three runs on eight hits in 6 2/3 innings.
Brewers 6, Orioles 5 (10 innings)
Sal Frelick singled home a 10th-inning run and visiting Milwaukee pulled out a victory against Baltimore.
Trevor Megill (3-3) was the winning pitcher despite a blown save. Chad Patrick retired the Orioles in order in the bottom of the 10th for his sixth save.
Milwaukee's Jackson Chourio and Baltimore's Pete Alonso hit three-run homers early in the game. Gunnar Henderson and Coby Mayo both collected three hits for the Orioles.
Dodgers 8, Giants 2
Mookie Betts homered twice, including his 53rd career leadoff homer, and Josue De Paula hit a tiebreaking double to help Los Angeles produce a victory over visiting San Francisco.
The Dodgers socked five home runs while winning for the 12th time in the last 15 games. Max Muncy and Kyle Tucker hit back-to-back homers in the eighth, and Betts and Will Smith repeated the feat later in the frame. Tyler Glasnow (5-1) gave up two runs and three hits while striking out a season-high 10 in six innings.
Jung Hoo Lee homered and Jonah Cox had an RBI single as the Giants fell for the fifth time in seven games.
Yankees 9, Diamondbacks 2
George Lombard Jr. had two hits and three RBIs, and his two-run single capped a five-run first-inning outburst as New York cruised past Arizona in Phoenix.
Ben Rice and Lombard homered and Rice added a triple as the Yankees won for the fourth time in five games. Gerrit Cole (9-9) gave up two runs on four hits in six innings.
Corbin Carroll homered and doubled for the Diamondbacks, who have lost five of six to see their NL wild-card chances fade. Eduardo Rodriguez (15-7) yielded seven runs in 5 1/3 innings.
Red Sox 4, Rays 2
Roman Anthony homered and had three RBIs, Jahmai Jones went deep and Boston cooled off first-place Tampa Bay in St. Petersburg, Fla.
Anthony went 2-for-5 while Caleb Durbin was 2-for-3 for the Red Sox. Boston starter Ranger Suarez (8-4) fought control issues but allowed one run on three hits in 5 2/3 innings.
Junior Caminero doubled, walked twice and drove in a run for the Rays, who had only five hits as their six-game winning streak ended. Ian Seymour (9-7) allowed four runs on seven hits in five innings.
Rangers 7, Blue Jays 1
Corey Seager capped a four-run second inning with an RBI double as Texas topped Toronto in Arlington, Texas.
The Rangers drew 10 walks and moved into a first-place tie with Houston in the American League West. Jake Burger had two RBIs for Texas, which won for the fifth time in six games. Texas took a 4-0 lead in the second inning against Dylan Cease (11-6), who allowed four runs (one earned) on three hits over 2 2/3 innings.
The Blue Jays fell two games back of the White Sox for the final AL wild-card spot. Myles Straw had two hits with an RBI for Toronto, which committed three errors and lost for the third time in four games.
Tigers 11, White Sox 8
Dillon Dingler delivered the go-ahead single and Riley Greene followed with a two-run homer in a five-run eighth inning as visiting Detroit stormed back from six runs down to beat Chicago.
Hao-Yu Lee went 4-for-5 with a homer, three RBIs and two runs for the Tigers. Kevin McGonigle finished 2-for-5 with four RBIs. Drew Sommers (2-4) threw two shutout innings, fanning five, and Kenley Jansen blanked the White Sox in the ninth for his 21st save.
Colson Montgomery and Miguel Vargas each had two hits and three RBIs for the White Sox, who have lost three out of four. Sean Newcomb (2-5) got only two outs in relief while allowing three runs.
Pirates 8, Royals 5
Konnor Griffin had four hits and two RBIs and Spencer Horwitz delivered a tiebreaking two-run single in the seventh as Pittsburgh rallied to beat visiting Kansas City.
Pittsburgh trailed 4-0 after the top of the third inning and 5-2 entering the bottom of the fourth. The Pirates won their second straight after losing four of their previous five.
Vinnie Pasquantino and Michael Massey each homered as the Royals scored five runs against Pittsburgh ace Paul Skenes, who scattered six hits in his six innings. Royals starter Randy Dobnak allowed four runs on seven hits over 3 2/3 innings.
Nationals 9, Cardinals 1
Cade Cavalli pitched five scoreless innings and recorded the 200th strikeout of his first full major league season, leading Washington to a victory at St. Louis.
Cavalli (13-5), who agreed with the Nationals earlier in the day on a four-year, $47 million contract extension, allowed four hits and struck out six. Dylan Crews hit a two-run homer and Yohandy Morales added a two-run double for Washington.
Cardinals starter Kyle Leahy (10-5) allowed seven runs, six earned, on five hits over three innings. Leo Bernal went 3-for-4.
Mariners 5, Rockies 4
Lazaro Montes homered leading off the top of the ninth, J.P. Crawford went deep to open the game, and Seattle beat Colorado in Denver.
Randy Arozarena finished with three hits as the Mariners logged their second win in a row. Carlos Vargas (2-0) recorded one out in relief, and Andres Munoz earned his 28th save with a scoreless ninth inning.
Cole Carrigg, Connor Norby and Jake McCarthy had three hits apiece and Ezequiel Tovar contributed two hits for the Rockies, who have lost three in a row and 11 of 12. Jordan Romano (0-4) served up Montes' homer.

Title: Ed Sheeran changes Philadelphia concert time as protests planned after Macklemore fallout
Article_Text:
Ed Sheeran changes Philadelphia concert time as protests planned after Macklemore fallout
The concert was originally scheduled to begin at 5:30pm local time, but the start time has since been moved to 8pm
Ed Sheeran has changed the start time of his Philadelphia concert as the fallout from Macklemore’s removal from his Loop Tour continues, with pro-Palestinian protesters also planning a demonstration outside the venue.
Sheeran is scheduled to perform at Lincoln Financial Field on Saturday, September 19. The concert was originally scheduled to begin at 5:30pm local time, but the start time has since been moved to 8pm on Ticketmaster. The change follows the withdrawal of the tour’s supporting acts, leaving Sheeran without announced opening performers for the Philadelphia show.
Macklemore was removed from the remaining US dates of the tour after making pro-Palestinian comments during his performance at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium earlier this month. Sheeran has said the decision was made by the promoter after upcoming venues communicated that they would pull the shows if Macklemore remained on the line-up.
Following Macklemore’s departure, Finneas, Lukas Graham, Aaron Rowe and Sheeran’s backing band Beoga all withdrew from the remaining dates. Beoga said it fully supported Macklemore’s message, while the other departures further reshaped the remaining tour schedule.
The Philadelphia concert is also expected to draw protests. Local pro-Palestinian groups have announced plans to rally outside Lincoln Financial Field ahead of the show, with organisers saying the demonstration will focus on Palestinian advocacy and concerns over the treatment of Macklemore’s comments.
Ticket resale prices for the Philadelphia show have also fallen as the concert approaches. Tickets that were listed at $91 on Thursday were available for as little as $66.30 on Friday, while other reporting put the cheapest available ticket at around $67. TicketData founder Keith Pagello cautioned that falling resale prices are common immediately before concerts and do not necessarily indicate an effect from the controversy.
Sheeran has said he has personal views about the Israel-Palestine conflict but does not want his concerts to become political forums. He has also denied being responsible for Macklemore’s removal from the tour.
