Title: Revenge of the labor movement: Democrats with union backgrounds aim to retake Congress
Article_Text:
Revenge of the labor movement: Democrats with union backgrounds aim to retake Congress
default
The US labor movement is having a banner election year.
More than three dozen nominees for open House and Senate races across the US have backgrounds as labor union representatives or members.
Several nominees are running in heavily blue districts, making it almost certain they will win the seat in November’s midterms, while others are in highly contested races that are likely to determine control of the House and possibly the Senate. Most are Democrats, though some are running as independents.
The early success of so many candidates with ties to labor comes as Democrats work to rebuild their support among working-class voters, centering their campaign messaging around affordability issues.
But the messenger matters, too.
“In a political environment that’s been dominated by wealthy elites for decades, union candidates provide a level of trust and credibility that’s simply unmatched,” Steve Smith, a spokesperson for the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of labor unions in the US, told the Guardian. “These candidates are at long last returning the levers of power to the people.”
A 2024 study by Cal State and UCLA researchers found working-class voters are 6.4 percentage points more likely to prefer a political candidate with a working-class occupation over one with an upper-class occupation.
These candidates are at long last returning the levers of power to the peopleSteve Smith, AFL-CIO
Yet a 2026 report by the Center for Working-Class Politics found working-class candidates make up just 8-14% of Democratic and 5-8% of Republican congressional candidates.
Union candidates invoked pro-worker themes 159% more than non-union candidates, the report found. Running more union members as candidates, its authors argued, could increase the representation ordinary Americans have in Congress, by elevating people who can speak to and deliver on issues that affect the working class.
“Voters want elected leaders who understand the struggles working people face in an economy rigged against us,” Smith said. “In every area of the country, at every level, union members are running for office and winning because they bring lived experience in leveling the playing field for workers and creating a brighter future for our families.”
Americans overwhelmingly favor labor unions, according to recent annual Gallup polls, with 68% approving labor unions in 2025. But union density has been on a decline in recent decades, from more than 30% in the 1950s to 10% in 2025, correlating to a drastic increase in wealth and income inequality in the US.
Related: ‘They’re ready to come home’: the movement to bring young voters back to Democrats
In 2024, Donald Trump sought to woo labor leadersandblue-collar voters with populist trade promises. But exit polls and surveys conducted after the presidential election foundlittleevidence that union members had shifted toward Trump.
According to the VoteCast survey conducted for the Associated Press and Fox News after the 2024 election, union members preferred Harris over Trump by 16% in 2024, 57% to 41% for Trump, matching Biden’s 16% lead over Trump with union households in 2020.
Trump was formerly a union member, but he resigned from the Screen Actors Guild in February 2021 rather than facing disciplinary charges from the union for violating its constitution regarding his actions and role in inciting the attack on the US Capitol on 6 January 2021.
In his resignation letter, Trump wrote “Who cares!” and accused the union of never doing anything for him. In response to his resignation, the union issued a two-word statement: “Thank you.”
Meet the Senate and House candidates identified as having labor union backgrounds who are running to join the roughly 25 current members of Congress who have previously worked in the labor movement or in a job represented by a union.
default
***
Todd Achilles
Candidate for US Senate, Idaho
Independent Todd Achilles, a former American Federation of Teachers member from his work as a public policy professor and lecturer, is running for the US Senate in a race where the Democratic nominee withdrew in July.
***
Abdul El-Sayed
Candidate for US Senate, Michigan
Abdul El-Sayed is a former American Association of University Professors member and other higher education unions from his time working as a professor and scholar at Columbia University, Harvard University, the University of Michigan, Wayne State University and American University. The union made its first ever national political endorsement in endorsing his Senate campaign.
In an interview with the Guardian in July, El-Sayed explained his critique of the economy and the impact of concentrated corporate power.
“If the markets actually worked the way they’re supposed to, you might have some efficient movement of money,” he said. “The problem is, we don’t live in capitalism, we live in oligopoly.”
***
Troy Jackson
Candidate for US Senate, Maine
Troy Jackson worked several past union jobs as a member of the unions of Painters and Allied Trades (IUPAT), the Machinists (IAM), Operating Engineers (IUOE), United Auto Workers (UAW), and Laborers’ International Union of North America (Liuna).
“Everything Troy fights for comes from his working-class roots as a logger from Allagash and the 1998 blockade, when he stood up to powerful landowners undercutting Maine workers,” Jackson’s campaign manager, Dan Gottlieb, said in a statement.
Gottlieb added: “Mainers know whose side Troy is on: theirs. For him, solidarity isn’t a slogan – it’s how he’s lived his life.”
***
Angie Nixon
Candidate for US Senate, Florida
Angie Nixon is a state legislator in Florida and the Democratic nominee for Senate in a special election to fill Marco Rubio’s vacated seat. She previously has worked as a union organizer, directing the Florida Public Services Union’s (FPSU) higher education campaign.
***
Dan Osborn
Candidate for US Senate, Nebraska
Dan Osborn, a former president of Bakery, Confectionery, Tobacco Workers and Grain Millers International Union (BCTGM) Local 50G, which represents Kellogg’s workers, is running for the US Senate in Nebraska as an independent. He faces Republican Pete Ricketts, the heir to billionaire Joe Ricketts, co-founder of TD Ameritrade.
***
James Talarico
Candidate for US Senate, Texas
As a public school teacher, James Talarico was a member of the San Antonio Alliance of Teachers and Support Personnel. He is also a longtime member of the Texas State Employees Union (TSEU – CWA Local 6186).
***
Colin Allred
Candidate for Texas’s 33rd congressional district
The former congressman Colin Allred is runningagain this cycle in a newly redrawn Democratic-dominant district in Texas. He is a formermember of the NFL Players Association, the union representing National Football League players.
Chris Backemeyer
Candidate for Nebraska’s first congressional district
Chris Backemeyer, a former US state department employee and the Democratic nominee for Nebraska’s first congressional district, is a member of American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE) Local 1534.
Mitchell Berman
Candidate for Wisconsin’s first congressional district
Mitchell Berman worked a union job in college at UPS, where he was a member of Teamsters Local 344. As a nurse, he has worked several union jobs including as a member of the Wisconsin Federation of Nurses & Health Professionals and National Nurses United.
“Coming from a working-class background, understanding what folks are going through [and] having walked a mile in my neighbor’s shoes gives me the ability to look at legislation from the perspective of having some empathy and understanding for what people are dealing with,” Berman said in August.
***
Bob Brooks
Candidate for Pennsylvania’s seventh congressional district
Bob Brooks, a former president of the Pennsylvania Professional Fire Fighters Association, is running to flip one of the state’s swing districts.
“We need to change who’s representing us and who’s making the rules and the laws,” Brooks said in June. “That’s what inspired me to do this. I think we need more everyday people down there, because everyday people are the ones that are struggling.”
***
Connie Chan
Candidate for California’s 11th congressional district
A former member of the International Federation of Professional and Technical Engineers (IFPTE) Local 21, Connie Chan is in a general election runoff to replace Nancy Pelosi’s vacated seat in California’s 11th congressional district.
***
Darializa Avila Chevalier
Candidate for New York’s 13th congressional district
In one of the biggest primary upsets in 2026, Darializa Avila Chevalier defeated Adriano Espaillat, the incumbent congressman and chair of the Congressional Hispanic caucus, and she is expected to easily win the general election in a district that leans heavily in favor of Democrats.
She is a union member of the United Auto Workers Local 2325.
“That really changed the course of my education and my PhD program, to be able to be part of a union that fought for me, my work conditions, my wage, and made it possible for me to continue my program,” she said in June, reflecting on her experience joining the union. “I was able to teach at a pace that was manageable, right, with a workload that was manageable, but also be paid enough to actually lead a dignified life.”
***
Carmela Conroy
Candidate for Washington’s fifth congressional district
Carmela Conroy was a union member represented by the American Foreign Service Association.
***
Sam Forstag
Candidate for Montana’s at-large congressional district
Sam Forstag served as the vice-president of the Forest Service Council Local 60, an arm of the National Federation of Federal Employees.
“There is genuinely a fundamental lack of representation for working people in federal office right now, and that has serious, substantive effects on what kind of policies they actually prioritize and what they pass,” Forstag said in February. “The primary function of government is to step in when the market is not meeting a need and to make people’s lives materially better. And it seems like some people at the national level forgot about that.”
***
Chris Gallant
Candidate for New York’s first congressional district
Chris Gallant served as the president of his local union with the National Air Traffic Controllers Association.
***
Vince George
Candidate for West Virginia’s first congressional district
Vince George was a member of the West Virginia Education Association and is a retired union member of American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees (Afscme).
***
Bob Harvie
Candidate for Pennsylvania’s first congressional district
A teacher for more than 20 years, Bob Harvie is a former member of the Bucks County Technical High School Education Association.
***
Missi Hesketh
Candidate for Missouri’s seventh congressional district
Missi Hesketh is a teacher and a member the National Education Association and a former member of the Missouri State Teachers Association.
***
Bill Hill
Candidate for Alaska’s at-large congressional district
Bill Hill, an independent, is a former unionconstruction worker. The leading Democrat in the race dropped out and endorsed his campaign.
***
Amanda Hollowell
Candidate for Georgia’s first congressional district
Amanda Hollowell was the state director for 9to5 in Georgia, a worker-led organization that arose from women-led worker organizing in the 1970s.
***
Jake Johnson
Candidate for Minnesota’s first congressional district
A high school math teacher, Jake Johnson served as an official with his local teachers’ union.
“To me, a lot of the great things that happen in public schools happen because of unions. We’re the ones fighting for smaller class sizes. We’re the ones fighting for reasonable wages,” Johnson said in July. “That’s happening because of teachers’ unions. We’re the ones that are raising the bar as far as teacher quality.”
***
Tanya Lloyd
Candidate for Texas’s 27th congressional district
Tanya Lloyd is a former union member of the Texas American Federation of Teachers.
***
Donavan McKinney
Candidate for Michigan’s 13th congressional district
A former organizer with the Service Employees International Union, Donavan McKinney defeated incumbent representative Shri Thanedar in the Democratic primary and is expected to easily win the district that favors Democrats by 22 percentage points, according to Cook Political Report’s Partisan Voting Index.
***
Analilia Mejia
Candidate for New Jersey’s 11th congressional district
Analilia Mejia, who won a special election in New Jersey’s 11th congressional district in April, is a former union organizer with the Service Employees International Union, Unite Here, and United Food and Commercial Workers.
***
Jena Nelson
Candidate for Oklahoma’s fifth congressional district
The former Oklahoma teacher of the year in 2020, Jena Nelson is a teachers’ union member. The district last flipped blue under Trump’s first term in 2018, but Republicans took back the district in 2020.
***
Richard Pan
Candidate for California’s sixth congressional district
Richard Pan, a pediatrician, is a member of the Union of American Physicians and Dentists – Afscme Local 206.
***
Brian Poindexter
Candidate for Ohio’s seventh congressional district
An ironworker, apprenticeship instructor and former organizer, Brian Poindexter is running to unseat Max Miller, the congressman who is facingcalls to resign due to domestic assault allegations from his ex-wife, the daughter of Republican senator Bernie Moreno, and similar allegations made against him by Stephanie Grisham, a former White House press secretary under Trump’s first administration.
“People are working harder and harder. We’re getting less and less and we’re getting more and more of the burden,” Poindexter said. “I’d like to see an economy that works for all of us, not just the wealthy. We need to build an economy that rewards work, not just wealth.”
***
Chris Rabb
Candidate for Pennsylvania’s third congressional district
ChrisRabbhelped organize adjuncts at Temple University with the United Academics of Philadelphia, while he worked as an adjunct professor at the university.
***
Kyle Rable
Candidate for Texas’s 19th congressional district
Kyle Rable is a member of the Texas State Employees Union, CWA Local 6186.
***
Lauren Reinhold
Candidate for Kansas’s first congressional district
A former federal employee, Lauren Reinhold served as a union steward and officer while working at the Social Security Administration and National Labor Relations Board (NLRB).
***
Ceretta Smith
Candidate for Georgia’s 12th congressional district
Ceretta Smith is a past president and current member of AFGE Local 2017 and also serves as the fair practices coordinator and women’s coordinator for AFGE Council 172, which represents Defense Commissary Agency workers. The US army veteran has worked as federal employee for more than 20 years.
***
Katy Padilla Stout
Candidate for Texas’s 23rd congressional district
Katy Padilla Stout is a former teachers’ union member with the American Federation of Teachers, which has endorsed her campaign.
***
Trina Swanson
Candidate for Minnesota’s eighth congressional district
Trina Swanson was a member of the American Federation of Government Employees while she worked at US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). She is running against the Republican incumbent representative, Pete Stauber.
“Northern Minnesota taught her that unions strengthen our middle class,” Swanson’s campaign website states.
***
Claire Valdez
Candidate for New York’s seventh congressional district
Claire Valdezwon the Democratic primary for New York’s seventh congressional district after the retirement of Nydia Velázquez. Valdez served as an organizer with United Auto Workers Local 2110 at Columbia University.
***
Mai Vang
Candidate for California’s seventh congressional district
A union member of the California Faculty Association, progressive Mai Vang edged past the 82-year-old Democratic incumbent Doris Matsui in the primary for California’s seventh congressional district. They will face each other again in the November general election.
***
Randy Villegas
Candidate for California’s 22nd congressional district
Randy Villegas is a former United Auto Workers Local 4811 member, which represents higher-education workers.
***
Brandon Wade
Candidate for Oklahoma’s second congressional district
Brandon Wade is an official with International Union of Operating Engineers Local 351, where he has held several different roles while working more than 20 years in the oil and gas industry.
***
Marni von Wilpert
Candidate for California’s 48th congressional district
Marni Von Wilpert is a former NLRB attorney who helped write the comprehensive labor law reform legislation, the Protecting the Right to Organize (Pro) Act, and a member of the Nonprofit Professional Employees Union while working at the Economic Policy Institute.
“One of my biggest priorities for running for Congress myself is to finish this work, to come back as a member of Congress and finally get labor law reform across the finish line,” von Wilpert said.
Her Republican opponent, Jim Desmond, worked as a pilot for Delta Air Lines, where he was a member of the pilots’ union, Air Line Pilots Association, but has opposed unions on project labor agreements.

Title: MLB roundup: Braves top Astros, wrap up postseason berth
Article_Text:
Field Level Media
                
19 Sep 2026, 13:25 GMT+10
            
(Photo credit: Troy Taormina)
Michael Harris II, Ronald Acuna Jr. and Matt Olson slugged two-run home runs and deadline acquisition Tyler Mahle continued his exceptional pitching for the visiting Atlanta Braves, who secured a postseason berth with a 6-2 victory over the Houston Astros on Friday.
Atlanta qualified for the postseason for the eighth time in nine seasons. The Braves lowered their magic number to clinch the National League East to three over the Philadelphia Phillies.
Harris provided Mahle a 2-0 lead when he followed a one-out single by Matt Olson with an opposite-field blast to left off Astros starter Peter Lambert (8-10) in the fourth inning. Harris (3-for-5) drove a first-pitch slurve from Lambert 367 feet for his 26th homer of the year.
Mahle (7-10) improved to 4-1 with a 1.28 ERA over eight starts since his acquisition from the Giants. He allowed one run on three hits and one walk with six strikeouts over six innings.
Guardians 5, Athletics 3
Jose Ramirez hit a solo homer in the sixth inning for his 1,000th career RBI after rookie Travis Bazzana went deep in the fifth, fueling host Cleveland to a victory over the Athletics.
The Guardians have won three in a row to move a game ahead of the second-place Chicago White Sox in the American League Central. Joey Cantillo (10-9) threw six scoreless innings in relief, and Cade Smith handled the ninth for his 38th save.
Zack Gelof belted a three-run homer in the first inning for the Athletics, whose losing skid reached four games. Reliever Scott Blewett (2-1) permitted one run on one hit in 1 2/3 innings.
Padres 8, Marlins 2
Ty France clouted a three-run homer to cap a six-run fifth inning as San Diego stopped visiting Miami to forge a three-way tie atop the National League wild-card standings.
Winning for the 11th time in 12 games, the Padres pulled even with the Chicago Cubs and Philadelphia Phillies, who both lost. San Diego's magic number for clinching a playoff spot dropped to four.
San Diego starter Nick Pivetta (3-2) worked five innings, yielding four hits and a run. Marlins reliever Cade Gibson (5-2) was charged with the first two runs in the game-changing fifth. The Padres' Jackson Merrill and the Marlins' Agustin Ramirez homered.
Mets 6, Phillies 3
Zac Thornton tossed six solid innings, Juan Soto homered among his three hits and host New York beat Philadelphia.
Soto went 3-for-5 for the Mets, while Francisco Lindor and Carson Benge each collected two hits. Thornton (5-5) gave up two runs on five hits.
Edmundo Sosa finished 3-for-3 with a homer and Derek Hill also went deep for the Phillies, who fell to 7-9 this month. Newly acquired Jose Urquidy threw 4 2/3 shutout innings after opener Tim Mayza (3-4) surrendered three runs while getting just one out.
Reds 6, Cubs 4
Cincinnati scored three times in the sixth inning in a back-and-forth win over visiting Chicago.
Elly De La Cruz had two hits, two walks and two runs for the Reds. Cincinnati starter Chase Burns and reliever Julian Aguiar (1-0) each allowed two runs on four hits in three innings.
Cubs starter Clay Holmes (6-8) surrendered six runs on three hits in 5 1/3 innings. Ian Happ homered for Chicago, and Michael Conforto amassed three hits.
Twins 3, Angels 0
Connor Prielipp allowed two hits over a career-high seven innings and fellow rookie Walker Jenkins went 3-for-4 with a home run as Minnesota topped Los Angeles in Anaheim, Calif.
Travis Adams pitched a 1-2-3 ninth inning to pick up his third save. Jenkins, who began his career going 4-for-45, homered for the second straight game on his sixth consecutive hit in the series.
Jose Siri had two hits for the Angels. Grayson Rodriguez (4-8) gave up three runs on eight hits in 6 2/3 innings.
Brewers 6, Orioles 5 (10 innings)
Sal Frelick singled home a 10th-inning run and visiting Milwaukee pulled out a victory against Baltimore.
Trevor Megill (3-3) was the winning pitcher despite a blown save. Chad Patrick retired the Orioles in order in the bottom of the 10th for his sixth save.
Milwaukee's Jackson Chourio and Baltimore's Pete Alonso hit three-run homers early in the game. Gunnar Henderson and Coby Mayo both collected three hits for the Orioles.
Dodgers 8, Giants 2
Mookie Betts homered twice, including his 53rd career leadoff homer, and Josue De Paula hit a tiebreaking double to help Los Angeles produce a victory over visiting San Francisco.
The Dodgers socked five home runs while winning for the 12th time in the last 15 games. Max Muncy and Kyle Tucker hit back-to-back homers in the eighth, and Betts and Will Smith repeated the feat later in the frame. Tyler Glasnow (5-1) gave up two runs and three hits while striking out a season-high 10 in six innings.
Jung Hoo Lee homered and Jonah Cox had an RBI single as the Giants fell for the fifth time in seven games.
Yankees 9, Diamondbacks 2
George Lombard Jr. had two hits and three RBIs, and his two-run single capped a five-run first-inning outburst as New York cruised past Arizona in Phoenix.
Ben Rice and Lombard homered and Rice added a triple as the Yankees won for the fourth time in five games. Gerrit Cole (9-9) gave up two runs on four hits in six innings.
Corbin Carroll homered and doubled for the Diamondbacks, who have lost five of six to see their NL wild-card chances fade. Eduardo Rodriguez (15-7) yielded seven runs in 5 1/3 innings.
Red Sox 4, Rays 2
Roman Anthony homered and had three RBIs, Jahmai Jones went deep and Boston cooled off first-place Tampa Bay in St. Petersburg, Fla.
Anthony went 2-for-5 while Caleb Durbin was 2-for-3 for the Red Sox. Boston starter Ranger Suarez (8-4) fought control issues but allowed one run on three hits in 5 2/3 innings.
Junior Caminero doubled, walked twice and drove in a run for the Rays, who had only five hits as their six-game winning streak ended. Ian Seymour (9-7) allowed four runs on seven hits in five innings.
Rangers 7, Blue Jays 1
Corey Seager capped a four-run second inning with an RBI double as Texas topped Toronto in Arlington, Texas.
The Rangers drew 10 walks and moved into a first-place tie with Houston in the American League West. Jake Burger had two RBIs for Texas, which won for the fifth time in six games. Texas took a 4-0 lead in the second inning against Dylan Cease (11-6), who allowed four runs (one earned) on three hits over 2 2/3 innings.
The Blue Jays fell two games back of the White Sox for the final AL wild-card spot. Myles Straw had two hits with an RBI for Toronto, which committed three errors and lost for the third time in four games.
Tigers 11, White Sox 8
Dillon Dingler delivered the go-ahead single and Riley Greene followed with a two-run homer in a five-run eighth inning as visiting Detroit stormed back from six runs down to beat Chicago.
Hao-Yu Lee went 4-for-5 with a homer, three RBIs and two runs for the Tigers. Kevin McGonigle finished 2-for-5 with four RBIs. Drew Sommers (2-4) threw two shutout innings, fanning five, and Kenley Jansen blanked the White Sox in the ninth for his 21st save.
Colson Montgomery and Miguel Vargas each had two hits and three RBIs for the White Sox, who have lost three out of four. Sean Newcomb (2-5) got only two outs in relief while allowing three runs.
Pirates 8, Royals 5
Konnor Griffin had four hits and two RBIs and Spencer Horwitz delivered a tiebreaking two-run single in the seventh as Pittsburgh rallied to beat visiting Kansas City.
Pittsburgh trailed 4-0 after the top of the third inning and 5-2 entering the bottom of the fourth. The Pirates won their second straight after losing four of their previous five.
Vinnie Pasquantino and Michael Massey each homered as the Royals scored five runs against Pittsburgh ace Paul Skenes, who scattered six hits in his six innings. Royals starter Randy Dobnak allowed four runs on seven hits over 3 2/3 innings.
Nationals 9, Cardinals 1
Cade Cavalli pitched five scoreless innings and recorded the 200th strikeout of his first full major league season, leading Washington to a victory at St. Louis.
Cavalli (13-5), who agreed with the Nationals earlier in the day on a four-year, $47 million contract extension, allowed four hits and struck out six. Dylan Crews hit a two-run homer and Yohandy Morales added a two-run double for Washington.
Cardinals starter Kyle Leahy (10-5) allowed seven runs, six earned, on five hits over three innings. Leo Bernal went 3-for-4.
Mariners 5, Rockies 4
Lazaro Montes homered leading off the top of the ninth, J.P. Crawford went deep to open the game, and Seattle beat Colorado in Denver.
Randy Arozarena finished with three hits as the Mariners logged their second win in a row. Carlos Vargas (2-0) recorded one out in relief, and Andres Munoz earned his 28th save with a scoreless ninth inning.
Cole Carrigg, Connor Norby and Jake McCarthy had three hits apiece and Ezequiel Tovar contributed two hits for the Rockies, who have lost three in a row and 11 of 12. Jordan Romano (0-4) served up Montes' homer.

Title: New laws trigger a fresh legal fight over Nazi-looted art in Los Angeles and Auschwitz museums
Article_Text:
New laws trigger a fresh legal fight over Nazi-looted art in Los Angeles and Auschwitz museums
			
By Canadian Press on September 19, 2026.
			
								
						
			
This undated photo provided by the Norton Simon Art Foundation on Friday, Sept. 18, 2026, shows two oil paintings, "Adam and Eve," painted in 1530 by Lucas Cranach the Elder, on display in the Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena, Calif. (Gerard Vuilleumier/Norton Simon Art Foundation via AP)
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Jewish heirs of 
Holocaust
 victims and their representatives have filed two lawsuits in California staking their claims to Nazi-looted paintings that still hang on the walls of prominent museums in Los Angeles and 
Auschwitz
.
This pair of lawsuits are the first to be filed after the recent passage of laws by California and Congress, which strengthen U.S.-based claims to artwork that were forcibly taken from Jewish families during World War II.
One lawsuit was filed in Los Angeles Superior Court on Monday by the Jewish Federation of Greater Los Angeles and its board chair Daniel Gryczman against Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena for the return of “Adam and Eve.” These are two life-size oil-on-panel masterpieces created by Lucas Carnach the Elder in 1530.
The other lawsuit was filed in federal court in Los Angeles the same day by the daughters of the late Dinah Gottliebova Babbitt, a Holocaust survivor and California-based animator who was held in Auschwitz. It demanded the return of watercolors of fellow prisoners that the artist was forced to paint for Josef Mengele, a Nazi physician who had earned the nickname the “Angel of Death.”
Spokespersons for both museums say the museums legally hold titles to the works, and intend to continue displaying them to the public. The lawsuits don’t specify the monetary value of the paintings.
Artworks pit Jewish families against museums 
The issue of 
Nazi-looted art
 is an emotional, legally and ethically charged topic that pits Jewish families that have suffered inter-generational trauma against museums that say they are trying to preserve a painful, yet important, chapter of history. Between 1933 and 1945, the Nazi regime orchestrated the largest art theft in world history, seizing over 600,000 works of art across Europe from Jewish families, collectors and museums. Decades later, many of these masterpieces reside in prominent museums around the world, making the push for their recovery more complex than a simple property dispute.
Rabbi Noah Farkas is president and CEO of the Jewish Federation of Los Angeles, the organization to which Marei von Saher, sole heir of Dutch Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker, has signed over her rights. The paintings were seized from Goudstikker’s collection by Hermann Goring, Adolf Hitler’s second-in-command and changed a number of hands before being sold in the 1960s to the Pasadena Museum of Modern Art, which was renamed Norton Simon Museum in honor of its benefactor.
Farkas said the federation plans to use most of the net proceeds from the recovered art to provide much-needed help to the about 2,500 Holocaust survivors living in the Los Angeles area.
“These are incredibly beautiful European masterpieces stolen from a Jewish family to enrich the Nazi party and fund the war and death machine against the people,” he said. “It’s our honor to take on this role on behalf of the community and use most of the proceeds to help these elderly survivors live out the last years of their lives in dignity, comfort and peace – something their family members were denied during the Holocaust.”
Marei von Saher, in a statement, said she is grateful to the Jewish organization for taking up her family’s cause.
“This effort represents a meaningful step toward justice for Holocaust survivors and victims of Nazi era atrocities,” she said.
New legislation gives lawsuits second wind
California Assemblyman Jesse Gabriel, D-Woodland Hills, wrote Assembly Bill 2867, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom in September 2024, which requires that the state law must apply in lawsuits brought by California residents or their heirs to recover art seized during the Holocaust or during other acts of persecution. Gabriel, who co-chairs the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, introduced the legislation in response to a federal court ruling, which allowed the state-owned Thyssen-Bornemisza National Museum in Madrid to keep a multimillion-dollar 
Camille Pissarro impressionist masterpiece
.
That painting had been taken by the Nazis from the Cassirer family in 1939. This case, which prompted this new law, is expected to be heard in federal court in California next month.
Gabriel said it’s time for museums to “do some deep introspection on whether they want to be on the right side of history.”
Museums want to preserve paintings for posterity
Norton Simon Museum released a statement pointing out that a federal court in 2018 unanimously determined that the museum had proper title to the Cranach paintings. In May 2019, the U.S. Supreme Court 
declined to get involved in the case
, leaving in place lower court rulings.
They said the Cranach paintings, which originally belonged to the Stroganoff family, were put up for sale in 1931 by the Soviet Union in an illicit auction in Berlin where they were purchased by Goudstikker. After a complicated journey, the paintings were sold to the museum by a Stroganoff family descendant. The museum later restored and preserved the pieces.
“For nearly 50 years, they have been on view at the Norton Simon Museum and will continue to be accessible to the public for years to come,” the statement said.
Pawel Sawicki, a spokesperson for the Auschwitz Memorial, said the watercolors of Roma victims that Gottliebova Babbitt was forced to paint by Mengele to document his horrendous experiments and racial research, “must remain in the Memorial” to document the man’s crimes. He said these paintings must not be mischaracterized as “Nazi-looted art” because Gottliebova Babbitt painted them against her will as a prisoner and therefore didn’t have ownership of the watercolors.
While he understands the family’s sentiments, Sawicki said the portraits of Roma and Sinti victims are among the few remaining documents of Mengele’s criminal experiments and should be treated as unique documents related to the history of the Auschwitz concentration camp.
“While fully respecting the rights of people who created some of the documents here, we are of the opinion that any loss in the collections of the Memorial will constitute irreparable harm,” he said. “ … The loss of even the smallest part of the documentation is an irreparable loss and blemish on the memory of the victims of Auschwitz.”
Advocates hope cases will now be heard on their merit
Joel Greenberg, founder of Art Ashes, a Philadelphia-area nonprofit that helps Jewish families track down and recover Nazi-looted art, said in addition to the California law, President Donald Trump signed into law and updated the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025. This new law permanently eliminated the expiration date to allow Holocaust survivors and their heirs to indefinitely pursue the recovery of these works of art.
Greenberg said the new federal law gave families the right to reclaim their art for up to six years from the time they find out in whose possession they are.
“These new laws mean that technical defenses will no longer stick in court,” he said. “Every case will be heard on its merits.”
He said the new legislation also ensures that these Jewish families have their day in court and a fair process to determine ownership of the stolen art.
“It will make sure the stories of what happened to European Jewry is not lost and forgotten,” he said. “The art can still be returned to the rightful owner.”

Title: Why does some rain fall harder than other rain? - Shelbyville Times-Gazette
Article_Text:
Curious Kids is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to curiouskidsus@theconversation.com.
Why does some rain fall harder than other rain? – Naomi B., age 9, San Fancisco, California
There are some days when the rain falls peacefully and gently, nourishing the Earth. But on some other days the rain comes down in a torrential downpour that meteorologists like me call a cloudburst. Standing outside in one of these intense rainstorms can feel like being smothered in a heavy, wet towel. These storms can flood the lands below them and lead to great destruction.
So what causes this difference?
All rain comes from a combination of two things: moisture in the air – usually in the form of clouds – and currents of air moving upwards. As moist air rises up through a cloud, the air cools and the water in it turns into tiny raindrops.
This is the same thing that happens when you can see your breath on a cold evening. The temperature change from warm to cool causes water droplets to form in your breath.
In a cloud, these tiny raindrops are very light and float as the rising air pushes them up. But the higher they go, the larger and heavier they get. Eventually, they get so heavy that they fall to the Earth as rain.
Cold air can hold much less moisture than warm air, so wintertime clouds don’t have much water in them; they are thin and layered rather than puffy and tall and full of water.
Since cold air likes to sink to the ground, it’s difficult to get that air to rise quickly, so these wintertime clouds have only gentle upward air currents. As these slow currents sweep up through the thin clouds that don’t have much moisture, small raindrops form. Gravity easily pulls them down against the air current before they get too big. When clouds are thin and the air is moving slowly, you get nice calm rain.
Hard rainstorms happen when there is a lot of moisture in the air and the air moves upwards very fast. Summer thunderstorms are the perfect example.
The warm, moist air rises very quickly – like a hot air balloon – and can be moving as fast as 30 to 40 miles per hour. The air also holds much more moisture than winter clouds – up to five times as much.
All of this creates very tall, thick clouds that are full of moisture. Water droplets form quickly as the air moves up through the clouds. But since the wind is blowing upwards so fast, the droplets can get huge before gravity drags them down to Earth. When the weight of all the water droplets gets to be too much for the wind, the wind current collapses, and all the raindrops in the cloud come crashing down at once. These are summer thunderstorms.
Thunderstorms can drop one, two or even three inches of rain in less than an hour. These sudden torrential downpours, called cloudbursts, can lead to flash flooding that can overflow streams and roads and trap people wherever they are.
[The Conversation’s science, health and technology editors pick their favorite stories. Weekly on Wednesdays.]
Thankfully, because thunderstorms are so violent and relatively small, they don’t last very long. Once the rain falls from the clouds and squashes the upward air currents, the clouds disappear and you often see a nice blue sky.
Of course, winter can deliver some strong storms too – especially over the warmer ocean water. When strong winter storms drop lots of heavy rain, the same principles are at work: lots of moisture in the air, fast upwards wind currents and tall clouds.
No two rainstorms are ever the same. Sometimes clouds can rain so hard it feels like you are standing in the shower. Other times they bring only a nice peaceful drizzle. Now, whether you are soaked or singing in the rain, you’ll know why.

Please tell us your name, age and the city where you live. We won’t be able to answer every question, but we will do our best.

Title: Stabbing of Sikh truck driver at Wyoming rest area has community on edge
Article_Text:
Sikh truck driver stabbed more than a dozen times in Wyoming rest stop attack
FORT COLLINS, Colo. (AP) — The stabbing of a truck driver at a remote Wyoming rest stop had U.S. Sikhs on edge Friday amid rising anti-immigrant vitriol against the community and its truck drivers in particular.
The Sikh victim was attacked from behind early Sunday while in a restroom at the Bitter Creek rest stop on Interstate 80 midway between Cheyenne and Salt Lake City, according to court documents. He suffered stabs to the neck and chest and over a dozen other cuts but survived.
While police say the motive is unknown, the attack came after deadly crashes involving Sikh truck drivers led to debate about commercial driver’s licensing requirements — sparking hatred toward Sikhs as a group, community leaders said.
Anti-Sikh sentiment has been especially severe on truck-driving forums, said one Sikh in the trucking industry, Harsimran Singh, CEO of Gillson Trucking in Stockton, California.
“I’ve been here for the last 25-plus years,” Singh said. “I never felt this kind of hate before.”
Police were still investigating what prompted the Wyoming attack by a man who left the rest area driving a truck-trailer combination, Sweetwater County Sheriff’s Department spokesperson Jeff Sheaman said.
“We have zero motive,” Sheaman said.
The victim allegedly told police he was trying to use the restroom when he was attacked from behind. He pushed the attacker, he said, and didn’t see the knife at first, according to the police affidavit filed in the case.
Within hours, police arrested Andrew Kris Bzdak in nearby Carbon County, Wyoming. A family at the rest area who heard the attack allegedly followed Bzdak’s truck back onto the highway and tipped off police to help find him, according to the affidavit.
Video taken from a truck at the rest area showed the victim walk casually into the restroom, followed by a man police said was Bzdak. Soon after, Bzdak allegedly was recorded running from the restroom, followed by the stumbling, wounded victim who fell at least once, according to the affidavit.
Bzdak remained jailed on $1 million bond Friday in Rock Springs, on suspicion of attempted murder, a crime punishable in Wyoming by up to life in prison. An initial appearance was scheduled for Thursday.
A phone message left at an address for Bzdak in Catawissa, Pennsylvania, wasn’t immediately returned, nor was a phone message for him at the jail and for his Wyoming public defender, Gary Arnell.
Despite no evident motive, the attack was unnerving for Sikhs, who number around 750,000 in the U.S. Many live in California.
Sikh men wear beards, uncut hair and turbans, and many work as truck drivers. Advocacy groups estimate at least 150,000 Sikh truck drivers work in the U.S.
In August 2025, authorities said a Sikh truck driver’s U-turn on a Florida turnpike caused a crash that killed three people. The crash prompted investigations as well as reports about Sikh truck drivers being harassed.
Then last October, a Sikh truck driver accused of being under the influence of drugs caused a fiery crash that killed three people, authorities said.
Both drivers were in the U.S. illegally, according to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which Singh, the trucking CEO, blamed for stirring anti-immigrant hatred with social media posts.
One such post, since taken down, showed a dark-skinned man with a beard that read, “Get off our roads, you don’t know how to drive Mr. Singh.” DHS officials have said the post referred specifically to the driver in the Florida crash. But Sikh community representatives pointed out that a large number of Sikhs — well over 100,000 in the U.S. and millions worldwide — have the last name Singh.
No matter what motivated the attack, the crime is difficult to separate from racism toward Sikhs, said Jasjit Singh, legal services director for the Sikh community group Jakara Movement and a representative of the victim.
“We were making noise about this,” Jasjit Singh said. “That is how the community feels. Until something really bad happens to us, nothing is going to really happen.”
The victim was headed home Friday after five days in a Casper hospital and hopes to drive his truck across Wyoming again, Jasjit Singh said.
But Harsimran Singh, the trucking CEO, also remained apprehensive.
“We are probably going to see more of this,” Harsimran Singh said. “I’m not surprised that it has happened.”

Title: AP Trending SummaryBrief at 7:28 a.m. EDT
Article_Text:
Munich’s Oktoberfest roars to life as the mayor taps the first keg
MUNICH (AP) — Munich's Oktoberfest has kicked off with the city's mayor tapping the first beer keg, marking the start of the 191st edition of the festival. Thousands of revelers in traditional Bavarian attire flocked to the beer tents on Munich's Theresienwiese fairground. They enjoyed brass music, freshly tapped beer, pretzels and sausages. The festival runs for 16 days, expecting around six million visitors from Munich, southern Germany and worldwide. German authorities have tightened security, using AI-powered cameras to detect large crowds. There are bans on knives, drones and large bags, with more than 600 police officers on duty.
Italy sees mosquitos spread the West Nile virus farther and longer as Europe warms
ROME (AP) — Italian health authorities are seeing evidence that rising temperatures and longer warm seasons are helping mosquitoes spread West Nile virus across a wider area, during more months of the year. Warmer temperatures favor mosquito reproduction and can mean the transmission season sometimes lasts as late as November. Areas once largely unaffected are increasingly reporting infections, reflecting a gradual expansion of the virus across the country. Italy’s experience with the virus is drawing attention from European countries located farther north. More than 650 infections have been reported in Italy so far this year, accounting for roughly half of all cases recorded in Europe.
Princess Diana's famous 'revenge dress' goes on show ahead of Sotheby's auction
LONDON (AP) — A striking black dress worn by Princess Diana on the day her estranged husband admitted adultery is going up for auction at Sotheby’s. Known as the “revenge dress,” it has a presale estimate of up to $300,000. Diana wore the off-the-shoulder silk dress, designed by Christina Stambolian, to a gala in London on June 29, 1994, the day the then-Prince Charles' TV interview was broadcast. Sotheby’s Morgane Halimi says Diana used the dress to seize control of her story. The dress will tour internationally before its sale in New York on December 9. Diana's enduring appeal continues to captivate collectors and fans worldwide.
A truck driver built a model of NYC with over 800,000 structures for fun. Now it's a museum exhibit
NEW YORK (AP) — A truck driver who spent two decades building a massive scale model of his native New York City was delighted when it went viral on TikTok. Now, Joe Macken’s sprawling balsa wood and foam board creation is on display at the Museum of the City of New York. The immense model is 50 feet long and nearly 30 feet wide, covering all five boroughs, parts of New Jersey and suburban Long Island. More than 800,000 balsa wood structures are laid out in street-level detail across more than 300 large foam boards like interconnecting puzzle pieces. The exhibit runs through Oct. 12.
Mets' Jared Young has concussion symptoms, CT scan negative after scary collision with Nolan McLean
NEW YORK (AP) — Mets first baseman Jared Young was carted off the field  in the sixth inning of a 3-0 loss to Philadelphia after he was knocked out when struck on the head by a knee of pitcher Nolan McLean as the two converged on Justin Crawford’s slow grounder. New York manager Andy Green said a CT scan at a hospital was negative and Young had concussion symptoms and full use of his extremities. With the Phillies ahead 1-0, McLean broke to first on contact and Young initially moved back toward the bag. McLean briefly paused, at which point Young reached for the ball with his right hand as he tried to keep a foot on the base.
Knicks pause ticket sales after mistake caused them to be listed at prices too high
NEW YORK (AP) — The New York Knicks are pausing ticket sales after a mistake caused them to be listed for amounts that were too high. The NBA champions put individual game tickets for the 2026-27 season on sale this week. The get-in price for the Oct. 20 season opener against Philadelphia was more than $1,000. The team said Thursday they are rolling back to last year’s prices plus an average increase of 12%. They added that sales will restart shortly with the correct prices, and anyone who already purchased individual tickets would be refunded the difference.
Holdout juror in Clancy trial didn't have 'any doubts' that she was responsible for killing her kids
BOSTON (AP) — The lone juror who wanted to convict Lindsay Clancy of murder for killing her three children said he was certain of her guilt, but that other jurors wouldn’t listen to him. That's according to a statement released Friday by juror Michael Desronvil in his first public comments on the case. Eleven of 12 jurors were ready to clear Clancy of criminal responsibility, with the majority feeling the Massachusetts mom was in the grip of a rare condition called postpartum psychosis when she strangled her kids. But juror Desronvil sided with the prosecutors, who had argued that Clancy knew what she was doing. Desronvil says “I didn’t have any doubts.”
Buckingham Palace hits back at claims in a book by Princess Diana's brother
LONDON (AP) — Buckingham Palace is denying a claim by Princess Diana's brother that King Charles III said she would soon be forgotten after her death. In a new book, Charles Spencer recounts arguing with the then-Prince Charles over plans for Prince William and Prince Harry to walk behind Diana's coffin in 1997. Spencer claims Charles said: “Rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough.” The palace issued a strong statement late Wednesday, suggesting grief can affect judgment and memory. Tensions between the palace and Diana’s family after her death have been dramatized in programs, including “The Crown.” The book, “Swan Song: Diana, My Sister,” is set to be published next week.
The psychedelic pop artist Peter Max has died at 88, his son says
NEW YORK (AP) — The artist Peter Max has died at age 88. Max was known for colorful, psychedelic pop art that expressed the optimism of the “flower power” movement of the 1960s and graced everything from postage stamps to a cruise ship. His son said he died Monday. No cause was given, but he had advanced dementia. Max began his career in graphic design in the 1960s, and his swirly, colorful, instantly recognizable designs epitomized the era’s “flower power” art. Max’s work remained well known and popular well into the 21st century. Max was the official artist for the Olympics, the Super Bowl and other events. His portrait subjects ranged from U.S. presidents to Taylor Swift.
Paralyzed A's minor leaguer Ryan Lasko leaves hospital more than two months after spinal-cord injury
WEST ORANGE, N.J. (AP) — Ryan Lasko, a minor league prospect with the Athletics who was paralyzed in an outfield collision more than two months ago, has been released from an in-patient rehabilitation hospital. He will continue his recovery from home. The 24-year-old Lasko was released exactly two months after arriving at the Kessler Institute for Rehabilitation in New Jersey. It's about 35 miles from where he attended college at Rutgers and became a second-round draft pick by the A’s in 2023. Staff members at the facility celebrated his departure with a “clap out” farewell ceremony as he exited the building’s main entrance.

Title: Media man takes a spin on 'Wheel of Fortune,' show airs Thursday
Article_Text:
MEDIA — Tony Oriente has spun the wheel on “The Price Is Right.” He took his chances on “Deal or No Deal.” And now, he’s getting ready to take a spin on the most famous wheel of them all.
The Media resident will appear as a contestant on “Wheel of Fortune” at 7:30 p.m. Thursday, Sept. 24, on ABC, giving Delaware County viewers a chance to watch one of their own compete on one of television’s longest-running and most popular game shows.
For Oriente, it’s the latest — and perhaps most memorable — chapter in a rather unique game-show history.
“I am in a very rare club that has spun both ‘The Price is Right’ wheel and the ‘Wheel of Fortune’ wheel, as well as one of the very few people to be on three game shows in one lifetime,” Oriente said.
Born and raised in Philadelphia, Oriente moved to Delaware County in 2006, living in Sharon Hill and Chester before settling in Media. He currently works as assistant county clerk and administrative assistant to the executive director for Delaware County.
Away from work, Oriente is involved in the local arts and his church community.
He has performed with the Players Club of Swarthmore, Viviana Theatre Company and the Candlelight Theatre in Arden, Del. He is a member of the choir at Holy Trinity Lutheran Church of Wallingford, serves on the church council and volunteers twice a month leading a grief group.
Oriente also enjoys traveling, playing piano, baking and — perhaps fittingly — watching old game shows. That passion for game shows has taken Oriente to television sets far beyond the Delaware County area.
In September 2016, he was a Showcase winner on “The Price Is Right,” taking home more than $26,000 in prizes, including a car. He was the first winner of a car in a Showcase during Season 45.
Three years later, in 2019, he was selected as a contestant on CNBC’s “Deal or No Deal.” That game didn’t go quite as well, but didn’t lessen his fondness for game shows. Oriente went home with just $70, which he donated to a local animal shelter.
Then came “Wheel of Fortune.” Oriente applied in October 2025. He quickly received a second interview and subsequently took the show’s online test. Then, about six months later, came the email he had been waiting for: He was going to be a contestant.
He traveled to California and filmed his episode in May 2026. The show is currently produced by Sony Pictures Television and taped at Sony Picture Studios in Culver City, Calif.
“The taping of the show was exciting, a lot of fun, and everyone on the set was so supportive and nice,” Oriente said. “I nearly felt like I had celebrity status for a day.”
One of the highlights came before the cameras even started rolling.
“Meeting Vanna White,” he said, “was a dream come true.”
White greeted the contestants while they were in hair, makeup and wardrobe, and Oriente described her as “wholesome, charming and elegant.”
After each contestant had a practice turn, they were assigned the shows that they would tape on that day. Five episodes were filmed during the day.
When it was Oriente’s turn, he was introduced to host Ryan Seacrest.
“Ryan Seacrest was gracious, charming and down-to-earth,” Oriente said.
And then came the moment he had been waiting for: stepping onto the stage and facing the famous wheel.
“There was a special energy when Vanna and Ryan took to the stage,” Oriente said. “It was overwhelming.”
The wheel, he discovered, is heavy. But with nerves and adrenaline pumping, Oriente said, “it makes it seem so light.”
For someone who has watched the show since its early days — when contestants would “shop” through various departments for prizes — being there in person was something entirely different, he explained.
“I have been a fan of ‘Wheel of Fortune’ ever since the early days of ‘shopping in various departments for prizes’ and have been a regular ‘Wheel’ watcher ever since,” he said.
Now, millions of other viewers will have the opportunity to watch Oriente take his turn.
Although he is not permitted to give any other details about the show on Sept. 24, or to say how he fared, Oriente said the experience itself was one of the best in his life.
“Though I have been on game shows before, being on ‘Wheel of Fortune’ was truly one of the most exciting experiences of my life,” he said. “To represent Delco and to appear in millions of homes on one of America’s top-rated game shows is an honor and a once-in-a-lifetime event that I will cherish for the rest of my life.”
For Oriente, the experience is about more than the outcome of one game. It’s about a lifelong love of game shows, an unforgettable day on a television set, and bringing a little bit of Delaware County along for the ride.
Tune in
Tony Oriente will appear as a contestant on “Wheel of Fortune” at 7:30 p.m. Thursday, Sept. 24, on ABC, locally Channel 6.

Title: CWA rebuffed after asking state to end receivership for city
Article_Text:
The Chester Water Authority asked Pennsylvania authorities to end the receivership in Chester and the state responded that not at this time, although the receiver himself said no one is looking more forward to it ending than himself.
CWA solicitor Francis Catania sent the Pennsylvania Department of Community and Economic Development two letters, one on Aug. 27 and another on Sept. 8, to end the receivership, among other things.
The state Department of Community and Economic Development oversees the Act 47 Receivership program.
“It is time for the Receivership to end,” Catania wrote in August. “The Receivership has lasted six years. This is an unacceptably long time for the citizens of Chester to be deprived of local control of their City. It is time to return control of Chester to the people’s duly elected leaders, the Chester City Council.”
While the current receivership program has been in place in Chester since 2020, the city has been under some sort of financial oversight since 1995.
A week ago, Catania followed up with his request.
“The DCED and Receiver have had notice of the same core problems for years, yet the Receiver with the DCED’s support remains preoccupied with attacking CWA rather than addressing them,” he said. “CWA is neither the cause of the City’s financial problems nor a cure for them.”
In his opinion, Catania said the receiver has not been productive.
“The Receiver has already wasted years of time, energy and taxpayer money unsuccessfully attacking CWA through the City’s bankruptcy proceedings and the protracted lawsuit finally concluded by the Pennsylvania Supreme Court,” the CWA solicitor said. “The solution to the City’s financial troubles is not to perpetuate this failure and try to create a boogeyman out of CWA, but rather, to really and truly focus on solving the structural problems affecting the City.”
A day later, on Sept. 9, the state Department of Community and Economic Development responded.
The agency noted that the Commonwealth Court approved Kapoor’s term to start on July 1, 2025 and end on Dec. 28, 2027. Prior to Kapoor, Michael Doweary had served as receiver since 2020 and left last year to take an executive position at York College.
In the responding letter, Michael K. Hanna Jr., DCED’s Executive Deputy Secretary, said Kapoor “remains independent from DCED and does not take direction from DCED on how to fulfill his responsibilities as receiver.”
He also noted that the time to address this would have been when the court was considering Kapoor’s appointment.
“CWA had the opportunity to object to both the appointment of Receiver Kapoor and the extension of the City’s receivership last year,” Hanna wrote. “(H)owever, the CWA did not raise any issues before the Commonwealth Court.”
He provided a list of accomplishments the receivers had attained.
Those included having the Chester Police Pension Fund on track to be able to fund 55 months of checks by year’s end compared to two months of checks in 2022.
He noted Chester’s budget last year had no layoffs or service cuts and studies are being completed that relate to the city’s economic development, public safety and parking. Annual 3% pay increases have also been implemented for city employees.
Hanna said vital improvements had been done to public works, including trash collection, LED lights, equipment modernization, road repairs and facility upgrades.
He spoke of the new 12-hour police shifts putting more officers out on the streets as well as new body and dash cameras and vehicles.
The executive deputy secretary also said improvements have been made to tax-revenue collection, outsourced payroll and institutional financial controls.
Hanna concluded, “While Receiver Kapoor and his predecessor, Receiver Doweary, have made substantial progress towards improving the financial strength and operational efficiency of the City, the City’s fiscal emergency is ongoing; thus, it is inappropriate to seek termination of the receivership at this time.”
Noel Brandon, chairman of the Chester Water Authority, agrees with Catania.
Noting that the city has been under DCED oversight for 30 years, he added, “If it’s a country, they might call it an occupation.”
He said the CWA has posted on ChesterWaterFacts.com that Pennsylvania has spent more than $21 million by the DCED over the last six years for the receivership.
“That’s a lot of money dished out by the DCED,” Brandon said. “To us, it seems like wasteful spending on the part of the government.”
In the meantime, he said, the CWA has had to defend itself against a strategy to sell it despite its strong financial viability.
“They can use any synonym they want,” Brandon said. “They want to extract money from CWA ratepayers. The DCED needs to come up with a completely new strategy.”
He said the office needs to work with Chester City Council and someone who can actually help them over the next six years.
Brandon said that in the corporate world, if someone came in to do a turnaround, they’d have 18 months.
“A change is needed,” he added. “The next step for DCED is to take some sort of action, whatever it is. That action needs to better the city. We think the ball is in their court.
“What we’re not going to stop doing is informing our ratepayers,” he said.
Kapoor’s view
Receiver Vijay Kapoor said he, too, wants the receivership to end, but in a way that the city won’t financially collapse when he leaves.
“Nobody wants a successful receivership to conclude more than me,” he said.
He noted two things are critical to setting the city on a viable course.
“We have to find a way of addressing that $43 million in past due pension payments plus interests,” Kapoor said.
Then, he said what is needed from a financial end is the city needs an ongoing stream of revenues that meets expenses on an ongoing basis and that is in the best interest of the residents.
“There’s no one path that leads to the end,” Kapoor said.
After recent court decisions, his office in the process of determining a range of what those numbers would be and what the gap is. He said he anticipates that range to be available in the next month and a half.
“The financial information that was here was not great,” he said of the receiver’s arrival six years ago. Now, he said, there is a very good chief financial officer with a very good professional staff in place.
Areas they are evaluating to come to that range include how much infrastructure spending should be allocated annually to care for the city’s roads and bridges and, also, what should be budgeted for long-term health care costs for active and retired employees.
Kapoor provided a metaphor of where the city was six years ago financially to where it is today.
“When we first got here, the city had flatlined,” he said. “We basically spent the past couple of years getting a heartbeat back. Now, in my mind, we’re in the hospital. We’re in the recovery room.”
Using this metaphor, he said the goal is to get the city out of the hospital and not have to return.
The key to that, Kapoor said, is transparency.
“We need to be able to help the city with a plan to get out of the hospital and not get back in,” he said, adding that they need to ensure that some of the things that hurt the city don’t come back.
With the Chester Water Authority, he said his concern is transparency, in particular after a 14% rate hike last year, a move he said wasn’t explained with enough information.
He said the city does appoint one-third of the nine members to the CWA board and the authority does provide water to all of the city residents.
Kapoor said he also exercised scrutiny with the Stormwater Authority of Chester around the number of its board members and other issues. With DELCORA, he said, the city doesn’t appoint members to its board.
“My feeling on transparency extends to all of those entities,” Kapoor added.
He offered some recommendations to the CWA, including livestreaming meetings and taking up city Mayor Stefan Roots’ offer to have their board meetings at Chester City Hall.
“I have never seen a board disrespect a governing body,” Kapoor said, noting treatment of the mayor and the city’s CWA board appointment, Thomas Moore. “I have never seen a board try and kick off a member. I’ve never seen (such) a lack of transparency.
“It’s not personal thing for me,” Kapoor said. “My focus is and has always been on transparency. The fastest way to shut me up is to be transparent.”
Asked if amid all the legal and other wrangling there is a way for the city to emerge successfully from the receivership, Kapoor said he believes there is.
“If I didn’t, I would have resigned by now,” he said. “I do see a path forward here. I see my role as developing the parameters. Within those parameters, we work and try and figure it all out. I do think there are reasonable people in this commonwealth who can find common ground to figure out a way forward.”

WASHINGTON (AP) — The appeal of telehealth is easy to explain: Instead of calling a doctor, booking an appointment and hoping to eventually get a prescription, you can log onto an app or website and get approved for a new medication within minutes.
Since the COVID-19 pandemic, scores of online health services have launched with the promise of quick, convenient access to drugs for ADHD, sexual dysfunction, anxiety, weight loss and more.
Increasingly, though, government regulators are accusing these companies of deceptive, unethical business practices, including disclosing their customers’ health data, signing them up for hard-to-cancel subscriptions and bypassing real-time consultations with doctors.
The Federal Trade Commission’s latest lawsuit alleges that telehealth pioneer Hims & Hers engaged in all of those tactics, running afoul of U.S. consumer protection laws.
Hims has disputed the government’s claims, calling them “an effort to generate headlines at our expense.”
In recent years, FTC officials have filed similar cases against more than a half-dozen telehealth companies, including online therapy provider BetterHelp and pharmacy discount service GoodRx. In both cases, regulators said the companies shared users’ health data with online platforms such as Meta and Google, without getting permission.
Experts say part of the problem is that federal laws that govern the handling of health information generally don’t apply to telehealth companies.
“There’s an entire universe of companies collecting huge amounts of consumer health data every day that aren’t covered by our current health sector-specific laws,” said Andrew Crawford, an attorney with the nonprofit Center for Democracy and Technology.
Here are some things to know before signing up for a telehealth service:
Don’t expect to actually talk to a physician
Nearly all telehealth visits begin with a questionnaire in which users provide details about their medical history and possible medications they’re interested in.
According to the FTC’s lawsuit, Hims customers were automatically enrolled and billed for recurring prescriptions with “virtually no opportunity to review the provider’s recommended treatment.”
Researchers have documented similar practices across the industry, even for injectable weight-loss drugs that typically require a physical exam and other precautions before beginning treatment.
A recent analysis of nearly 50 telehealth companies selling GLP-1 drugs found that less than a third actually required any real-time video or audio consultation with a physician. In some cases, the prescriptions were approved within minutes.
“What we saw overwhelmingly was that it was incredibly easy to get access to the GLP-1s,” said Dr. Reshma Ramachandran of Yale University, who led the study. “Most of the time, the prescription was automatically sent, without even an opportunity to stop the dispensing.”
The lack of a real-time conversation means many patients aren’t getting the type of care recommended by medical societies that prescribe GLP-1s, including discussions about weight-loss goals, past efforts and eating disorders.
Only a little more than half the websites had a question about eating disorders — which GLP-1 drugs can induce or worsen — on their intake questionnaires, the researchers found.
Your data may be shared with advertisers, social media companies and others
Americans often assume that any personal health information they share is protected by HIPAA, the federal privacy law that governs the handling of medical information. But the law generally only applies to specific types of health businesses, including medical offices, hospitals and insurers, not telehealth companies offering prescriptions, counseling, DNA tests and other online services.
Privacy experts say that legal gap is one reason companies continue to disclose sensitive health information to advertisers and search engines.
“There isn’t a clear federal law saying: ‘Don’t do this,’” said Justin Brookman, Consumer Reports’ director of technology policy. “There’s just a body of soft law and settled cases with the FTC that many companies probably aren’t even aware of.”
Because HIPAA does not cover every direct-to-consumer health platform, the FTC has generally used its broader authority to take action against “fraudulent, deceptive or unethical business methods.” In practice, that means showing that telehealth companies disclosed their customers’ health information after initially saying they wouldn’t.
Hims told customers that its platform offered a “100% online, private and secure” means of sharing information with the company’s medical professionals, according to the FTC complaint. But instead the company shared the data with Meta and other online platforms, the FTC alleges.
Still, experts say the penalties available to regulators are limited. In most cases, companies sign a legal agreement stating that they’ll stop the practices cited by regulators.
Lawmakers in California, Connecticut, Maryland and other states have passed new online privacy laws that include special protections for health information. But there’s been little enforcement against telehealth companies that break those rules.
Online privacy tools offer a bit of protection
For now, privacy experts recommend using ad blockers and private web browsers — sometimes called “incognito” windows — when logging onto telehealth websites. Those tools can make it harder for companies to track your location, online history and other personal information.
It’s also a good idea to read any user agreements to get a sense of how the company plans to use your personal data, said Crawford. Some telehealth sites, for example, explicitly state in their privacy policies that they have the right to sell data about users’ sex lives.
The only surefire way to protect your information may simply be to decline the terms of service, usually one of the first steps required before accessing telehealth.
“The system we have now overly burdens consumers to do a ton of work in terms of understanding how each piece of technology collecting their personal data is going to handle it,” he said. “But even if you do all that work, you often have little agency.”

Title: Ed Sheeran Concert Time Changed As Ticket Prices Plunge, Protests Planned
Article_Text:
Ed Sheeran’s Philadelphia concert will begin later than originally scheduled on Saturday, while organizers of planned pro-Palestinian protests outside the stadium say their demonstration will go ahead at its original time.
The concert at Lincoln Financial Field is now scheduled for 8 p.m., moved back from the previously advertised 5:30 p.m. start after the remaining opening acts withdrew from Sheeran’s U.S. Loop Tour.
Stadium parking lots are scheduled to open at 3 p.m. and doors at 6 p.m., according to event information reported by FOX 29 Philadelphia.
SEPTA said it would run additional Broad Street Line express trains and deploy transit police, station attendants and other personnel at NRG Station as the city prepares for both the rally and the concert.
Local station 6abc also reported that the show would proceed without support acts.
What Is The Ed Sheeran Controversy About?
Sheeran's tour lineup began unraveling after U.S. rapper Macklemore used an opening set at MetLife Stadium on September 4 to express support for Palestinians and lead the crowd in chants of “Free Palestine.”
The fallout widened after Macklemore was removed from the remaining U.S. dates. Every other support act then pulled out in solidarity with the rapper, leaving Sheeran without Finneas, Aaron Rowe, Lukas Graham or Beoga for their scheduled appearances.
Macklemore said Sheeran told him that Robert Kraft, the owner of Gillette Stadium, opposed his scheduled appearances and that other venue owners had taken a similar position.
Sheeran said forthcoming venues told the tour that their shows would not proceed with Macklemore on the bill, and that Messina Touring Group ultimately removed him under the promoter’s contract.
Sheeran said he tried to broker a solution but maintained that the final decision belonged to the promoter and venues rather than him.
He added: "I am appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine, I am not complicit. I have my personal views on this devastating conflict."
The departures left the Philadelphia concert without its advertised support bill. Nicole Tedesco of Pittston told 6abc she feels "disappointed" adding that she wanted the "whole experience."
Protests Planned
Pro-Palestinian protest group Shutdown DZ Philly has called supporters to gather outside the Lincoln Financial Field stadium at 4:30 p.m., three and a half hours before the revised concert time.
In an Instagram update, the organizers said they were aware of the change but “will not be changing the start time of our rally,” adding that their focus was drawing attention to Gaza.
Philadelphia police told 6abc that staffing would be adjusted amid the planned demonstration.
Some fans told the station that concerns surrounding the protest, the altered lineup and refunds had affected their plans to attend.
Caitlin Smith, of Hatboro, had planned to attend the concert with her husband. Both use power wheelchairs. However, despite Philadelphia police saying they would work to maintain safety, Smith has decided to stay home.
"The Ed Sheeran song 'Perfect' was our wedding song," Smith said. "My ultimate dream would have been for us both to meet him, but going to this concert was essentially the next best thing. Because of everything being so unsure, it kinda sucks."
"With us both being in chairs trying to get into the city, we don't want to take that risk," she added.
No blanket refund policy for the Philadelphia concert had been publicly announced by Ticketmaster, Lincoln Financial Field or the tour organizer by Saturday morning.
Smith told 6abc that she had been unable to secure a refund from StubHub, although the station reported that some customers had received refunds through Ticketmaster.
Ticketmaster said the event organizer, Messina Touring Group, controlled the refund policy.
Newsweek reached out to Messina Touring Group and the Lincoln Financial Field via a website contact form and email, respectively, for comment on Saturday morning and is awaiting a response.
Resale Tickets Plunge Further
Resale prices have fallen further. StubHub listings viewed Saturday showed tickets from $53 including fees, with TicketData showing resale prices at $56. Prices and availability can change rapidly.
That is below the $75 get-in price recorded at midday Friday, when prices for the Philadelphia show had already fallen 45 percent over the previous week.
Keith Pagello, founder of TicketData, cautioned that prices often soften as concerts approach, but said the Philadelphia decline was pushing beyond the tour’s typical pattern.
